subjects.name: Command Terms & Academic Language
subjects.subtitle: The words every VCE subject, SAC and exam uses — whatever you study

units.name: Command terms — the essential ones

words.meaning: Break something into its parts and show how the parts work together. In VCE: name the parts, then spend your marks on the LINKS between them — cause, effect, relationship. If your answer has no 'because' or 'which leads to', you have described, not analysed.
words.example: Analyse how the writer builds tension in the opening chapter.

words.meaning: Judge how good, useful or successful something is, and give reasons for your judgement. In VCE: give strengths AND limitations, then commit to a judgement ('overall, … because …'). Sitting on the fence loses the judgement mark — the verdict is what makes it evaluation.
words.example: Evaluate the effectiveness of the government's response to the crisis.

words.meaning: Give the main features of something in detail. You are not judging it. In VCE: features and characteristics only — no reasons, no judgement. Usually low-mark questions: be accurate and quick, and save the 'why' for explain questions.
words.example: Describe the structure of a plant cell.

words.meaning: Make something clear by giving reasons or showing how it works. In VCE: every explain answer needs a 'because' chain — state the point, give the reason, link it back to the question. Marks are usually one per link in the chain.
words.example: Explain why the price of housing rose in this period.

words.meaning: Look at more than one side of an idea before reaching a view. In VCE: present more than one side or factor with evidence, and show tension between them. One-sided answers cap out early; you usually finish with a considered position.
words.example: Discuss whether the law achieves justice for victims.

words.meaning: Show how two or more things are similar, and usually how they differ. In VCE: similarities AND differences, point by point — 'X does this, whereas Y does that'. Writing two separate paragraphs about X then Y is the classic way to lose these marks.
words.example: Compare the two experiments' results.

words.meaning: Show how two or more things are different from each other. In VCE: differences only, drawn sharply — 'whereas', 'while', 'unlike'. You still need both things in every sentence; describing only one is not contrasting.
words.example: Contrast life in the city with life in the country.

words.meaning: Give the main points only, without the detail. In VCE: the main points in order, briefly — a sketch, not an essay. Depth earns nothing here; coverage and sequence do.
words.example: Outline the three stages of the water cycle.

words.meaning: Name or point out exactly what something is. A short answer is enough. In VCE: name or point to it — often one word or phrase, worth one mark. Do not explain; a paragraph on a 1-mark identify question steals time from the 10-markers.
words.example: Identify two features of a persuasive text.

words.meaning: Give the exact meaning of a term — where its limits are. In VCE: give the precise meaning as your subject uses it — the study design's wording, not everyday English. In sciences and business, learned definitions are free marks.
words.example: Define 'opportunity cost'.

words.meaning: Show clearly how two things are different from each other. In VCE: state the difference between two things — the boundary line, not full descriptions of each. 'X is …, whereas Y is …' in one or two sentences usually earns full marks.
words.example: Distinguish between weather and climate.

words.meaning: Look closely at something and say what you find. In VCE: inspect closely and question as you go — how it works, why it matters, where it falls short. Sits between analyse and evaluate; evidence is expected.
words.example: Examine the causes of the Great Depression.

words.meaning: Decide how important, valuable or successful something is, and say why. In VCE: like evaluate — weigh importance, effectiveness or value against evidence and reach a judgement. Often paired with a criterion ('assess the impact on …'): judge against THAT, not in general.
words.example: Assess the impact of social media on teenagers' sleep.

words.meaning: Explain what something means, especially data, a source or a text. In VCE: say what the data, text or source MEANS, not what it shows. Translate the pattern into significance: 'the sharp rise suggests …'. Restating numbers is not interpreting.
words.example: Interpret the trend shown in the graph.

words.meaning: Give the main ideas briefly, in your own words. In VCE: the essential ideas only, in your own words, shorter than the original. No new information, no opinion — selection is the skill being marked.
words.example: Summarise the article in three sentences.

words.meaning: Give reasons that show your answer or choice is the right one. In VCE: defend a position with evidence and reasoning — why THIS choice and, often, why not the alternative. Every claim needs support; 'I think' without grounds earns nothing.
words.example: Justify your choice of method.

words.meaning: Show clearly that something is true, usually by using evidence or an example. In VCE: prove it by showing, with evidence or worked reasoning — 'demonstrate your understanding' means apply the concept to the case, not recite the definition.
words.example: Demonstrate how the formula is applied.

words.meaning: Make an idea clear by giving an example. (It does not mean 'draw a picture'.). In VCE: make the point concrete with an example, case or diagram. The example IS the answer — a general statement without one has not illustrated anything.
words.example: Illustrate your point with an example from the text.

units.name: Command terms — higher-order thinking

words.meaning: Put ideas from several sources together to make one new whole. In VCE: combine ideas from different sources or areas into one coherent whole — the mark is for the connections you build, not for retelling each source in turn.
words.example: Synthesise the findings of the three studies.

words.meaning: Judge the strengths and weaknesses of something carefully. In VCE: judge strengths and weaknesses against criteria, with evidence. It is not 'criticise' — a fair critique acknowledges what works before weighing what does not.
words.example: Critique the artist's use of colour.

words.meaning: Support a claim with evidence so it stands up. In VCE: back the claim with specific evidence — data, quotes, cases. 'Substantiate your answer' means: no evidence, no marks, however good the argument sounds.
words.example: Substantiate your argument with data from the table.

words.meaning: Use what you know to work out what happens beyond the data you have. In VCE: extend the pattern beyond the data you were given — and flag the assumption you are making. Common in graphs: continue the trend, and say why that is (or is not) reasonable.
words.example: Extrapolate the population trend to 2050.

words.meaning: Suggest an explanation that can be tested. In VCE: propose a testable explanation BEFORE the evidence is in — usually 'If X, then Y, because Z'. It is marked on logic and testability, not on being right.
words.example: Hypothesise why the plants in the dark grew taller.

words.meaning: Put an idea, plan or question into a clear, careful form. In VCE: build something precise from the material — an equation, a research question, a plan. The wording is the work: vague formulations lose the mark even when the idea is right.
words.example: Formulate a research question for your investigation.

words.meaning: Put forward an idea or plan for others to consider. In VCE: put forward a course of action or solution and give your reasons. Usually wants something specific and workable, tied to the scenario — not 'they should raise awareness'.
words.example: Propose a solution to the traffic problem.

words.meaning: Say what you think should be done, and why. In VCE: choose the best option and defend the choice — criteria, evidence, and often why the alternatives lose. A recommendation without a reason is just a preference.
words.example: Recommend a strategy for the business to increase sales.

words.meaning: Add more detail to an idea you have already given. In VCE: take the point further — more detail, an example, an implication. Repeating the same sentence in new words is the classic non-elaboration.
words.example: Elaborate on your second reason.

words.meaning: Judge the worth or quality of something. In VCE: weigh value or quality against evidence and land on a judgement — evaluate's formal twin, common in Business and HHD.
words.example: Appraise the reliability of this source.

words.meaning: Show what makes two things different. (In Maths Methods it also means 'find the derivative'.). In VCE: show precisely what separates two things that look similar — definitions, then the distinguishing feature. (In Maths it also means find the derivative — check which subject you are in.)
words.example: Differentiate between mass and weight.

words.meaning: Sort things into groups that share features. In VCE: sort items into groups AND name the principle you sorted by — the classification scheme is what earns the marks, not the sorting.
words.example: Categorise the responses as positive, negative or neutral.

words.meaning: Put things in order of importance, most important first. In VCE: rank by importance or urgency and justify the order — especially the top choice. An unranked list is not prioritising.
words.example: Prioritise the three risks for the committee.

words.meaning: Work out an answer by reasoning from what you already know. In VCE: reason from the general rule to the specific case — 'all X are Y; this is X; so …'. Show the steps: the working is the answer.
words.example: Deduce the missing angle from the information given.

words.meaning: Work out something that is not stated directly, using clues. In VCE: read what is implied but not stated, from evidence — 'the data suggests …'. Name the evidence you inferred FROM, or it reads as a guess.
words.example: Infer the character's feelings from her actions.

words.meaning: Check that something is sound, accurate or acceptable. In VCE: check soundness against evidence or criteria — in science, whether the method measures what it claims; in data, whether results hold. Say HOW you checked.
words.example: Validate your results by repeating the experiment.

units.name: Exam and SAC instructions

words.meaning: How much, or how far, is something true? Your answer must take a position, not just describe. In VCE: never fully yes or no. Argue a POSITION on the spectrum ('to a significant extent, because … however …') — the counter-evidence paragraph is what separates high answers.
words.example: To what extent did the reforms improve living standards?

words.meaning: You must use the named source, text or material in your answer. In VCE: you MUST use the named source, case or text explicitly — quote it, cite its data, name its parts. An answer that never touches the reference fails the question even if otherwise correct.
words.example: With reference to Source B, explain the artist's purpose.

words.meaning: Answer by connecting your point to the thing named. In VCE: answer only within the named context — 'in relation to the Australian economy' means every point tied to Australia. General answers score general marks.
words.example: Discuss the result in relation to your hypothesis.

words.meaning: In the same order as the things just listed. In VCE: 'in the order given' — 'A and B scored 7 and 9 respectively' means A=7, B=9. Misreading it reverses the data; read twice in maths and science questions.
words.example: Groups A and B scored 12 and 15 respectively.

words.meaning: Answer in a few words or one or two sentences — long answers waste time. In VCE: one or two sentences, low marks, no development. The skill is stopping — time saved here is spent on the extended-response questions.
words.example: Briefly outline the purpose of the study.

words.meaning: Add short notes or labels onto a diagram, text or image. In VCE: add short labels or notes ON the diagram, graph or text itself — arrows, phrases, not paragraphs. Marks are per useful label.
words.example: Annotate the diagram to show where energy is lost.

words.meaning: Close to the real value, but not exact. In VCE: a sensible estimate is wanted, not a precise value — show the rounding or reading you made ('≈ 40 from the graph'). Precision theatre wastes time.
words.example: Give an approximate value to two decimal places.

words.meaning: Do this only in the places where it suits — not everywhere. In VCE: a signal that judgement is being assessed — include the thing (units, examples, working) exactly where it belongs, not everywhere. It usually means marks are attached to it.
words.example: Use a diagram where appropriate.

words.meaning: The source material — text, image, data or scenario — a question is built on. In VCE: the provided material — graph, photo, quote, case — that your answer must engage with. Stimulus questions are 'with reference to' in disguise: use it or lose it.
words.example: Read the stimulus material before answering Question 3.

words.meaning: A short piece taken out of a longer text. In VCE: a passage taken from a longer text. Questions on an extract are marked from THAT passage — evidence from elsewhere in the text usually earns nothing unless asked for.
words.example: Read the extract from the novel on page 4.

words.meaning: A described situation you must respond to as if it were real. In VCE: an invented case you must apply your knowledge to. Marks come from linking theory to the scenario's details by name — generic theory answers cap at half.
words.example: In this scenario, you are the manager of a small business.

words.meaning: Show what something is like by giving an example of it. In VCE: give a specific example that shows the concept in action — real or from the studied material. One well-chosen example beats three vague ones.
words.example: Exemplify each technique with a quotation.

words.meaning: Say exactly which one, or exactly how much — be precise. In VCE: state it exactly — the value, the name, the condition. Ranges and hedges ('around', 'maybe') lose the mark when a specific answer is asked for.
words.example: Specify the units in your answer.

words.meaning: Make something easier to understand by explaining it more clearly. In VCE: make the meaning plain — simpler terms, sharper boundaries, an example if it helps. You are being marked on removing ambiguity, not adding information.
words.example: Clarify what you mean by 'fair'.

units.name: How VCE works — the system words

words.meaning: The official VCAA document that says exactly what a subject teaches and assesses.
words.example: Every question on the exam comes from the study design.

translations.ja: スタディデザイン（教科要綱）

words.meaning: The whole course of study — everything you are taught across the years.
words.example: Civics is part of the Victorian Curriculum in Years 7 to 10.

words.meaning: The facts and ideas you have learned. 'Key knowledge' lists what you must know for each outcome.
words.example: Each area of study lists its key knowledge and key skills.

words.meaning: What you must be able to do by the end of an area of study. You must pass every outcome.
words.example: There are two outcomes in Unit 3.

words.meaning: SAC — work assessed by your teacher at school that counts towards your final score.
words.example: The first School-assessed Coursework is in week 6.

translations.vi: bài tập đánh giá tại trường (SAC)

words.meaning: SAT — a large piece of work, usually a folio or product, assessed at school over a long period.
words.example: Visual Communication Design has a School-assessed Task, not just SACs.

translations.vi: nhiệm vụ đánh giá tại trường (SAT)

translations.ps: د ښوونځي لخوا ارزول شوی دنده (SAT)

words.meaning: GAT — a test all VCE students sit, used to check that scores are fair.
words.example: The General Achievement Test is held in the middle of the year.

translations.vi: Bài kiểm tra thành tích chung (GAT)

words.meaning: Adjusting subject scores so that the same score means the same standard in every subject.
words.example: Scaling means your study score can change slightly.

translations.ja: スケーリング（得点調整）

words.meaning: Proving that the work you handed in is really your own.
words.example: Keep your drafts — they are used for authentication.

words.meaning: Something you must have done before you are allowed to start a course.
words.example: Units 1 and 2 are not a prerequisite for Units 3 and 4.

words.meaning: Passing a unit by showing you achieved every outcome — an S, rather than an N.
words.example: You need satisfactory completion of 16 units to get your VCE.

words.meaning: Extra help or time in assessment for students with illness, disability or hardship.
words.example: She applied for special provision because of her injury.

units.name: Building a written argument

words.meaning: The main point a writer argues for — what they want you to accept.
words.example: The writer's contention is that phones should be banned in class.

words.meaning: The central argument of your essay, usually stated in the introduction.
words.example: Your thesis should answer the question directly.

words.meaning: An idea you accept as true and build your argument on.
words.example: The argument rests on the premise that all students have internet at home.

words.meaning: Facts, data or quotations that show your point is true.
words.example: Support each idea with evidence from the text.

words.meaning: An argument against your own — you raise it so you can answer it.
words.example: A strong essay deals with the counterargument.

words.meaning: A result or meaning that follows from something, without being said directly.
words.example: Discuss the implications of the new policy for small business.

words.meaning: As a result of what was just said.
words.example: Rainfall fell sharply; consequently, the crop failed.

words.meaning: Looking at it the opposite way round.
words.example: City rents rose. Conversely, country rents fell.

words.meaning: After that; later.
words.example: The law passed in 1975 and was subsequently amended twice.

words.meaning: Prove that an argument is wrong.
words.example: She refutes the claim with evidence from the census.

words.meaning: Admit that part of the other side's argument is fair, before answering it.
words.example: The writer concedes that the cost is high, but argues it is worth paying.

words.meaning: Making sense as a whole, with ideas that fit together logically.
words.example: A coherent essay answers one question from start to finish.

words.meaning: Held together by words and phrases that link sentence to sentence.
words.example: Linking words such as 'however' make writing cohesive.

translations.vi: liên kết chặt chẽ (về câu chữ)

words.meaning: Your answer to an argument against you.
words.example: The final paragraph is a rebuttal of the opposing view.

words.meaning: A block of sentences developing one idea.
words.example: Start a new paragraph for each new point.

words.meaning: Put two things side by side so the difference between them stands out.
words.example: The film juxtaposes the wedding with the funeral.

translations.vi: đặt cạnh nhau để đối chiếu
translations.fa: کنار هم قرار دادن برای مقایسه
translations.ur: موازنے کے لیے پہلو بہ پہلو رکھنا
translations.ps: د پرتلې لپاره تر څنګ ایښودل

units.name: Describing data, graphs and trends

words.meaning: The general direction data moves in over time.
words.example: The graph shows an upward trend in temperature.

words.meaning: A relationship where two things change together. It does not prove one causes the other.
words.example: There is a strong correlation between study hours and results.

words.meaning: A part compared with the whole, often written as a fraction or percentage.
words.example: A large proportion of the sample was under 20.

words.meaning: Big enough to matter. In statistics it means the result is unlikely to be chance.
words.example: The difference between the groups was significant.

words.meaning: Go up and down repeatedly, without a steady direction.
words.example: Prices fluctuated throughout the year.

words.meaning: A period where a value stops changing and stays level.
words.example: Growth rose quickly, then reached a plateau in 2019.

words.meaning: A fall or decrease over time.
words.example: There was a steady decline in newspaper sales.

words.meaning: Happening slowly, in small steps.
words.example: The graph shows a gradual increase, not a sudden jump.

words.meaning: How big something is — its size or scale.
words.example: An earthquake of magnitude 6.5 struck the region.

words.meaning: Something that can change, and that you measure or control in an experiment.
words.example: Temperature was the independent variable.

words.meaning: The middle value when all values are put in order.
words.example: The median house price was $780,000.

words.meaning: How values are spread out across a range.
words.example: The distribution of scores was close to normal.

words.meaning: Growth that gets faster and faster as the amount gets bigger.
words.example: The population showed exponential growth after 1950.

translations.vi: đường, có khả năng hoạt động

words.meaning: How far a value moves away from the average.
words.example: The standard deviation tells you how spread out the data is.

words.meaning: Build up in amount over time.
words.example: Sediment accumulates at the mouth of the river.

words.meaning: A value or result that does not fit the pattern.
words.example: The reading of 92 is an anomaly and should be checked.

units.name: Hedging — showing how certain you are

words.meaning: Something that usually happens, but not always.
words.example: There is a tendency for prices to rise before Christmas.

words.meaning: Show or point to something — weaker than 'prove'.
words.example: The results indicate a link between sleep and memory.

words.meaning: Point towards a conclusion without proving it. Very common in academic writing.
words.example: The evidence suggests that the trend will continue.

words.meaning: Probably true or probably going to happen.
words.example: Rain is likely in the afternoon.

parts.meaning: in a way that can be

words.meaning: A reasonable case can be made for this, though others may disagree.
words.example: This is arguably the poet's finest work.

translations.ja: おそらく（議論の余地はあるが）
translations.hi: तर्कसंगत रूप से कहा जा सकता है

words.meaning: Mainly; more than any other reason.
words.example: The decline was primarily caused by drought.

words.meaning: Possibly, in the future — it could happen but has not yet.
words.example: The change is potentially damaging to small businesses.

words.meaning: Easy to see; or seeming true but perhaps not really true.
words.example: It became apparent that the sample was too small.

parts.meaning: in a way that can be

words.meaning: Probably, judging by what we know — though it has not been checked.
words.example: The author, presumably writing in 1890, describes the city.

translations.ja: おそらく（推定されるに）

words.meaning: Large and important enough to matter.
words.example: There was a substantial increase in demand.

words.meaning: So small that it can be ignored.
words.example: The effect on the result was negligible.

words.meaning: Neither large nor small; in the middle.
words.example: The study found a moderate improvement in scores.

words.meaning: Mostly; the largest part.
words.example: The population is predominantly under 30.

parts.meaning: in a way that can be

words.meaning: It is possible to imagine this, though it is not likely.
words.example: The result could conceivably be explained by measurement error.

units.name: Sources, evidence and reliability

words.meaning: Name the source where an idea or quotation came from.
words.example: Cite the author and year for every quotation.

words.meaning: You can trust it — it gives the same result again and again.
words.example: A single blog post is not a reliable source.

words.meaning: Sound and well founded — it really measures or shows what it claims to.
words.example: The conclusion is valid only if the sample was random.

words.meaning: Not leaning towards one side.
words.example: Try to find an unbiased account of the event.

words.meaning: The point of view a person writes or speaks from.
words.example: The diary gives a soldier's perspective on the battle.

words.meaning: Evidence made at the time by someone who was there.
words.example: A letter written in 1915 is a primary source.

words.meaning: An account written later by someone who was not there.
words.example: Your textbook is a secondary source.

words.meaning: How far a source deserves to be believed.
words.example: The author's expertise adds to the credibility of the report.

words.meaning: Support a claim with a second, independent source that says the same.
words.example: Two other witnesses corroborate her account.

words.meaning: Using someone else's words or ideas as if they were your own. It is cheating.
words.example: Referencing your sources protects you from plagiarism.

words.meaning: Put someone else's idea into your own words. You still name the source.
words.example: Paraphrase the passage rather than quoting all of it.

translations.vi: diễn giải lại bằng lời riêng

words.meaning: Saying who an idea, quotation or image came from.
words.example: The image was used without attribution.

words.meaning: Check that something is true.
words.example: Verify the figure against the official statistics.

words.meaning: Based on facts, not on personal feelings.
words.example: A report should be objective.

words.meaning: Based on personal feelings or opinions.
words.example: 'Beautiful' is a subjective judgement.

units.name: High-frequency academic nouns

words.meaning: One of the things that causes or affects a result.
words.example: Cost was the main factor in the decision.

words.meaning: One part or side of something you are looking at.
words.example: Consider the economic aspect of the problem.

words.meaning: A general idea.
words.example: The concept of supply and demand is central to economics.

words.meaning: A standard you judge something against. Plural: criteria.
words.example: Cost was one criterion; safety was another.

words.meaning: A structure of ideas used to organise thinking about a topic.
words.example: Use the four-step framework to analyse the case.

words.meaning: A basic rule or truth that other ideas are built on.
words.example: The principle of equality before the law.

words.meaning: Something that happens and can be observed. Plural: phenomena.
words.example: El Niño is a weather phenomenon.

words.meaning: A testable prediction you make before an experiment. Plural: hypotheses.
words.example: State your hypothesis before collecting data.

translations.fr: une façon de faire quelque chose
translations.hi: किसी काम को करने का तरीका
translations.ro: un mod de a face ceva
translations.tl: paraan ng paggawa ng isang bagay
translations.ur: کسی کام کو کرنے کا طریقہ
translations.vi: cách làm một việc gì đó

words.meaning: The whole approach and set of methods used in a study, and why they were chosen.
words.example: The methodology section explains how the data was gathered.

words.meaning: How important something is, and why it matters.
words.example: Explain the significance of the 1967 referendum.

words.meaning: A conclusion you reach from clues rather than from a direct statement.
words.example: Make an inference about the writer's attitude.

words.meaning: The situation around something, which helps explain it.
words.example: Read the quotation in the context of the whole speech.

words.meaning: A limit on what you can do.
words.example: Time was the biggest constraint on the project.

words.meaning: A fixed limit or setting within which something works.
words.example: The task set clear parameters for the design.

translations.ja: パラメーター（変数条件）

words.meaning: The reasons behind a decision or design.
words.example: Explain the rationale for your choice of materials.

words.meaning: General agreement among a group.
words.example: There is scientific consensus that the climate is warming.

units.name: High-frequency academic verbs

words.meaning: Make up or form something.
words.example: Women constitute 51 per cent of the population.

words.meaning: Be made up of; consist of.
words.example: The parliament comprises two houses.

words.meaning: Get or come from a source.
words.example: The word derives from Latin.

words.meaning: Weaken something gradually.
words.example: The scandal undermined public trust in the company.

words.meaning: Make something easier to happen.
words.example: Good roads facilitate trade between regions.

words.meaning: Make something bad less severe.
words.example: Planting trees can mitigate the effects of heat.

words.meaning: Make a bad situation worse.
words.example: The drought exacerbated food shortages.

words.meaning: Make room for something, or change to fit someone's needs.

units.name: Unit 1 AoS 1 · The business idea

words.meaning: To come into view, or to start to exist and be noticed.
words.example: A business idea often emerges from a problem the owner keeps running into.

words.meaning: The most important parts, on which everything else is built.
words.example: Price, quality and service are the cornerstones of the shop's reputation.

words.meaning: One part of the economy, such as retail, mining or health.
words.example: A cafe belongs to the services sector, not the manufacturing sector.

words.meaning: The point at which something is finished.
words.example: The plan needs completion before the bank will look at the loan.

words.meaning: Using new ideas or new ways of doing things.
words.example: An innovative packaging design can make a small business stand out.

words.meaning: The personal reason someone starts a business, such as independence or money.
words.example: Her personal motivation was to be her own boss, not to get rich.

words.meaning: How possible and realistic an idea is in practice.
words.example: Test the feasibility of the idea before you sign a lease.

words.meaning: Money given by a local council to help a business or project start.
words.example: Small council grants can pay for a new sign or a food handling course.

translations.vi: trợ cấp của hội đồng địa phương

words.meaning: A plan for a product or service that someone thinks they can sell for a profit.
words.example: Their business idea was a coffee cart for the train station car park.

words.meaning: A gap in the market where a business could sell something people want.
words.example: A suburb with no bakery is a clear business opportunity.

words.meaning: Coming up with a new idea, product or way of doing something.
words.example: Innovation is what keeps a business ahead of its competitors.

words.meaning: The willingness to take a risk and start a business from your own idea.
words.example: Entrepreneurship means accepting that the idea may fail.

words.meaning: A person who takes the risk of starting and running a new business.
words.example: The entrepreneur used her savings to buy the first delivery van.

words.meaning: A person employed to run the day-to-day operations of a business someone else owns.
words.example: The owner sets the goals; the business manager runs the roster.

words.meaning: A chance to sell something because customers want it and no one supplies it well.
words.example: Long queues at the only gym in town point to a market opportunity.

words.meaning: The way what people want to buy shifts over time, creating new business ideas.
words.example: Changing customer needs turned a video shop into a games cafe.

translations.vi: nhu cầu khách hàng thay đổi

words.meaning: Testing and improving new products or processes before they go on sale.
words.example: Two years of research and development went into the recyclable bottle.

words.meaning: New tools, equipment or systems that make new products or ways of working possible.
words.example: Technological development lets a one-person business sell worldwide.

translations.vi: quả bóng, hình cầu, thế giới

words.meaning: Customers and competitors in other countries, not just at home.
words.example: An online store opens up the global market to a small Melbourne maker.

words.meaning: Wanting to be your own boss instead of working for someone else.
words.example: A desire for independence is a common reason people start a business.

words.meaning: Deciding clearly what a business wants to achieve, and by when.
words.example: Goal setting turns a vague hope into a target you can measure.

words.meaning: A target about money, such as a level of profit or sales.
words.example: Their financial goal was to break even in the first year.

words.meaning: A target about helping the community or the environment, not just making money.
words.example: Hiring local school leavers is a social goal, not a financial one.

words.meaning: A target that matters to the owner as an individual, such as flexible hours.
words.example: Being home by four each day was her personal goal.

words.meaning: The basic idea of what a business will sell and how it will make money.
words.example: Explain the business concept in two sentences before you write the plan.

words.meaning: Collecting information from possible customers to see if an idea will work.
words.example: Market research showed that parents wanted after-school sessions.

words.meaning: A check done before starting a business to see if the idea is realistic.
words.example: The feasibility study found the rent was too high for the expected sales.

words.meaning: The good effect a business has on jobs, spending and tax in the country.
words.example: Small businesses make a large contribution to the economy through jobs.

translations.vi: đóng góp cho nền kinh tế

words.meaning: How much a business improves people's quality of life, not just its own profit.
words.example: A community garden run by a cafe adds to social wellbeing.

words.meaning: The money government collects from businesses and individuals in tax.
words.example: Taxation revenue pays for the roads and schools the business relies on.

words.meaning: A workplace where people are encouraged to try new ideas.
words.example: A culture of innovation means staff can suggest changes without fear.

units.name: Unit 1 AoS 2 · The external environment (1)

words.meaning: Inside the business, such as its staff, managers and equipment.
words.example: Internal factors are the ones a business can control.

words.meaning: Everything that surrounds a business and affects how it operates.
words.example: The external environment includes laws, the economy and technology.

words.meaning: Deciding in advance what a business will do and how it will do it.
words.example: Careful planning is what separates a business from a hobby.

words.meaning: Achieving what was aimed for, such as profit, growth or a social goal.
words.example: A successful business meets its objectives without running out of cash.

words.meaning: The things a business actually does from day to day.
words.example: Ordering stock and serving customers are daily activities.

words.meaning: The main areas of work in a business, such as operations, finance and marketing.
words.example: Each of the four functions supports the others.

words.meaning: Forces that push a business to change what it is doing.
words.example: Rising rent and cheaper imports are two pressures on the shop.

words.meaning: Affected or changed by something else.
words.example: The price was influenced by what the competitor charged.

words.meaning: Outside the business, and largely beyond its control.
words.example: Interest rates are an external factor, not an internal one.

words.meaning: Choices a business makes between different courses of action.
words.example: Big decisions about location are hard to undo.

words.meaning: Final, or most important of all.
words.example: The ultimate objective of most businesses is to make a profit.

words.meaning: The specific results a business is aiming to achieve.
words.example: Write objectives that can be measured, not just hoped for.

words.meaning: The period of time set for something to be done.
words.example: Give every objective a timeframe, such as twelve months.

words.meaning: The way two people, groups or businesses deal with each other.
words.example: A good relationship with a supplier can get you better terms.

words.meaning: A working arrangement in which two or more people or groups share the work and the rewards.
words.example: The cafe formed a partnership with a local bakery to supply its bread.

words.meaning: A business that brings goods in from another country to sell here.
words.example: The importer pays more when the Australian dollar falls.

words.meaning: A business that sells goods to customers in other countries.
words.example: A weak dollar is good news for an exporter.

words.meaning: To do with money — how it comes in, goes out and is recorded.
words.example: The financial side of the plan shows every start-up cost.

words.meaning: To do with machines, equipment and computer systems.
words.example: Technological change can make a whole product line out of date.

words.meaning: A duty to deal with something, and to answer for how it is done.
words.example: Workplace safety is the employer's responsibility.

words.meaning: Breaking information into parts to work out what it means.
words.example: The analysis showed that sales dropped every winter.

words.meaning: To do with the natural world and a business's impact on it.
words.example: Environmental laws limit what the factory can pour into the drain.

words.meaning: Set up as a company that is legally separate from its owners.
words.example: Once incorporated, the business can own property in its own name.

words.meaning: Not legally separate from its owner, like a sole trader or a partnership.
words.example: An unincorporated business has no legal life apart from its owner.

translations.vi: không có tư cách pháp nhân

words.meaning: Setting a business up so that it can begin trading.
words.example: Establishing a business takes longer than most owners expect.

parts.meaning: to be of use or value

words.meaning: Whether something, such as staff or stock, can be got when it is needed.
words.example: The availability of trained baristas decides where the cafe opens.

words.meaning: Fitting together so that each adds to the other — not 'complimentary', which means free.
words.example: A florist and a card shop are complementary businesses.

words.meaning: To do with the make-up of a population, such as age, income or language.
words.example: The demographic around the new estate is young families.

translations.ro: a căuta / a se îndrepta spre

words.meaning: Other businesses selling a similar product to the same customers.
words.example: Two competitors opened in the same street within a month.

words.meaning: Being able to keep going over time without using up resources or people.
words.example: Sustainability means the business can still be operating in ten years.

words.meaning: Careful thought about something before deciding.
words.example: Location deserves serious consideration before any lease is signed.

units.name: Unit 2 AoS 1 · Legal and financial set-up (1): registering a business, tax and safety

words.meaning: acting in line with laws, regulations and rules that apply to a business.
words.example: Compliance is not optional: a fine for ignoring a rule costs far more than following it.

words.meaning: laws made by parliament that a business must follow.
words.example: Federal legislation sets the minimum wage; the business cannot pay under it.

words.meaning: officially recording a business name, structure or website domain with an authority.
words.example: Registration must be finished before the shop opens its doors.

words.meaning: a business's commitment to operate ethically and consider its impact on society and the environment.
words.example: Corporate social responsibility goes beyond the law: it is what the business chooses to do.

translations.vi: trách nhiệm xã hội của doanh nghiệp

words.meaning: a business or person that provides goods or materials to another business.
words.example: One late supplier can shut a whole production line down.

words.meaning: a formal guideline a business sets to guide decisions and actions consistently.
words.example: The refund policy tells every staff member the same thing to say.

words.meaning: the specific steps staff follow to carry out a policy or task.
words.example: The policy says report accidents; the procedure says which form to fill in.

words.meaning: systems a business uses to manage, monitor and protect its money.
words.example: Financial control is how a small business notices money going missing.

words.meaning: systematically storing a business's financial and legal documents.
words.example: The tax office expects record-keeping to go back five years.

words.meaning: in business: the unique web address a business registers for its website — not a general 'area'.
words.example: Register the domain early: someone else may want the same one.

words.meaning: A unique 11-digit number that identifies a business to the tax office and to other businesses.
words.example: You cannot send an invoice to another business without an ABN.

words.example: Only a company has an ACN; a sole trader has an ABN alone.

translations.ja: オーストラリア法人番号

words.meaning: Officially recording a business's trading name so no other business can use it.
words.example: Business name registration lasts one or three years, then has to be renewed.

words.meaning: The national body that registers companies and business names and enforces company law.
words.example: A new company must lodge its details with ASIC before it can trade.
