units.name: This All Come Back Now · Genesis: comparing creation stories

words.meaning: An old word for the sky, imagined as a solid dome holding back water.
words.example: Compare the firmament of Genesis with the sky in a Dreaming account.

words.meaning: Total ruling power over something or someone.
words.example: Genesis grants humans dominion over animals; Country asks for care instead.

words.meaning: An old word for birds, especially birds kept or hunted for food.
words.example: The older translation says fowl where a modern one would say birds.

words.meaning: An old form of the verb 'creeps', used of small crawling creatures.
words.example: Creepeth sounds strange because the -eth ending left English centuries ago.

words.meaning: To conquer something or bring it under your control.
words.example: Being told to subdue the earth is a very different relationship from belonging to it.

words.meaning: To fill something up again.
words.example: The command to replenish the earth reads oddly beside stories of caring for Country.

words.meaning: When one text deliberately echoes or answers another.
words.example: Setting Genesis beside a creation story builds an intertextuality the unit wants you to notice.

units.name: This All Come Back Now · Myth This

words.meaning: A traditional story a culture treats as carrying deep truth, not a lie.
words.example: In Literature, calling something a myth is not calling it false.

words.meaning: To show that a popular belief is false.
words.example: The story debunks the outsider's tidy picture of Aboriginal culture.

words.meaning: A belief in luck or magic not based on evidence, often used to dismiss other people's beliefs.
words.example: Outsiders in the story call knowledge superstition because they do not hold it.

translations.es: costumbres transmitidas de generación en generación
translations.ro: obiceiuri transmise din generație în generație
translations.ru: обычаи, передаваемые из поколения в поколение
translations.tl: mga kaugaliang ipinasa sa mga henerasyon
translations.vi: phong tục truyền qua các thế hệ

words.meaning: Stories and knowledge passed on by speech across generations rather than in writing.
words.example: An oral tradition is not a rough draft of a written one.

translations.ja: 盛り合わせの皿（雑多な作）

words.meaning: Writing that mocks a person, belief or institution in order to criticise it.
words.example: The satire here is aimed at the visitors, not at the culture they misread.

units.name: This All Come Back Now · Clatter Tongue

words.meaning: A formal legal inquiry into how someone died.
words.example: The inquest closes the file without explaining the death.

words.meaning: An image or idea that repeats through a text and builds meaning.
words.example: Moths return often enough in this story to count as a motif.

words.meaning: An expression or image used so often that it has lost its force.
words.example: The writer takes a cliché about butterflies and turns it into something darker.

words.meaning: When the truth of a situation is the opposite of what is said or expected.
words.example: There is bitter irony in accusing her of theft over an object that was itself taken.

words.meaning: A collection of weapons, or the place where they are kept.
words.example: Old weapons fall out of the character like an armoury nobody admitted was there.

words.meaning: A settlement where Aboriginal people were forcibly moved and controlled by churches or governments.
words.example: The mission is a setting that carries its own history before anything happens in it.

words.meaning: To stand for something beyond the literal thing itself.
words.example: The objects spilling from her mouth symbolise a history nobody will say aloud.

units.name: This All Come Back Now · The Centre

words.meaning: A traditional Aboriginal carrying vessel, used for food, water or a baby.
words.example: Calling the site a digital coolamon says that it carries and protects culture.

words.meaning: Informal Aboriginal English for a non-Indigenous person.
words.example: The narrator's tone shifts whenever a gub enters the online space.

words.meaning: The online test that asks you to prove you are not a robot.
words.example: The story turns a captcha into a test of cultural belonging.

words.meaning: A spatial metaphor: being pushed to the edges of society while claiming a strong centre of your own.
words.example: Trace the fringes/the centre metaphor from the story's first page.

words.meaning: Taking back a word, space or identity that was taken away, and making it a source of pride.
words.example: Reclamation is why the spelling Blak matters to these writers.

words.meaning: A newly invented word or phrase, often made by blending existing ones.
words.example: Blak captcha is a neologism built from two very different worlds.

units.name: This All Come Back Now · Nimeybirra and Cloud Busting

words.meaning: A story told out of time order, jumping between moments instead of running start to finish.
words.example: A non-linear structure can make memory feel closer than chronology.

words.meaning: Breaking a story into disconnected pieces, which can mirror broken memory or history.
words.example: The fragmentation is doing work here, not just making the story hard.

words.meaning: The order and shape in which a story's events are arranged for the reader.
words.example: Map the narrative structure before you argue about its effect.

words.meaning: A long period with far too little rain for the land to keep going.
words.example: Drought sits behind almost every image of the sky in this story.

words.meaning: A piece of writing that mourns a loss.
words.example: Read the closing pages as an elegy for a place as much as for a person.

words.meaning: The ability to keep going and recover after hardship.
words.example: Resilience here refuses to let the story be only about damage.

words.meaning: Giving weather or landscape human feelings, such as clouds that seem to withhold rain.
words.example: Clouds that refuse to break are pathetic fallacy doing the story's emotional work.

units.name: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof · Act One

words.meaning: Lying, or a whole system of lies that a family lives inside.
words.example: Brick returns to the word mendacity whenever the family performs happiness.

words.meaning: Strong dislike or revulsion at something you find offensive.
words.example: Brick's disgust is aimed at himself as much as at anyone else.

words.meaning: Saying one thing and doing another, or pretending to a virtue you do not have.
words.example: The birthday party is built on hypocrisy that everyone can see.

words.meaning: Being part of something wrong by staying silent or going along with it.
words.example: Staying silent about the diagnosis is its own kind of complicity.

words.meaning: Refusing to accept a painful truth.
words.example: Denial keeps the whole household comfortable and dishonest.

words.meaning: The powerful male head of a family.
words.example: Big Daddy is the patriarch whose land everyone is quietly counting.

words.meaning: Greedily wanting something that belongs to someone else.
words.example: Gooper and Mae are openly covetous of the estate.

words.meaning: Not moving or changing; on stage, a scene that stays fixed in one place and time.
words.example: One bedroom and continuous time make the play feel static and airless.

words.meaning: A false, respectable front put up to hide an unpleasant truth.
words.example: The birthday celebration is a façade stretched over illness and resentment.

units.name: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof · Act Two

words.meaning: A whole system of lies; in Act Two it becomes Big Daddy's own verdict on his household.
words.example: In the long confrontation, mendacity turns into Big Daddy's word too.

words.meaning: A gentler word used to avoid naming something uncomfortable directly.
words.example: A polite euphemism keeps the word cancer out of the room.

words.meaning: A direct, tense clash between characters.
words.example: The confrontation forces Brick to say what he has been drinking to avoid.

words.meaning: When the audience knows something a character on stage does not.
words.example: We learn that Big Daddy is dying before he does, which is dramatic irony.

words.meaning: Pushing down feelings or desires instead of expressing them.
words.example: Repression, not honesty, is what holds this family together.

units.name: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof · Act Three

words.meaning: An uneasy coming back together after conflict.
words.example: Williams leaves the reconciliation unfinished on purpose.

words.meaning: The way things already are, before any change.
words.example: Argue whether the ending disturbs the status quo or restores it.

words.meaning: What a person leaves behind: property, reputation and unfinished relationships.
words.example: The plantation is only the visible part of Big Daddy's legacy.

words.meaning: Deliberate uncertainty of meaning that a text refuses to resolve.
words.example: The ambiguity of the final exchange is the point, not a flaw.

words.meaning: The powerful female head of a family.
words.example: As Big Daddy weakens, Big Mama and Maggie both reach for the matriarch's place.

units.name: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof · Dramaturgy and staging

words.meaning: The playwright's written instructions about movement, tone and set, which are not spoken aloud.
words.example: Williams's stage directions read almost like prose fiction.

words.meaning: A short remark a character makes that the others on stage are assumed not to hear.
words.example: An aside lets the audience in on something the room does not know.

words.meaning: A long, uninterrupted speech by one character.
words.example: Big Daddy's longest monologue runs almost without interruption.

words.meaning: A speech in which a character alone on stage says their inner thoughts aloud.
words.example: A soliloquy tells the audience what a character will not admit to anyone else.

words.meaning: Objects handled on stage, which often carry meaning beyond their practical use.
words.example: Brick's crutch and the liquor cabinet are props doing symbolic work.

words.meaning: The built stage environment, such as furniture and walls, that shows where characters live.
words.example: The whole play happens on one set, which traps the family in a single room.

words.meaning: The techniques a writer uses to build a character: speech, action, appearance and other people's reactions.
words.example: Maggie's characterisation depends as much on what she repeats as on what she says.

words.meaning: Everything visible on stage at once: set, lighting, costume and where the actors stand.
words.example: Read the mise-en-scène of the opening as carefully as the dialogue.

words.meaning: The emotional attitude a scene or line carries, and the way it shifts.
words.example: Track how the tone turns from teasing to threatening across Act Two.

units.name: Frankenstein · Letters 1–4: Walton's frame narrative

words.meaning: Full of burning enthusiasm for something.
words.example: Walton is ardent about reaching a place no one has seen.

words.meaning: A person's face, or the expression it holds.
words.example: Walton reads exhaustion in the stranger's countenance before he hears a word.

words.meaning: Fearless; not put off by danger.
words.example: Walton calls his crew dauntless, and the ice soon tests that.

words.meaning: Extremely distressing to go through or to watch.
words.example: The story Walton is about to record is a harrowing one.

words.meaning: In a way that cannot be undone.
words.example: Victor believes one choice changed his life irrevocably.

translations.ja: 取り返しのつかないほど

words.meaning: A sailor, especially one navigating a ship.
words.example: The lonely mariner of Coleridge's poem stands behind Walton's letters.

words.meaning: Steady determination to keep going despite difficulty.
words.example: Walton treats perseverance as a virtue; the novel is less sure.

words.meaning: A novel told through letters.
words.example: Frankenstein opens as an epistolary novel written home from the Arctic.

words.meaning: A story told inside another story.
words.example: Victor's account sits inside Walton's letters, so the letters are the frame narrative.

words.meaning: A reference to another work, person or event that adds meaning for readers who catch it.
words.example: The allusion to Coleridge's ancient mariner colours Walton's whole voyage.

units.name: Frankenstein · Chapters 1–10: ambition and the creation

words.meaning: Kind and generous in spirit.
words.example: Victor insists that his intentions were benevolent from the start.

words.meaning: To share in someone's sadness and say so.
words.example: Clerval arrives to commiserate with Victor after the illness.

words.meaning: Something that eases grief or disappointment.
words.example: There is no consolation for the family after Justine's trial.

translations.ja: ふるい分ける／識別する

words.meaning: To notice or work out something that is not obvious.
words.example: Readers discern Victor's guilt long before he names it.

words.meaning: An evil spirit or devil.
words.example: Victor calls his creation a fiend rather than a son.

words.meaning: Extremely ugly, in a way that causes horror.
words.example: Victor's word for the creature is hideous, before it has done anything.

words.meaning: A sign believed to predict good or bad luck to come.
words.example: The storm over the mountains reads as an omen the first time we meet it.

words.meaning: An old forerunner of chemistry that hunted for gold and for eternal life.
words.example: Victor's boyhood reading in alchemy shapes what he later wants from science.

words.meaning: Like Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire for humans and was punished for it.
words.example: The novel's subtitle makes Victor's ambition Promethean and doomed.

words.meaning: Dangerous overconfidence, especially in defying natural limits.
words.example: Hubris, not curiosity, is what the novel finally punishes.

words.meaning: The early-1800s idea that electricity could bring dead tissue back to life.
words.example: Galvanism was real scientific news while Shelley was writing.

words.meaning: A round character is complex and many-sided; a flat character stays simple and one-note.
words.example: Decide whether the creature is a round character or a walking argument.

translations.ja: 立体的人物と平板な人物
translations.vi: nhân vật đa diện và nhân vật phẳng

units.name: Frankenstein · Chapters 11–16: the creature's own narrative

words.meaning: A guess based on very little evidence.
words.example: The creature's first ideas about people are conjecture built from a gap in a wall.

words.meaning: Too unhappy to be comforted.
words.example: The creature is disconsolate after the cottagers drive him out.

words.meaning: Mysterious and hard to interpret.
words.example: The creature stays enigmatic even while he is explaining himself.

words.meaning: Shockingly obvious and offensive, with no attempt to hide it.
words.example: The rejection is a flagrant injustice in the creature's telling.

words.meaning: Deeply and often sadly thoughtful.
words.example: He grows pensive once he understands what he is.

words.meaning: Deserving deep respect, usually because of age or wisdom.
words.example: The blind cottager is the venerable figure the creature dares to approach.

words.meaning: Punishment you inflict in return for a wrong done to you.
words.example: Vengeance replaces companionship once the creature gives up hope.

words.meaning: Deliberately and with no care for the consequences.
words.example: He accuses Victor of abandoning him wantonly.

words.meaning: The creature's comparison of himself to both Adam and Satan from Milton's poem.
words.example: The Paradise Lost allusion lets him be innocent and monstrous at once.

translations.vi: ám chỉ Thiên đường đã mất

words.meaning: Someone who teaches themselves, without any formal schooling.
words.example: The creature is an autodidact who learns language by watching in secret.

units.name: Frankenstein · Chapters 17–21: the broken promise

words.meaning: Mean-spirited or morally low, in the older sense the novel uses.
words.example: Victor calls his own motives base when he destroys the second creature.

words.meaning: Impossible to stop or to talk out of something.
words.example: The creature's plan is inexorable once the promise is broken.

words.meaning: So great that it cannot be overcome, whatever you try.
words.example: Victor treats every obstacle as insurmountable except the one he made himself.

words.meaning: Annoying and tiring in a small, wearing way.
words.example: He finds ordinary company irksome after months of secrecy.

words.meaning: Having no energy or interest in anything.
words.example: Victor turns listless whenever the pursuit pauses.

words.meaning: Deliberately meaning to cause harm.
words.example: Whether the creature is malicious or was made malicious is the novel's hardest question.

words.meaning: A state of heavy, sluggish inactivity, close to sleep.
words.example: Grief drops him into a torpor that lasts for weeks.

words.meaning: To travel right across an area.
words.example: The chase makes both of them traverse half of Europe.

words.meaning: Hints planted early in a text about what is coming.
words.example: The threat about the wedding night is unmistakable foreshadowing.

words.meaning: The tense feeling of not knowing what will happen next.
words.example: Shelley builds suspense by telling us the date but not the victim.

units.name: Frankenstein · Chapters 22–24: the pursuit and Walton's return

words.meaning: An enemy or opponent, especially one you are set against for a long time.
words.example: By the end each man has made the other his only adversary.

words.meaning: A feeling of anxious confusion and dismay at bad news.
words.example: Walton's crew hear the story with consternation rather than admiration.

words.meaning: Very distinguished or famous, in a good way.
words.example: Victor still dreams of an illustrious name while he is dying.

words.meaning: Having unlimited power; able to do anything at all.
words.example: Victor wanted to be omnipotent over life and could not care for one creature.

words.meaning: A long journey made for a spiritual or deeply important purpose.
words.example: The hunt across the ice becomes Victor's grim pilgrimage.

words.meaning: A double or look-alike, often standing for a hidden side of a person.
words.example: Critics read the creature as Victor's doppelgänger rather than his opposite.

words.meaning: Punishment given in return for wrongdoing.
words.example: The creature calls the deaths retribution; Victor calls them murder.

words.meaning: Overwhelming natural vastness, such as mountains or ice, that inspires awe and terror at once.
words.example: The Alps give Victor the sublime, and no peace with it.

units.name: Look Who's Morphing · Reading the whole collection

words.meaning: The way one text is built out of references to other texts.
words.example: Cho makes his stories out of films and songs, so intertextuality is everywhere.

words.meaning: A reference to another text, person or event that the writer expects you to recognise.
words.example: Each story title is an allusion to a film the reader is meant to know.

words.meaning: Films, television, music and other entertainment that almost everybody knows.
words.example: The collection pulls its characters straight out of 1980s pop culture.

words.meaning: A style in which impossible or illogical events are told as if they were normal.
words.example: A boy becomes a giant monster and nobody blinks: that is absurdism.

words.meaning: A complete change of form or identity.
words.example: The title promises a metamorphosis, and every story delivers one.

parts.meaning: mixed offspring of two different types

words.meaning: Being a mix of two cultures, identities or forms instead of one fixed thing.
words.example: Hybridity means the narrator belongs to both worlds and to neither.

words.meaning: The quality of being able to change and flow rather than staying fixed.
words.example: Gender fluidity lets the narrator be someone different in every story.

words.meaning: An exaggerated imitation of a work or style, written to make fun of it.
words.example: The story is a parody of the musical, not a tribute to it.

words.meaning: Stories written by fans that borrow characters or worlds from an existing work.
words.example: These stories read like fan fiction that has turned strange and personal.

words.meaning: A narrator who tells the story as 'I', so we see everything through one character.
words.example: The first-person narrator blurs the line between the author and the character.

translations.vi: người kể chuyện ngôi thứ nhất

units.name: Look Who's Morphing · Dirty Dancing & The Sound of Music

words.meaning: A warm, sad longing for the past or for a place you cannot go back to.
words.example: The story runs on nostalgia for a film the narrator loved as a child.

words.meaning: A story about growing from childhood into adult understanding.
words.example: One summer changes everything, which gives the story its coming-of-age shape.

words.meaning: A work that imitates another artist's style, usually with affection rather than mockery.
words.example: The story is a pastiche of the film: same moves, same music, new meaning.

words.meaning: Changing to fit into the main culture around you, sometimes losing your own.
words.example: Assimilation comes easier to the children than to their parents.

words.meaning: A community living far away from the homeland its families came from.
words.example: The family kitchen is a small piece of the Chinese diaspora in suburban Australia.

words.meaning: Innocent, clean and morally safe, like an old family film.
words.example: Cho borrows the wholesome mood of the musical and then quietly breaks it.

units.name: Look Who's Morphing · The Exorcist & Today, On Dr Phil...

words.meaning: Being taken over and controlled by an outside force or spirit.
words.example: In horror films possession is literal; here it is what family pressure feels like.

words.meaning: A type of story built to frighten and unsettle its audience.
words.example: The horror genre supplies the demon, the bedroom and the terrified family.

words.meaning: A deliberately exaggerated, theatrical style that is funny and unsettling at once.
words.example: The costumes and the over-acting push the scene into pure camp.

translations.zh-Hans: 展示 / 展示 / 展示 zin2 si6
translations.zh-Hant: 展示 / 展示 / 展示 zin2 si6

words.meaning: A television format where a host questions guests about their private problems.
words.example: The talk show turns private shame into entertainment for a studio audience.

words.meaning: Revealing private, often shameful feelings, as if admitting them to someone.
words.example: The confessional tone invites us to judge the speaker as much as pity him.

words.meaning: Something staged to be watched, made big and dramatic for an audience.
words.example: Suffering becomes a spectacle once the cameras are pointed at it.

units.name: Look Who's Morphing · Cock Rock Country & Suitmation

words.meaning: The behaviour and qualities a culture expects from men.
words.example: The rock star persona tests masculinity by exaggerating it.

words.meaning: Loud, aggressive pride in being male.
words.example: All that machismo collapses the moment the narrator changes shape.

words.meaning: Mixing the rules of two different genres so that neither one holds.
words.example: The genre-bending mix of rock and country makes the singer impossible to place.

words.meaning: The Japanese genre of giant-monster films, performed by actors inside monster suits.
words.example: Kaiju films are why the narrator can imagine himself stepping over a city.

words.meaning: Something clever and made rather than natural: costume, trick or performance.
words.example: The zip up the back of the monster suit is artifice you are meant to notice.

words.meaning: A complete change of shape, form or identity.
words.example: The transformation into a monster is played for comedy and for fear at once.

units.name: Look Who's Morphing · Aiyo! & I, Robot

words.meaning: A short exclamation thrown into speech to show sudden feeling.
words.example: The title is an interjection: a word you say before you have time to think.

words.meaning: Moving between two languages or ways of speaking, often to signal who you are.
words.example: Code-switching at the dinner table marks the line between home and school.

words.meaning: A scattered community that keeps the words and habits of a homeland it left.
words.example: One shouted word carries a whole diaspora into an English sentence.

words.meaning: A robot built to look and behave like a human.
words.example: An android narrator lets the story ask what counts as a real person.

words.meaning: Stories that imagine future technology, robots or other possible worlds.
words.example: Borrowing a famous science fiction title warns you that robots are coming.

words.meaning: Treating a person as less than human, or a machine becoming more human.
words.example: Dehumanisation cuts both ways: the machine grows a self while the people lose theirs.

units.name: Introduction to Poetry — Billy Collins

words.meaning: Poetry that is itself about reading or writing poetry.
words.example: A poem that gives advice about poems is metapoetry.

words.meaning: One comparison stretched across many lines or a whole poem.
words.example: The extended metaphor holds a single image steady from the first line to the last.

words.meaning: Meant to teach a lesson or give instruction.
words.example: The poem is gently didactic: it shows students how not to read a poem.

words.meaning: Insisting that a text has one strict meaning and nothing more.
words.example: Literalism hunts for the one right answer and misses the poem.

units.name: Red Brocade — Naomi Shihab Nye

words.meaning: The generous, welcoming treatment of guests and strangers.
words.example: In this poem hospitality comes first: food and rest before any questions.

words.meaning: A traditional practice that belongs to one particular culture.
words.example: Feeding a stranger for days before asking their name is a cultural custom.

words.meaning: The form of a verb that gives an order or an instruction.
words.example: The imperative mood makes the poem sound like an invitation you cannot refuse.

words.meaning: Protective covering worn in battle; in the poem, the busyness people hide behind.
words.example: Being too busy to sit down is a kind of armour.

units.name: No Explosions — Naomi Shihab Nye

words.meaning: Placing two very different ideas or images side by side for effect.
words.example: The juxtaposition of fireworks and real bombs makes the celebration uneasy.

words.meaning: Saying one thing while meaning something different, often the opposite.
words.example: The irony of the title is that the poem is full of explosions.

words.meaning: Shortness: saying a great deal in very few words.
words.example: The poem's brevity does work that a long argument could not.

units.name: show me a girl at five — Maxine Beneba Clarke

words.meaning: Repeating the same words at the start of several lines in a row.
words.example: The anaphora at the head of each line builds like a drumbeat.

words.meaning: Writing that examines and challenges unfair treatment of women and girls.
words.example: The poem is a feminist critique of what girls are taught to want.

words.meaning: The way a society teaches people the roles and behaviour it expects of them.
words.example: Socialisation starts early: the poem follows a girl from the age of five.

units.name: The Last Apology — Ellen van Neerven

words.meaning: Words that say sorry for a wrong; here, the 2008 National Apology to the Stolen Generations.
words.example: The poem asks what an apology is worth if nothing else changes.

words.meaning: The process of repairing a relationship, here between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australia.
words.example: Reconciliation in this poem is unfinished, and the speaker knows it.

words.meaning: Action taken to put right a past wrong, such as compensation or repair.
words.example: An apology without redress leaves the harm exactly where it was.

words.meaning: Having two opposite feelings about the same thing at the same time.
words.example: The speaker's ambivalence keeps the poem from ending in easy gratitude.

units.name: My Last Duchess — Robert Browning

words.meaning: A poem spoken by one character to a silent listener, revealing more than the speaker means to.
words.example: The whole dramatic monologue is one man showing a visitor a portrait.

words.meaning: The invented character who speaks a poem, who is not the poet.
words.example: The persona is a duke; the poet stands quietly behind him.

words.meaning: When the reader understands more than the speaker or character does.
words.example: Dramatic irony lets us hear the threat the Duke thinks he is hiding.

words.meaning: A need to own and control another person.
words.example: His possessiveness treats a wife as one more object in the gallery.

words.meaning: The turn in a poem where the argument, tone or direction changes.
words.example: Mark the volta in the margin where the speaker's tone shifts.

units.name: Sonnet 18 — William Shakespeare

words.meaning: A fourteen-line poem with a set rhyme scheme, traditionally about love.
words.example: A sonnet has fourteen lines and no room to waste.

words.meaning: A line of five beats, each one a soft syllable followed by a stressed one.
words.example: Tap the desk five times a line and you can hear the iambic pentameter.

words.meaning: The turn partway through a sonnet where the argument changes direction.
words.example: After the volta the poem stops comparing and starts promising.

words.meaning: Two lines side by side that rhyme, often used to close a sonnet.
words.example: The final rhyming couplet snaps the whole argument shut in two lines.

words.meaning: Deliberate exaggeration that is not meant to be believed literally.
words.example: Promising that a poem will outlast stone is glorious hyperbole.

units.name: Still I Rise — Maya Angelou

words.meaning: Repeating the same opening words line after line to build force.
words.example: The anaphora returns like a wave that will not stop.

words.meaning: A line or phrase that comes back at intervals through a poem.
words.example: The refrain lifts the poem a little higher each time it returns.

words.meaning: The strength to recover and keep going after hardship.
words.example: Resilience here is not quiet: it is loud and public.

words.meaning: A bold refusal to obey or to be put down.
words.example: Every stanza answers an insult with defiance.

words.meaning: A single image developed across the whole poem to carry its meaning.
words.example: The extended metaphor of tides and oceans turns rising water into rising people.

units.name: Jabberwocky — Lewis Carroll

words.meaning: Poetry built from invented words, carried by rhythm and sound instead of meaning.
words.example: Nonsense verse still obeys grammar, which is why you almost understand it.

words.meaning: A newly invented word.
words.example: Some of Carroll's neologisms were so useful that dictionaries kept them.

words.meaning: A word made by packing two words into one, the way brunch packs breakfast and lunch.
words.example: A portmanteau word folds two meanings into a single sound.

words.meaning: A word that imitates the sound it describes, like buzz or crash.
words.example: The battle is mostly onomatopoeia: you hear it more than you see it.

words.meaning: A story poem in short verses with a simple rhyme scheme.
words.example: The ballad form promises a hero and a monster, and the poem delivers both.

units.name: If— — Rudyard Kipling

words.meaning: Written to teach a lesson or hand on advice.
words.example: The whole poem is didactic: a father listing rules for a son.

words.meaning: The verb form used for commands and instructions.
words.example: The imperative mood turns fatherly advice into orders.

words.meaning: The repetition of the same words at the start of line after line.
words.example: Anaphora stacks condition on condition until the last line pays them off.

words.meaning: Enduring hardship calmly, without complaining.
words.example: The poem's stoicism asks you to treat success and failure the same way.

words.meaning: A statement that seems to contradict itself but points to a truth.
words.example: Treating triumph and disaster as one thing is the poem's central paradox.

units.name: The Road Not Taken — Robert Frost

words.meaning: A comparison that says one thing is another, without using like or as.
words.example: The fork in the road is a metaphor for a choice that cannot be undone.

words.meaning: Deliberate uncertainty: a text that can honestly be read two ways.
words.example: The ambiguity is the point, and readers still argue about the last line.

words.meaning: Using an object or image to stand for a much larger idea.
words.example: The symbolism is simple: two roads, one life, no going back.

words.meaning: Looking back on something that has already happened.
words.example: The poem is framed as retrospection: the choice is told from years later.

units.name: Preludes — T. S. Eliot

words.meaning: A style built on sharp, exact images instead of explanation or emotion words.
words.example: Imagism gives us the smell of the street and lets us do the rest.

words.meaning: Breaking a text into disconnected parts, so the world it shows feels broken too.
words.example: The fragmentation into four short sections matches a city that never joins up.

words.meaning: A city falling into dirt and ruin, and the images a poet builds from it.
words.example: Urban decay fills the poem: smoke, grit and burnt-out days.

words.meaning: An early twentieth-century movement that broke old forms to show a broken modern world.
words.example: Modernism is why the poem hands you scraps of a city instead of a story.

words.meaning: Dirty, shabby and morally low.
words.example: The sordid details are chosen on purpose: stale smells, damp streets, tired feet.

units.name: Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night — Dylan Thomas

words.meaning: A nineteen-line poem with two repeating lines and a strict rhyme scheme.
words.example: A villanelle circles back on itself, which suits a poem about refusing to stop.

words.meaning: A repeated line that returns at fixed points and holds a poem together.
words.example: Two refrains take turns closing the stanzas until the last verse uses both.

words.meaning: The verb form that gives a command.
words.example: The poem is almost all imperative mood: do this, refuse that.

words.meaning: One image carried through a whole poem; here light stands for life and dark for death.
words.example: The extended metaphor of light and dark runs to the final line.

words.meaning: Refusing to give in quietly.
words.example: The poem answers death with defiance rather than comfort.

units.name: We Are Going — Oodgeroo Noonuccal

words.meaning: The repetition of the same opening words in line after line.
words.example: The anaphora lists everything being taken, one line at a time.

words.meaning: A poem that mourns a loss.
words.example: The poem is an elegy for a people's land, ceremony and story.

words.meaning: Having your land or belongings taken away from you.
words.example: Dispossession is not only losing land; it is losing the ceremonies held on it.

words.meaning: A traditional Aboriginal gathering with dance, song and ceremony.
words.example: The poem remembers the corroboree that the new town has covered over.

translations.ja: アボリジニの歌舞儀式
translations.vi: lễ hội ca múa thổ dân

words.meaning: A sacred circle of ground used for ceremony and initiation.
words.example: The bora ring in the poem now lies under a rubbish tip.

words.meaning: An expression of deep grief; a poem or song of mourning.
words.example: The tone is a lament, steady and quiet rather than angry.

units.name: Lady Lazarus — Sylvia Plath

words.meaning: Poetry that draws openly and intensely on the poet's own private life and pain.
words.example: Confessional poetry made private suffering a public subject.

words.meaning: One comparison developed across a poem; here dying is performed like a stage trick.
words.example: The extended metaphor turns survival into a magic act with an audience.

words.meaning: An image of rising from the dead that keeps returning through a poem.
words.example: The resurrection motif appears every time the speaker comes back.

words.meaning: Comedy used to talk about painful or frightening things.
words.example: The dark humour makes you laugh and then feel uneasy about laughing.

words.meaning: A reference to a real historical event, used to give a poem extra weight.
words.example: The historical allusion to the Holocaust is the poem's most argued-about choice.

words.meaning: A retelling of a traditional story from a new point of view.
words.example: The revisionist myth gives Eve the last word instead of the blame.

words.meaning: Writing that challenges the way women are treated or portrayed.
words.example: The feminist critique here is aimed at male pride, not at Eve.

words.meaning: A gap between what seems to be true and what actually is.
words.example: The irony is that the woman traditionally blamed becomes the wisest voice.

units.name: Mother — Kirli Saunders

words.meaning: Passing between generations, from grandparents to parents to children.
words.example: Intergenerational knowledge is handed down long before it is written down.

words.meaning: The responsibility of caring for something rather than owning it.
words.example: Custodianship means the land is looked after, not bought and sold.

words.meaning: The deep, ongoing relationship First Nations people have with their traditional land.
words.example: Connection to Country holds language, family and responsibility together, not just place.

units.name: from Throat — Ellen van Neerven

words.meaning: Poetry with no fixed rhyme scheme and no regular metre.

words.meaning: Comedy that comes from the gap between how characters see themselves and how they really are.
words.example: Chekhov's ironic humour lets an audience laugh at Vanya and pity him at once.

words.meaning: A group of characters of roughly equal importance, with no single hero.
words.example: An ensemble cast keeps the audience's sympathy moving around the room.

words.meaning: The loss of a belief you once held about a person, a career or a life.
words.example: Vanya's disillusionment with the professor poisons everything he gave up for him.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Love that the other person does not return.
words.example: Almost every character in the play is carrying an unrequited love.

words.meaning: Dull sameness, with nothing to mark one day off from the next.
words.example: The monotony of the estate is a setting and a state of mind at once.

words.meaning: A deep sense that life has no purpose worth the effort.
words.example: Under the jokes, the play keeps circling an existential despair.

units.name: Uncle Vanya · Acts 3–4: confrontation and resignation

words.meaning: A direct, angry clash in which what has been held back is finally said.
words.example: The confrontation in Act 3 releases years of resentment in a few minutes.

words.meaning: The quality of being pointless — effort that changes nothing.
words.example: Even the gunshot ends in futility: nothing about the household changes.

parts.meaning: revel-song (from the Greek for a village festival song)

words.meaning: A play that mixes tragic and comic elements, so that suffering is also absurd.
words.example: Chekhov called it a comedy, but tragicomedy is closer to what an audience feels.

words.meaning: Accepting an unwanted situation and stopping the struggle against it.
words.example: The play closes on resignation rather than on change.

words.meaning: Enduring hardship calmly, without complaining about it.
words.example: Sonya's stoicism is either comfort or defeat, depending on how you read it.

words.meaning: A plot that ends close to where it started, suggesting nothing will change.
words.example: The cyclical structure returns the estate to its account books and its silence.

words.meaning: An ending that avoids the big dramatic moment and lets tension leak away.
words.example: The anticlimax is the point: life goes on without resolution.

translations.ja: アンチクライマックス

units.name: King Lear · Acts 1–2: the love test and its betrayals

words.meaning: Pride so great that it blinds a person to good sense.
words.example: Lear's hubris makes him demand love out loud before he will hand over land.

words.meaning: Praise that is excessive and insincere, offered to get something.
words.example: Goneril and Regan win kingdoms with flattery; Cordelia loses hers by refusing.

words.meaning: A child's cruelty or disrespect toward a parent.
words.example: Filial ingratitude is the wound Lear keeps returning to on the heath.

words.meaning: The custom of the eldest child inheriting the whole estate.
words.example: By dividing the kingdom, Lear breaks with primogeniture and invites chaos.

words.meaning: Foolish behaviour, or a badly judged decision.
words.example: The play measures Lear's folly against the Fool's uncomfortable good sense.

words.meaning: Breaking the trust of someone who relied on you.
words.example: Edmund's betrayal of his brother runs alongside the sisters' betrayal of their father.

words.meaning: Deliberately causing pain to someone who cannot stop you.
words.example: Putting Kent in the stocks is a small cruelty that promises worse.

words.meaning: Hiding who you are by changing how you look or speak.
words.example: Kent and Edgar both survive in disguise, watching what they cannot prevent.

words.meaning: Hints planted early in a text about events that are still to come.
words.example: The gathering storm is foreshadowing: the kingdom breaks before the weather does.

units.name: King Lear · Act 3: the storm and madness

words.meaning: The loss of clear, rational thought.
words.example: Lear's madness arrives as his power and his family fall away together.

words.meaning: The tempest on the heath, used to mirror the chaos in Lear's mind and kingdom.
words.example: The storm is weather, but it is also everything Lear can no longer control.

words.meaning: The belief that life has no built-in meaning, order or value.
words.example: The play's nihilism sits inside the word "nothing", which keeps coming back.

words.meaning: The licensed jester who is allowed to tell a king uncomfortable truths.
words.example: The Fool says what no courtier dares, and only the joking protects him.

words.meaning: A small thing that stands for something much larger.
words.example: The heath becomes a microcosm of a kingdom with no order left in it.

units.name: King Lear · Acts 4–5: blindness, pathos and the tragic end

words.meaning: Restoring a broken relationship after harm has been done.
words.example: The reconciliation between Lear and Cordelia is brief and almost unbearable.

words.meaning: Being unable to see — literally, or unable to see the truth about people.
words.example: Gloucester's blindness is physical; Lear's was there from the first scene.

words.meaning: Winning back your moral worth, or a relationship, after doing wrong.
words.example: Edgar's care for his father is the closest the play comes to redemption.

words.meaning: The quality in a scene that makes an audience feel pity and sadness.
words.example: The pathos of the last scene comes from how ordinary the old man's grief sounds.

words.meaning: The emotional release a tragedy's ending is meant to give the audience.
words.example: Whether this ending offers catharsis at all makes a good essay question.

words.meaning: The sense that the deaths in a tragedy are far greater than anyone deserved.
words.example: Cordelia's death is the clearest tragic waste in Shakespeare.

words.meaning: The view that suffering carries no lesson and the universe offers no justice.
words.example: The unresolved ending leaves the nihilism of the storm scenes standing.

words.meaning: Putting order back in place at the end of a tragedy — here, only partly.
words.example: Edgar's last speech gestures at restoration without promising very much.

units.name: Medea · Prologue & Parados: the Nurse and the Chorus

words.meaning: The background information an audience needs before the action can begin.
words.example: The Nurse delivers the exposition: the marriage, the betrayal, the danger.

words.meaning: A strong feeling that something bad is about to happen.
words.example: The Nurse's foreboding about the children is the audience's first warning.

words.meaning: The killing of one's own child.
words.example: The whole play moves toward a filicide the audience can see coming.

words.meaning: A familiar character type that audiences recognise from many plays.
words.example: The loyal Nurse is a stock character doing a job the plot needs done.

words.meaning: A group of performers who comment on the action and speak for the community.
words.example: The chorus of Corinthian women judges Medea and pities her by turns.

words.meaning: The Chorus's entrance song, and the side passage they enter by.
words.example: The parados brings the women on stage and sets the play's moral frame.

words.meaning: A formal, elevated poem meant to be sung.
words.example: Between episodes the Chorus sings an ode that widens the play's argument.

units.name: Medea · Episodes I–III: the agon, the oath and the deception

words.meaning: The formal debate scene in Greek drama where two characters argue opposite sides.
words.example: The agon between Medea and Jason is an argument that neither of them wins.

words.meaning: The art of speaking persuasively to win an audience over.
words.example: Jason's rhetoric is smooth, which is exactly what makes it hard to trust.

words.meaning: The Greek duty of hospitality between host and guest, protected by the gods.
words.example: Medea is a foreigner in Corinth, so xenia is the only shelter she has.

words.meaning: Being forced to leave your home or country.
words.example: Creon orders exile, and the single day he grants becomes the play's clock.

words.meaning: Protection and refuge given to someone fleeing danger.
words.example: Aegeus offers asylum in Athens, and the revenge suddenly becomes possible.

words.meaning: A solemn promise, sworn so that breaking it offends the gods.
words.example: Medea makes Aegeus swear an oath before she will trust his offer.

words.meaning: A sudden, often divine device that resolves a plot from outside it.
words.example: Aegeus's arrival is a small deus ex machina that sets up a much larger one.

translations.ja: デウス・エクス・マキナ

words.meaning: Deliberate deception: saying one thing while planning another.
words.example: Medea's duplicity with Jason is the coldest scene in the play.

words.meaning: Controlling someone by managing what they believe and feel.
words.example: Her apology is pure manipulation, and Jason swallows every word of it.

words.meaning: When the audience knows something a character on stage does not.
words.example: The dramatic irony is unbearable: we already know what the gifts will do.

units.name: Medea · Messenger Speech & Exodus: the off-stage horror and the escape

words.meaning: A long report in Greek drama describing violence that happened off stage.
words.example: The messenger speech makes the audience picture the deaths instead of watching them.

words.meaning: In Greek tragedy, kept off stage: violence is described, never shown.
words.example: The deaths are obscene in the technical sense — they happen where we cannot see.

translations.ja: 舞台裏（暴力は語られる）

words.meaning: Writing designed to move an audience to pity and horror.
words.example: The pathos of the messenger's report lands before anyone has time to judge.

words.meaning: The emotional release an audience is meant to feel as a tragedy ends.
words.example: Euripides denies easy catharsis by letting Medea escape unpunished.

words.meaning: Arrogance that ignores what is owed to other people and to the gods.
words.example: Jason's hubris is his confidence that he could set Medea aside without cost.

words.meaning: Punishment that arrives as the inevitable answer to pride.
words.example: A Greek audience would read the revenge as nemesis for a broken oath.

words.meaning: A god or machine that ends a play from outside its human logic.
words.example: The chariot is a literal deus ex machina, and it denies the audience justice.

translations.ja: デウス・エクス・マキナ

units.name: Literature metalanguage · Devices 1: figurative language, imagery and sound

words.meaning: A reference to another text, person or event that adds meaning for readers who catch it.
words.example: One allusion to an old story can carry a whole argument in four words.

words.meaning: Using an object, colour or image to stand for an idea beyond its literal meaning.
words.example: Track the symbolism of light and dark before you write about the ending.

words.meaning: An image, phrase or idea that keeps returning across a text.
words.example: A motif becomes an argument only when you can say what its repetitions build.

words.meaning: Placing two contrasting things side by side so that the difference shows.
words.example: The juxtaposition of the feast and the funeral makes both of them look worse.

words.meaning: A gap between what is said or expected and what is actually true.
words.example: Name the kind of irony you mean: dramatic, verbal or situational.

words.meaning: Giving weather or landscape human feeling so that it matches a scene's mood.
words.example: Rain at a funeral is pathetic fallacy doing very obvious work.

translations.vi: gán cảm xúc cho thiên nhiên

words.meaning: Descriptive language that appeals to the senses.
words.example: Quote the imagery, then say which sense it works on and why that matters.

words.meaning: A direct comparison that says one thing is another, without "like" or "as".
words.example: A metaphor claims more than a simile does, because it drops the comparing word.

words.meaning: A comparison that uses "like" or "as".
words.example: A simile keeps the two things apart; a metaphor collapses them together.

words.meaning: Giving human qualities to something that is not human.
words.example: Personification of the city as a sleeping animal sets the mood of the scene.

words.meaning: The writer's or narrator's attitude to the subject, heard in the word choice.
words.example: Decide on the tone first; the rest of the analysis follows from it.

words.meaning: The emotional atmosphere a piece of writing creates for the reader.
words.example: Tone belongs to the speaker; mood belongs to the reader.

words.meaning: Repeating the same words at the start of line after line.
words.example: Anaphora builds pressure, which is why speeches and protest poems use it.

words.meaning: A line of poetry that runs into the next one without a pause.
words.example: Enjambment makes the reader's eye travel faster than the sentence does.

words.meaning: The turn in a poem where its argument, tone or perspective shifts.
words.example: Find the volta and you have found the poem's structure.

words.meaning: A pause cut into the middle of a line of poetry.
words.example: A caesura can make a line stop breathing halfway through.

units.name: Literature metalanguage · Devices 2: structure, narration and genre

words.meaning: Hints planted earlier in a text about events that are still to come.
words.example: Foreshadowing is only worth writing about if you can say what it prepares.

words.meaning: The techniques a writer uses to build and reveal a character.
words.example: Characterisation happens through speech and silence, not just description.

words.meaning: The particular way a story is told, shaped by who is telling it and how.
words.example: Narrative voice is not the author; it is the teller the author built.

words.meaning: A narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted.
words.example: With an unreliable narrator, the gaps in the telling become the evidence.

translations.vi: người kể chuyện không đáng tin

words.meaning: Written as a series of letters, diary entries or other documents.
words.example: An epistolary novel makes the reader feel they are opening someone's post.

words.meaning: A story enclosed inside another story.
words.example: A frame narrative always raises the question of why this teller was chosen.

words.meaning: A style that follows the loose, unfinished flow of a character's thoughts.
words.example: Stream of consciousness drops punctuation and logic to keep up with thinking.

words.meaning: A story whose characters and events stand for a larger moral or political meaning.
words.example: In an allegory the surface story is never the point.

translations.ja: 盛り合わせの皿（雑多な作）

words.meaning: Writing that mocks a person, institution or belief, often to provoke change.
words.example: Satire needs a target: say what the writer wants changed.

words.meaning: An exaggerated, comic imitation of another work or style.
words.example: A parody has to love its target enough to copy it accurately.

words.meaning: A work that imitates another style, usually with respect rather than mockery.
words.example: Pastiche borrows a style; parody sends it up.

words.meaning: The way texts refer to, echo or depend on other texts for meaning.
words.example: Intertextuality is not a hunt for references; it is an argument about meaning.

words.meaning: Fiction that draws attention to itself as something written and made up.
words.example: When the narrator mentions the reader, you are in metafiction.

units.name: Literature metalanguage · Close reading and essay writing

words.meaning: A detailed, line-by-line examination of language, structure and technique in a short passage.
words.example: Close reading means starting from the words, not from what you already think.

words.meaning: A grouped set of lines in a poem, like a paragraph in prose.
words.example: Say which stanza your quotation comes from.

words.meaning: A short extract of text chosen for detailed analysis.
words.example: Read the whole passage twice before you annotate a single line.

words.meaning: Notes written on or beside a text to record what you notice.
words.example: Good annotation names the technique and its effect, not just the device.

translations.ja: ～された（過去形の形容詞を作る）
translations.ro: care a fost (formează adjectiv la trecut)
translations.ur: جو ہو چکا (ماضی کی صفت بناتا ہے)
translations.vi: đã được (tạo tính từ quá khứ)
translations.zh-Hans: 已被……的（构成过去式形容词）
translations.zh-Hant: 已被……的（構成過去式形容詞）

words.meaning: A short quotation woven into your own sentence rather than left standing alone.
words.example: An embedded quote should read smoothly as part of your own grammar.

words.meaning: A precise verb that names exactly how a technique makes meaning.
words.example: Replace "shows" with an analytic verb such as "undercuts" or "juxtaposes".

words.meaning: The central argument or interpretation an essay sets out to prove.
words.example: If your thesis cannot be argued against, it is not yet a thesis.

words.meaning: A reasoned reading of what a text means, always arguable rather than simply correct.
words.example: Two interpretations can both be defensible; only one of them is yours.

units.name: Literature metalanguage · Critical frameworks (Literary Perspectives)

words.meaning: Reading a text for how it represents gender and power between men and women.
words.example: A feminist reading asks who speaks, who is looked at, and who stays silent.

words.meaning: Reading a text for how it represents class, wealth and power between social groups.
words.example: A Marxist reading of the novel starts with who owns the house.

words.meaning: Reading a text for how it represents colonisation, empire and the colonised "other".
words.example: A postcolonial reading asks whose land the story is standing on.

translations.ja: ポストコロニアル的読解

words.meaning: Reading a text using ideas about the unconscious mind, desire and repression.
words.example: A psychoanalytic reading treats the dream sequence as evidence, not decoration.

words.meaning: Reading a text for how it represents, or excludes, identities outside heterosexual norms.
words.example: A queer reading often works from what a text will not say directly.

words.meaning: Reading a text in the light of the historical period in which it was written.
words.example: A historicist reading puts the play back into the year it was first performed.

words.meaning: An approach that treats meaning as something each reader builds, not something fixed.
words.example: Reader-response criticism takes your reaction seriously, then asks you to justify it.

translations.vi: lý thuyết phản hồi độc giả

units.name: Literature metalanguage · Adaptation and transformation

words.meaning: Reworking a text into a new form or medium while keeping much of its content.
words.example: A film adaptation has to turn private thought into something an audience can see.

words.meaning: A more radical reworking of a text's content, setting, perspective or form.
words.example: A transformation can keep one character and change everything else.

words.meaning: The original work that an adaptation or transformation is based on.
words.example: Quote the source text when you explain what your creative response changed.

words.meaning: How closely an adaptation stays faithful to its source text.
words.example: Judging an adaptation only on fidelity misses what the new form can do.

words.meaning: Moving a story's setting to a different time or place while keeping its core plot.
words.example: Setting the play in a modern high school is a transposition, not a new plot.

words.meaning: Retelling a story from a new angle, often with changed values or a changed ending.
words.example: A reimagining usually hands the voice to a minor character.

units.name: Literature metalanguage · Views and values

words.meaning: The beliefs and priorities inside a text, whether it endorses them or criticises them.
words.example: Write about views and values by showing how the text treats them, not by guessing.

words.meaning: What an author meant to communicate — one useful reading, but not the only one.
words.example: Authorial intent cannot settle an argument the text itself leaves open.

words.meaning: The historical, social or cultural circumstances that shape a text's meaning.
words.example: Context explains why an audience in 1606 heard the storm differently.

words.meaning: The general mood and dominant attitudes of a particular period in history.
words.example: The novel captures the zeitgeist of a decade that believed the money would last.

words.meaning: A connected system of beliefs and values that shapes how people see the world.
words.example: Every text carries an ideology, including the ones that claim to be neutral.

words.meaning: The interpretation a culture treats as the natural or obvious one.
words.example: Naming the dominant reading is the first step to arguing against it.

words.meaning: The particular standpoint a reader or character sees and understands events from.
words.example: The narrator's subject position decides what the reader is allowed to know.

units.name: Literature metalanguage · VCAA command terms for SACs and the exam

words.meaning: Break something into its parts and show how the parts work together.
words.example: Analyse how the poet builds tension across the final stanza.

words.meaning: Look at more than one side of an idea before reaching a view.
words.example: Discuss whether the ending offers the audience any comfort.

words.meaning: Examine an idea openly and in depth, without forcing one fixed conclusion.
words.example: Explore the way the text presents belonging.

words.meaning: Show how two or more things are similar, and usually how they differ.
words.example: Compare the two poems' treatment of Country.

words.meaning: Show how two or more things are different from each other.
words.example: Contrast the Fool's honesty with Goneril's flattery.

words.meaning: Judge how good, useful or successful something is, and give reasons for your judgement.
words.example: Evaluate how convincingly the adaptation carries the novel's views and values.

words.meaning: Look closely at something and say what you find.
words.example: Examine the imagery in the passage line by line.

words.meaning: Explain what something means, especially where the meaning is not obvious.
words.example: Interpret the last two lines of the poem.

words.meaning: Give reasons that show your answer or choice is the right one.
words.example: Justify your choice of passage for close analysis.

deliberately breaking or twisting the usual rules of a genre to surprise or challenge the audience.
the technical elements (like camera angle, lighting or editing) used to create meaning in media.

how involved and interested an audience is with a media product.
in media: the act of watching, reading or otherwise taking in a media product.
in media: how an audience receives, interprets and responds to a media product.
the specialist vocabulary used to analyse and discuss how media products create meaning.

the process of building or putting something together, such as a narrative, from its individual parts.
the process of making a media product, covering everything from planning to filming or recording.
relating to the practical skills and equipment needed to operate a tool, process or piece of technology.

the process of getting a finished media product out to its audience.

the codes, conventions and techniques that media makers combine to create meaning for an audience.

the different types or categories of media, such as film, radio, print, photography or digital and interactive media.
to communicate with and respond to something, such as when an audience interacts with a media product instead of just watching passively.
the people who watch, read, listen to or otherwise engage with a media product; in new media, audiences often also produce and share content themselves.
relating to the tools, equipment and systems created by applying scientific and practical knowledge, such as new media platforms and devices.

the companies and organisations that create, own and distribute media products, such as television networks, film studios or social media platforms.
the typical features or qualities that make something identifiable, such as the features that define a new media audience.

words.meaning: the planning stage of making a media product, before filming or creating begins.
the stage after filming/recording where a media product is edited and finished.

the way media portrays people, places or ideas, shaping how audiences see them.
in media production: to finalise and complete a media product to a professional standard.
in media: to turn a planned idea or design into an actual finished product.
in media production: thinking critically about your own work to identify what to improve.
in media: the message or effect a creator plans for their product to have on its audience.

words.meaning: the power of a person or group to act independently and make choices that have an effect on others.
the power to affect what someone thinks, believes or does, without directly forcing them.
an official rule or system of control that governs how something must operate.
an established organisation, such as a media company or government body, with a recognised structure and purpose.

words.meaning: made to operate or connect across the whole world rather than within one country.
belonging to or happening in the present time.
the power to direct, limit or manage how something operates.

translations.vi: tính cách đạo đức, phong tục

words.meaning: relating to what is morally right or wrong in a particular situation.
the codes, conventions and techniques that media makers combine to create meaning for an audience.

units.name: Unit 2 AOS 1 — Performing

words.meaning: the basic building blocks of music, such as rhythm, melody, harmony and dynamics.
a specific technique a composer uses to shape and develop musical ideas.
the practical skills and understanding needed to perform and interpret music well.
a person who adapts an existing piece of music for different instruments or performers.
the specific physical skills required to play a particular musical instrument well.
relating to the distinctive style or manner in which a piece of music is performed.
a practice session to prepare a musical performance.

words.meaning: Great anger, especially the anger of God as the villagers imagine it.
words.example: They read the plague as the wrath of heaven rather than the work of fleas.

words.meaning: The group of people gathered to worship together in a church.
words.example: The congregation thins week by week as the deaths mount.

words.meaning: Showing very strong, passionate feeling, especially about religion.
words.example: Her fervent prayers fill the church long after the service has ended.

words.meaning: A person or animal that passes on a disease without necessarily looking ill.

words.meaning: A sign that something significant, usually bad, is about to happen.

units.name: Year of Wonders · Part 2: Sign of a Witch to Venom in the Blood

words.meaning: A person unfairly blamed for problems that are not really their fault.

words.meaning: A wave of extreme, uncontrolled fear or excitement spreading through a group.

words.meaning: Poison from an animal; also the bitter hatred carried in what someone says.
words.example: There is venom in the way the neighbours now speak of her.

words.meaning: The intention to harm or upset someone on purpose.
words.example: Old malice between two families turns deadly in a frightened village.

words.meaning: A long-running, bitter quarrel between people or families.
words.example: A feud over a boundary stone is still remembered thirty years later.

words.meaning: A feeling that someone has done something wrong, held without solid proof.
words.example: Suspicion falls on anyone who knows more about herbs than her neighbours.

units.name: Year of Wonders · Part 2: Wide Green Prison to So Soon to be Dust

words.meaning: The boundary the villagers agree not to cross, so the disease cannot spread outward.

words.meaning: The state of being trapped somewhere you are not able to leave.
words.example: The green hills become an image of entrapment rather than freedom.

words.meaning: Being cut off from other people or places.
words.example: A year of isolation changes how the village sees the world outside.

words.meaning: Giving up your own safety, comfort or interests for the good of other people.
words.example: Staying inside the boundary is an act of self-sacrifice by a whole village.

words.meaning: The fact that everyone must die; also the number of deaths in one place.

words.meaning: Deep sorrow, especially after someone close to you has died.
words.example: Anna's grief for her sons runs under every page of her narration.

words.meaning: The slow rotting or falling apart of something once living or well kept.
words.example: Empty cottages fall into decay within a single season.

words.meaning: The pointlessness of an effort that cannot possibly work.
words.example: The futility of charms and spells becomes clear as the deaths go on.

units.name: Year of Wonders · Part 2: The Poppies of Lethe to The Body of the Mine

words.meaning: A drug made from poppies, used to dull pain or bring on sleep.
words.example: An opiate can quiet the pain, but it also blurs the mind.

words.meaning: In Greek myth, the river of the underworld whose water makes you forget everything.
words.example: The poppies promise a kind of Lethe: forgetting instead of feeling.

words.meaning: A drug or substance that takes away pain or feeling.
words.example: With no real anaesthetic, a broken bone is set with strong drink and courage.

words.meaning: A feeling of having almost no hope left, which pushes people into extreme acts.
words.example: Desperation drives the villagers to remedies they would once have laughed at.

words.meaning: A brief reference to another text or story that adds meaning without explaining itself.
words.example: The chapter title is an allusion to a psalm about sailors in danger.

words.meaning: The belief that God sees ahead and cares for what happens in the world.
words.example: Some villagers trust providence; others trust vinegar and a locked door.

words.meaning: Serious danger, especially danger you cannot easily escape.
words.example: Every household faces the same peril once the sickness is inside the walls.

words.meaning: Courage and strength of mind shown while enduring pain or hardship.
words.example: The rector praises the fortitude of those who stay to nurse the dying.

words.meaning: A vertical or sloping tunnel dug down into the ground to reach minerals.
words.example: A lead miner works alone at the bottom of the mine shaft.

words.meaning: The work of digging earth out, whether to mine ore or to bury the dead.
words.example: The excavation of new graves goes on from dawn until dark.

words.meaning: Existing or happening below the surface of the ground.
words.example: The village's wealth comes from subterranean lead, cut out by hand.

words.meaning: The way a person earns a living and supports a family.
words.example: When a miner dies, his family loses its livelihood as well.

units.name: Year of Wonders · Part 2: The Press of Their Ghosts to Deliverance

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Troubled by memories of the dead, as though the dead kept visiting you.
words.example: Anna is haunted by the faces of the people she could not save.

translations.ur: مُردوں کی یادوں سے ستایا ہوا
translations.ps: د مړو په یادونو کې ښکېل

words.meaning: The state of having lost someone you love to death.

words.meaning: The inner sense of right and wrong that makes a person feel guilty.
words.example: His conscience will not let him leave the village to save himself.

words.meaning: A heavy responsibility or weight, whether physical or emotional.

words.meaning: Making something clean or pure again, often through a ritual or by burning it.

words.meaning: A pile of wood built to burn a body or a heap of possessions.

words.meaning: To treat something sacred with violent disrespect, or damage it on purpose.

words.meaning: Punishment handed out in return for a wrong that someone has done.

words.meaning: Being rescued or set free from danger or suffering.
words.example: The last death feels less like deliverance than exhaustion.

words.meaning: Being saved from sin, error or a hopeless situation, often through sacrifice.
words.example: Anna looks for redemption in useful work rather than in prayer.

words.meaning: The release of strong, built-up emotion, often at the climax of a story.
words.example: The final chapters offer the reader a catharsis after months of grief.

words.meaning: A moment when past actions are finally judged or paid for.
words.example: The rector faces a reckoning for the promises he made from the pulpit.

units.name: Year of Wonders · Part 3: Apple-Picking Time to the Epilogue

words.meaning: When a story ends by returning to the image or scene it began with, showing change.
words.example: The apple harvest returns at the end, giving the novel a cyclical structure.

words.meaning: Returning to and rejoining normal life or a community after a crisis.

words.meaning: The guilt felt by someone who lived through a disaster that killed others.

translations.ja: サバイバーズ・ギルト
translations.vi: mặc cảm của người sống sót
translations.ps: د ژوندي پاتې کېدو د ګناه احساس

words.meaning: What is left behind and remembered after an event or a person's life.
words.example: The village's legacy is a story about choosing to stay.

words.meaning: A short final section after the main story that shows what happens afterwards.

words.meaning: Being forced, or choosing, to live away from your home country or community.
words.example: Anna's new life abroad is a kind of chosen exile.

words.meaning: Remaking yourself into someone new, especially after great loss.
words.example: The ending is a reinvention: a new name, a new country and new work.

translations.ur: خود کو نئے سرے سے بنانا

words.meaning: The ability to recover and keep going after hardship.

units.name: Year of Wonders · Writing a personal response

words.meaning: The marking guide that spells out what the examiners are looking for.

words.meaning: The two or three main points your personal response essay is organised around.
words.example: Choose three arguments and give each one its own body paragraph.

words.meaning: Quotations or specific details from the text used to support an argument.
words.example: Every claim you make about Anna needs evidence from the novel.

words.meaning: The exact words copied from a text, used as evidence and always kept short.
words.example: Weave a short quotation into your own sentence rather than dropping it in.

words.meaning: A brief outline of your topic sentences and evidence, written before you draft.
words.example: A five-minute skeleton saves you twenty minutes of rewriting.

words.meaning: The opening paragraph that sets up the text, its context and your contention.
words.example: Name the novel and its author in the introduction, then state your contention.

words.meaning: The final paragraph that restates your contention and pulls the essay's ideas together.
words.example: A conclusion should not introduce a brand-new argument.

words.meaning: Behaving the way a group or society expects, rather than following your own judgement.
words.example: The novel asks what conformity costs when a whole village is afraid.

words.meaning: Someone rejected or shut out by their own community.
words.example: A healer can become an outcast overnight once the deaths begin.

words.meaning: An intensely difficult or dangerous situation that tests people and forces choices.
words.example: A crisis shows which characters act and which look away.

units.name: The Memory Police · Key word list 1: erasure, power and what is left behind

words.meaning: The complete wiping out of something so it no longer exists or is remembered.
words.example: On the island, erasure is official policy, not an accident.

words.meaning: The state of things being ordinary, or the way people expect them to be.
words.example: After each disappearance the islanders return to a strange kind of normalcy.

words.meaning: The way things currently are, especially when people resist changing them.
words.example: Nobody on the island questions the status quo out loud.

words.meaning: A reader's choice to accept impossible story events as real for the sake of the story.
words.example: The novel asks for suspension of disbelief: objects vanish and no one can remember them.

translations.fa: کسی که قدرت را در دست دارد

words.meaning: Describing a government or person that demands total obedience and allows no disagreement.
words.example: The Memory Police are the clearest sign of an authoritarian regime.

words.meaning: Shared by, or belonging to, a whole group rather than one person.
words.example: The island loses its collective memory one object at a time.

words.meaning: The cruel or unfair use of power to keep a group of people down.
words.example: Write a paragraph on how the novel shows oppression through silence rather than violence.

words.meaning: A careful, structured judgement of what something does well and does badly.
words.example: Your critique should weigh the novel's strengths against its slow middle chapters.

words.meaning: Able to be touched or physically felt.
words.example: A photograph is tangible; the memory inside it is not.

words.meaning: Not physical, and hard to grasp or hold on to.
words.example: What the islanders lose is intangible: the feeling a rose used to carry.

words.meaning: A small remaining piece of something that used to be bigger or whole.
words.example: A remnant of ribbon is all that survives the disappearance.

words.meaning: Remaining after most of something has gone.
words.example: The narrator feels a residual sadness she cannot name.

words.meaning: Lasting only a very short time.
words.example: Snow on the island is ephemeral, and so is everything else.

units.name: The Memory Police · Key word list 2: silence, complicity and resistance

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Broken up into disconnected pieces that no longer make a whole.
words.example: The narrator's memory of her mother is fragmented and full of gaps.

words.meaning: A lack of interest, concern or emotion about things that should matter.

words.meaning: Emotional distance; not letting yourself feel connected to something.
words.example: The calm voice of the narrator creates a chilling detachment.

words.meaning: Having something — land, memories, identity — taken away from you.
words.example: Each disappearance is another act of dispossession.

words.meaning: Stopping someone from speaking or being heard.
words.example: The silencing of the voice is the novel's cruellest disappearance.

words.meaning: The act of clearly expressing an idea or feeling in words.
words.example: Once the words go, articulation of loss becomes impossible.

words.meaning: Knowing everything; used of an all-seeing narrator or authority.
words.example: The Memory Police behave as if they were omniscient.

words.meaning: The overall mood or feeling a text creates in the reader.
words.example: The quiet, snowy atmosphere makes the danger feel closer, not further away.

words.meaning: Being partly responsible for a wrong because you helped or allowed it to happen.
words.example: Burning what has disappeared makes every islander share in the complicity.

words.meaning: Disagreement with, or opposition to, an official policy or ruling power.
words.example: Open dissent on the island ends with a knock at the door.

words.meaning: Close watching of people by an authority, usually without their consent.
words.example: Constant surveillance turns neighbours into people you cannot trust.

words.meaning: Quietly refusing to cooperate with authority, without open or violent rebellion.

translations.vi: chủ nghĩa xét lại lịch sử

units.name: The Memory Police · Background and Chapters 1–2: the island and the first disappearance

words.meaning: A story whose characters and events stand for a bigger real-world idea.

words.meaning: Describing a regime that seeks total control over public and private life.

words.meaning: An imagined society that is frightening or oppressive, used to comment on our own.

words.meaning: Land surrounded by water; here, the unnamed setting cut off from the rest of the world.

words.meaning: In this novel, when a thing vanishes from existence and from everyone's memory, not just from sight.

words.meaning: A publishing professional who works with a writer to prepare a book.

words.meaning: A sudden, forceful search of a place by an authority.

words.meaning: An empty gap left behind, physically or emotionally, by something missing.
