units.name: The Memory Police · Chapters 3–9: the old man, the world outside, writing within writing

words.meaning: Something a person's mind keeps returning to; an ongoing concern.

words.meaning: A source of creative ideas that makes someone want to write.

words.meaning: Nervous or anxious, as if stretched tight.

words.meaning: The style of printed or typed letters.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de

words.meaning: Weakened, as if watered down; used here for feelings growing fainter.

words.meaning: Information deliberately kept hidden from other people.

words.meaning: To reveal information that had been kept private.

words.meaning: Tight control over something or someone.

units.name: The Memory Police · Chapters 17–22: the safe room, the searches and the earthquake

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de

units.name: The Memory Police · Chapters 23–28: the cabin, the old man's death and the ending

words.meaning: A ceremony held for a person who has died.

words.meaning: Certain to happen and impossible to prevent.

words.meaning: The painful feeling of being alone or cut off from other people.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Having come to accept a difficult situation, even if it still hurts.

words.meaning: The people who live in a particular place.

words.meaning: To be gradually taken in or swallowed up by something larger.

units.name: The Memory Police · Themes and analytical vocabulary

words.meaning: In analysis, the meaning created by what a text leaves out or refuses to explain.
words.example: The novel's negative space — the reason for the disappearances — is where its power sits.

words.meaning: A story that draws attention to being a story, often by holding a story inside itself.

words.meaning: The background information a text gives to explain its world.
words.example: Ogawa withholds exposition on purpose: we never learn who rules the island.

words.meaning: Sharing a name with the title of the work.
words.example: The eponymous Memory Police are barely described, which makes them worse.

words.meaning: A person's capacity to act and make choices for themselves.
words.example: Argue whether the narrator has any real agency by the final chapter.

units.name: Crafting texts · Getting started: what identity and belonging mean

words.meaning: The qualities, beliefs and experiences that make a person or group who they are.
words.example: Your first piece should explore one part of identity, not all of it.

words.meaning: The feeling of being accepted as part of a place, group or community.
words.example: Write about a moment when belonging was offered to you and you refused it.

words.meaning: Quick, unstructured writing done to produce raw material and ideas, not a finished piece.
words.example: Ten minutes of generative writing will give you more than an hour of planning.

words.meaning: A published text studied as a model for techniques you can borrow in your own writing.
words.example: Choose a mentor text whose voice is nothing like yours.

words.meaning: Reading a text to notice how it was made, not only what it says.
words.example: Reading as a writer means asking why the paragraph breaks where it does.

words.meaning: An early, unfinished version of a piece of writing.
words.example: Bring a full draft to the workshop, not a plan.

words.meaning: A written explanation, also called a reflective statement, justifying the choices in your own text.
words.example: Your commentary should name the mentor text you borrowed the structure from.

units.name: Crafting texts · Purpose, context and audience: planning non-fiction

words.meaning: What a text is trying to do: express, reflect, explain or argue.
words.example: Decide the purpose before the first sentence, or the piece will drift.

words.meaning: The situation or setting in which a text is written and read.
words.example: The same essay changes meaning in a different context.

words.meaning: The way a text is delivered: read silently, read aloud, performed or published online.
words.example: Choosing spoken mode changes your sentence length immediately.

words.meaning: The people a text is written for, and what they already know or need.
words.example: Name your audience in one sentence before you plan anything else.

words.meaning: The level of formality of language, and how well it suits the audience and purpose.
words.example: The register slips when a formal essay suddenly uses slang.

translations.vi: mức trang trọng của lời nói

words.meaning: A sentence putting two ideas in friction, to give a piece something real to explore.
words.example: Try a tension statement: I wanted to belong there, and I wanted to leave.

words.meaning: Asking "so what?" about an idea again and again, to dig down to its real significance.
words.example: Use the "so what" ladder until the answer surprises you.

units.name: Crafting texts · Cohesion in non-fiction: five strategies

words.meaning: The quality of a text holding together as a connected whole, not just staying on topic.
words.example: Cohesion is what makes a reader trust that you know where you are going.

words.meaning: Returning at the end to an image from the opening, changed by what came between.
words.example: An echo structure lets the last line do the work of a conclusion.

words.meaning: The language that links one paragraph or idea to the next.
words.example: A good transition shows a shift in thinking, not just a change of subject.

words.meaning: Moving deliberately between close personal detail and wide general reflection.
words.example: The zoom takes you from one cracked tile to a whole idea about home.

words.meaning: A short personal story used as evidence or illustration.
words.example: One anecdote, told well, beats three general claims.

words.meaning: General, conceptual ideas that are not tied to any concrete example.
words.example: Too much abstraction and the reader has nothing to hold.

words.meaning: The distinct personality and style that comes through in how someone writes.
words.example: Your voice is what survives when the topic is taken away.

units.name: Crafting texts · A structuralist approach to narrative

words.meaning: A theory that meaning comes from pairs of opposite ideas rather than from single ideas.

words.meaning: A pair of opposite ideas, such as freedom and entrapment, that define each other by contrast.
words.example: Map the central binary of your mentor text before you plan your own.

words.meaning: A division into two opposed parts; another name for a binary.
words.example: The dichotomy of insider and outsider runs through the whole piece.

words.meaning: A recurring image, object or idea that runs through a text and builds meaning.
words.example: Doors work well as a motif in writing about belonging.

words.meaning: A struggle inside one character's mind, between two competing ideas or desires.
words.example: Her internal conflict is that she wants to be seen and wants to hide.

words.meaning: A struggle between a character and something outside themselves.
words.example: External conflict can be as small as an argument on a bus.

words.meaning: The moment of greatest tension or drama in a story.
words.example: Put the climax late, then stop soon after it.

words.meaning: The set of colours a writer or filmmaker deliberately uses to build mood and symbolism.
words.example: The film's cold blue colour palette does half the work of the script.

units.name: Crafting texts · Repetition: rhetorical and literary devices

words.meaning: A technique used to make persuasive language more convincing or memorable.
words.example: Name the rhetorical device, then explain what it does to the listener.

words.meaning: A phrase or line repeated at intervals through a text, anchoring a central idea.
words.example: A refrain gives a speech something the audience can carry home.

words.meaning: Repeating a similar grammatical structure in successive phrases, to create balance and rhythm.
words.example: Parallelism makes a list of three feel like an argument.

words.meaning: Repeating the same word or words at the start of successive phrases or sentences.
words.example: Anaphora builds pressure: I remember, I remember, I remember.

words.meaning: Repeating the same word or words at the end of successive phrases or clauses.
words.example: Epistrophe lands the emphasis on the last word every time.

words.meaning: Repeating words at both the start and the end of successive phrases.
words.example: Symploce is anaphora and epistrophe used at once.

words.meaning: Repeating the last word of one clause at the start of the next, making a chain.
words.example: Anadiplosis links ideas the way one hand passes to another.

words.meaning: Repeating a word or phrase with only a few words in between, for emphasis.
words.example: Diacope: home, my kind of home.

words.meaning: Placing two contrasting ideas close together, often in parallel structure, to sharpen the contrast.
words.example: Antithesis works best when the two halves are the same length.

words.meaning: Repeating the same consonant sound at the start of nearby words.
words.example: Use alliteration sparingly, or the sentence starts to sound like an advertisement.

words.meaning: Repeating similar vowel sounds in nearby words, creating a rhyme inside the line.
words.example: Assonance slows a line down without adding a single word.

words.meaning: Repeating consonant sounds anywhere in nearby words, not only at the start.
words.example: Consonance is harder to hear than alliteration, and often more effective.

words.meaning: Deliberately repeating conjunctions where they could be left out, to slow the reader down.
words.example: Polysyndeton makes a list feel endless: and the heat and the noise and the dust.

words.meaning: Leaving conjunctions out of a list, making it feel fast and relentless.
words.example: Asyndeton speeds a sentence up: she packed, she left, she never wrote.

words.meaning: Repeating a key word at emotionally important moments, without a fixed pattern.
words.example: Conduplicatio returns to one word whenever the feeling rises.

units.name: Crafting texts · Monologue as a textual form

words.meaning: A text in which a single character speaks, alone or to someone who does not reply.
words.example: A monologue needs a reason for the character to keep talking.

words.meaning: A character's private thoughts written as if we can hear their mind.
words.example: Interior monologue lets the reader hear what the character will never say aloud.

words.meaning: A stage convention in which a character, alone, speaks their thoughts to the audience.
words.example: A soliloquy assumes nobody else on stage can hear it.

words.meaning: A poem in which a character speaks to a silent listener, revealing more than they mean to.
words.example: In a dramatic monologue the gap between what is said and what is true does the work.

words.meaning: A standalone piece written to be performed live in front of an audience.
words.example: A performance monologue has to survive being heard once, with no rereading.

words.meaning: The constructed character or voice a writer or performer speaks through.
words.example: The persona in your piece does not have to be you.

words.meaning: The moment a character can no longer stay silent and finally speaks out.
words.example: Build the whole monologue towards one breaking point.

words.meaning: The way words and clauses are arranged into sentences.
words.example: Short syntax for panic; long, folded syntax for memory.

parts.meaning: a mark pricked into the skin

words.meaning: Shame or disapproval that society attaches to a circumstance, quality or person.

words.meaning: Bold refusal to obey or accept something.

words.meaning: Informal, everyday language, of the kind used in casual speech.

words.meaning: Saying or showing one thing while meaning or revealing something different.

words.meaning: A mild or indirect word used in place of a harsh or blunt one.

translations.ja: マイクロアグレッション

words.meaning: For a group to take back and use positively a word once used to insult them.

words.meaning: The accepted rules or normal features of a form or genre.

units.name: Rear Window · Film technique metalanguage: the Evidence Bank

words.meaning: Moving the camera sideways across a scene while filming.

words.meaning: Everything visible inside the frame — set, props, lighting, costume and where the actors stand.

words.meaning: A shot that shows what a character is looking at, as if through their eyes.

words.meaning: Objects placed in a scene or handled by actors, often chosen for their meaning.

words.meaning: The techniques a writer or filmmaker uses to build and reveal a character.

words.meaning: Two or more storylines shown alongside each other so the audience compares them.

words.meaning: A character whose opposite qualities make another character's traits stand out.

words.meaning: Editing that jumps between two scenes happening at the same time, usually to build tension.

words.meaning: A feeling of tense uncertainty about what is going to happen next.

words.meaning: When the audience knows something a character does not, which creates tension or unease.

words.meaning: A shot taken from the opposite angle, often used when a look is returned.

words.meaning: Taking pleasure in secretly watching other people, without their consent.
words.example: The film keeps asking whether the audience shares Jeff's voyeurism.

units.name: Rear Window · Key vocabulary and theory: the gaze and the watcher

words.meaning: The central argument your essay makes about the film.

words.meaning: A film theory that Hollywood films are shot from a man's viewpoint, placing women there to be looked at.

words.meaning: Being unable to move — here, the broken leg that keeps Jeff in his chair.

units.name: Rear Window · Lessons 1–3: the opening, expectations and energy shifts

words.meaning: The opening part of a film that sets up its world, characters and situation.

words.meaning: A conclusion you work out from clues, because the film shows it instead of stating it.

words.meaning: Any deliberate motion of the camera — panning, tracking or zooming — that shapes what we see.

words.meaning: What a viewer predicts will happen next, based on clues the film has already given.
words.example: The opening builds an expectation that the romance will end happily.

words.meaning: A guess about what will happen next, made from the evidence you already have.
words.example: Write your prediction in the margin, then check it after the next scene.

words.meaning: To show that an earlier expectation was right — one of three things a later scene can do to it.
words.example: The salesman's late-night trips confirm what Jeff already suspects.

words.meaning: To make an earlier expectation messier by adding something that does not quite fit it.
words.example: Lisa's arrival complicates the idea that Jeff is simply a lonely man.

words.meaning: To show that an earlier expectation was wrong by proving the opposite.
words.example: Doyle's report seems to contradict everything Jeff has told us.

words.meaning: A noticeable change in a scene's pace, tension or mood.
words.example: Mark the energy shift in the scene where the music suddenly stops.

words.meaning: A group of characters who together build a bigger picture or idea.
words.example: The courtyard ensemble shows every possible version of marriage and loneliness.

words.meaning: A lighter, funny moment put into a serious story to ease the tension.
words.example: Stella's blunt jokes work as comic relief between the tense scenes.

units.name: Rear Window · Lessons 4–8: moral judgment, thresholds and building the argument

words.meaning: A decision about whether an action or a character is right or wrong.

words.meaning: Being partly responsible for something wrong by watching or allowing it instead of stopping it.

words.meaning: The study of what counts as right and wrong behaviour.

words.meaning: The exact moment a film overturns what the audience believed up to that point.

words.meaning: A moment where a story's direction, or a character's understanding, changes completely.

words.meaning: A complete change in a situation, an expectation or a character's fortune.

words.meaning: An argument that keeps asking what a technique or symbol is really for, past the obvious plot reading.

words.meaning: An imagined, often wished-for scene, kept separate from what is real.

words.meaning: Support for an essay claim, taken from how the film is made or from what characters say.

words.meaning: The closing sentence of a body paragraph, which ties the point back to your contention.

units.name: Exploring arguments · The 'Australian values' debate

words.meaning: To blend into the dominant culture by giving up your own cultural traditions.

words.meaning: To join and take part in a community while keeping your own cultural identity.

words.meaning: An unfair opinion or attitude about someone, formed before you really know them.

words.meaning: Treating someone unfairly in practice because of prejudice against a group they belong to.

words.meaning: Discrimination or prejudice based on someone's race or ethnicity.

words.meaning: Persuasive language — sometimes used critically, to mean language that sounds good but says little.

words.meaning: A fond, sometimes unrealistic longing for the past.

words.meaning: In this debate: the sense that a society holds together as one, with shared trust and belonging.

words.meaning: To firmly reject something, or refuse to accept it.

words.meaning: Love of, and pride in, your own country.

words.meaning: The belief that your own nation is superior and should come before all others.

units.name: Exploring arguments · Persuasive language and argument analysis

words.meaning: A reasoned case put forward to support a particular point of view.

words.meaning: The central position or claim a persuasive text argues for.
words.example: Name the contention in your first sentence, then work through the arguments.

words.meaning: To push a reader towards a particular view or feeling through language choices.
words.example: The headline positions the reader to feel afraid before the article even begins.

words.meaning: The group of people a persuasive text is aimed at influencing.

words.meaning: Facts, statistics, expert opinion or examples used to support an argument.

words.meaning: A short personal story used to make an argument feel relatable or urgent.

words.meaning: Language designed to make the reader feel something — fear, sympathy, anger — rather than think.

words.meaning: Persuasion built on reasoning, facts and evidence.

words.meaning: Persuasion that works because the writer or speaker seems trustworthy or expert.

words.meaning: Answering an opposing argument directly and showing why it fails.

words.meaning: A broad claim applied to a whole group, usually without enough evidence.

words.meaning: Words such as 'we' and 'us' that make the reader feel part of the writer's group.

words.meaning: Deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis or effect.

words.meaning: The writer's attitude towards their topic, shown through word choice and style.

words.example: Under the weather is idiomatic language for feeling unwell.

units.name: Born a Crime · Apartheid and history: the chapter prefaces

words.meaning: South Africa's system, from 1948 to 1994, of separating and oppressing people by race in law.
words.example: The narrator is born near the end of apartheid but grows up in its shadow.

words.meaning: Keeping racial or social groups apart by law or by custom.
words.example: Segregation decided which bus, school and suburb a person could use.

words.meaning: Officially sorting people into racial categories, as the apartheid government did.
words.example: Racial classification decided a family's rights before a child could speak.

words.meaning: Racism built into laws, systems and institutions, not just individual attitudes.
words.example: Pass laws are institutionalised racism, written into the statute book.

translations.vi: phân biệt chủng tộc thể chế

translations.es: relativo al bien y al mal
translations.fr: concernant le bien et le mal
translations.ps: د سم او ناسم په اړه

words.meaning: The apartheid law banning relationships and marriage between people of different races.
words.example: The Immorality Act made the narrator's own birth a crime.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Under apartheid, an official racial category for mixed-race people, treated differently from black and white South Africans.
words.example: Being classified coloured placed a child between two worlds and inside neither.

words.meaning: A poor, racially segregated urban area black South Africans were forced to live in.
words.example: The family moves between the township and the city as money runs out.

translations.vi: khu định cư người da đen

words.meaning: Apartheid laws forcing black South Africans to carry papers that limited where they could go.
words.example: Pass laws turned an ordinary walk home into a crime.

words.meaning: Being denied the right to vote or to take part in political life.
words.example: Disenfranchisement kept most of the country out of its own elections.

words.meaning: Being partly responsible for something wrong by going along with it instead of opposing it.
words.example: The memoir asks quiet neighbours to face their own complicity.

words.meaning: The lasting effects of a system, such as apartheid, that continue after it officially ends.
words.example: Poverty and segregated suburbs are part of the legacy of apartheid.

units.name: Born a Crime · Identity, language and belonging: Noah's story

words.meaning: The book's title phrase: the narrator's birth itself broke the law, because his parents were different races.
words.example: The title phrase born a crime turns a legal charge into an identity.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Having parents from more than one racial background.
words.example: A mixed-race child had no legal place in the apartheid system.

words.meaning: A lizard that changes colour to blend in, used here for changing how you present yourself.
words.example: He becomes a chameleon, switching languages to fit whichever group he is with.

words.meaning: Blending into a dominant culture, sometimes losing parts of your own.
words.example: Assimilation can buy safety at the price of your first language.

words.meaning: Changing the language, accent or manner you use depending on who you are speaking to.
words.example: Code-switching lets him greet a shopkeeper in one language and his mother in another.

words.meaning: Someone who does not fully belong to the group around them.
words.example: He is an outsider in every group, and at home in the gap between them.

words.meaning: The ability to recover from hardship and keep going.
words.example: His mother's resilience carries the family through years of danger.

words.meaning: Not having enough money for basic needs such as food, housing and transport.
words.example: Poverty decides which suburb the family can live in.

words.meaning: Violence committed inside the home by a family member or a partner.
words.example: The memoir does not hide the domestic violence in the household.

words.meaning: The drive to do whatever is needed to stay safe or stay alive.
words.example: Survival instinct teaches him when to speak and when to disappear.

words.meaning: Quick, inventive work done to earn money or get by, often outside a proper job.
words.example: Selling copied CDs at school is the hustle that keeps the group in cash.

units.name: Born a Crime · Essay writing: analytical vocabulary

words.meaning: A non-fiction book in which the author tells the true story of part of their own life.
words.example: A memoir chooses scenes; it does not report every year of a life.

words.meaning: The main character of a story; here the author is also his own protagonist.
words.example: The protagonist grows from a small boy into a young comedian.

words.meaning: A short quote placed at the start of a text or chapter to set its tone.
words.example: Each chapter opens with a historical epigraph before the personal story begins.

words.meaning: A story told using I, from the narrator's own point of view.
words.example: First-person narrative lets us hear the joke and the fear at once.

words.meaning: A short, vivid scene or episode inside a larger story.
words.example: Each chapter is built from vignettes rather than one long plot.

words.meaning: A short personal story told to illustrate a point.
words.example: He turns a frightening anecdote into a joke, then back again.

translations.ja: 盛り合わせの皿（雑多な作）

words.meaning: Comedy, sometimes called satirical humour, used to criticise something serious such as an unjust system.
words.example: The satire is gentle on people and hard on the laws they lived under.

words.meaning: Placing two things side by side so the contrast between them stands out; the verb is juxtapose.
words.example: The juxtaposition of a legal notice and a family photograph is deliberate.

words.meaning: To criticise something strongly as wrong; a common verb in analytical essays.
words.example: The memoir condemns the system without condemning every person inside it.

words.meaning: To declare publicly that something is bad or wrong.
words.example: In an essay you might say the author denounces the pass laws.

words.meaning: To reveal something hidden or uncomfortable so that readers have to see it.
words.example: Humour is the tool he uses to expose how absurd the law was.

words.meaning: To try to explain or justify something with reasons, often to excuse it.
words.example: Characters rationalise their silence by saying nothing could be changed.

words.meaning: To give the background a reader needs in order to understand something.
words.example: The chapter openings contextualise each story with a piece of history.

words.meaning: The state of being harmed or wronged by something outside your control.
words.example: The memoir refuses victimhood and insists on humour instead.

words.meaning: A verb that names what an author is doing, such as portrays, critiques or reveals.
words.example: Swap shows for a sharper analytical verb such as exposes.

units.name: Creating texts: Protest · What is protest: defining terms

words.meaning: A strong, public statement or action showing disagreement with something.
words.example: The march was a protest against a law nobody had voted for.

words.meaning: Disagreement, especially with people in authority or with an official position.
words.example: The government treated any dissent as a threat to order.

words.meaning: Deliberately breaking a law as a form of peaceful protest.
words.example: Sitting down in the road is civil disobedience, not violence.

words.meaning: Taking direct action to bring about political or social change.
words.example: Her activism began with a petition and ended in parliament.

words.meaning: A real or believed cause for complaint or unfair treatment.
words.example: List the protesters' grievances before you judge their methods.

words.meaning: Unity and mutual support between people who share a cause.
words.example: Workers in other cities stopped work in solidarity.

words.meaning: Unintended harm caused as a side effect of an action such as a protest or a conflict.
words.example: Broken shopfronts became the collateral damage of one angry night.

words.meaning: Someone willing to suffer or die for a cause they believe in.
words.example: The movement treated her death as the death of a martyr.

words.meaning: The way things are now; the existing state of affairs.
words.example: Protest is uncomfortable because it refuses to accept the status quo.

units.name: Creating texts: Protest · Writing purposes: argue, explain, express, reflect

words.meaning: To write in a way that takes a position and tries to convince the reader.
words.example: If your purpose is to argue, every paragraph must push one contention.

words.meaning: To write in a way that makes clear how or why something is the case.
words.example: Writing to explain a protest is different from writing to defend it.

words.meaning: To write in a way that conveys personal feeling or experience.
words.example: A poem written to express grief does not need an argument.

words.meaning: To write in a way that looks back on an experience and considers its meaning.
words.example: Writing to reflect asks what the march taught you, not what happened.

words.meaning: The reason a piece of writing exists; what it is trying to do.
words.example: Decide your purpose before you choose a form.

words.meaning: The people a piece of writing is written for.
words.example: Your audience is a school assembly, so keep the sentences short.

words.meaning: The circumstances of time, place and culture surrounding a text.
words.example: The same speech means something different in a new context.

units.name: Creating texts: Protest · Mentor text — Freedom or Death (Pankhurst)

words.meaning: A woman who campaigned for women's right to vote, especially in early 1900s Britain.
words.example: A suffragette speaker had to win over a hostile crowd.

translations.vi: nhà đấu tranh quyền bầu cử nữ
translations.ur: ووٹ کے حق کی خاتون کارکن
translations.ps: د ښځو د رایې حق فعاله

words.meaning: Willingness to use forceful or confrontational methods for a cause.
words.example: The speech defends militancy as a last resort, not a first choice.

translations.vi: tinh thần đấu tranh quyết liệt

words.meaning: A comparison developed and carried through a whole piece of writing.
words.example: The extended metaphor of an army runs from the first line to the last.

words.meaning: A rallying call to battle, used figuratively for a passionate call to fight for a cause.
words.example: The final sentence works as a war-cry the audience can repeat.

words.meaning: Refusing to eat as a form of protest, often while in prison.
words.example: The hunger strike moved the argument from the street to the newspaper.

words.meaning: Deliberately damaging or disrupting something to hinder an opponent.
words.example: Cutting telegraph wires was sabotage aimed at the government, not at people.

words.meaning: An indirect reference to another event, person or work.
words.example: The allusion to a famous battle flatters the listeners who recognise it.

words.meaning: A comparison between two different things based on a feature they share.
words.example: She builds an analogy between a protest movement and an army at war.

words.meaning: An imagined situation used to make an argument, not a real one.
words.example: The hypothetical asks listeners what they would do in her place.

words.meaning: A person or group with an interest in an issue, or affected by it.
words.example: Name every stakeholder before you decide whose voice your piece will use.

units.name: Creating texts: Protest · Mentor text — identity, racism and speaking out

words.meaning: Including someone from a minority group only for appearances, without real inclusion.
words.example: One photograph on the website is tokenism, not change.

words.meaning: A small, often unintended comment or action that carries prejudice.
words.example: Being asked where you are really from is a common microaggression.

translations.ja: マイクロアグレッション

words.meaning: Racism built into everyday systems and institutions rather than single actions.
words.example: Systemic racism shows up in the numbers long before it shows up in words.

translations.vi: phân biệt chủng tộc hệ thống

words.meaning: Being true to yourself rather than performing the identity other people expect.
words.example: The writer's authenticity is what makes the piece hard to dismiss.

words.meaning: Accepting a situation without challenging it, even when it is unjust.
words.example: The article attacks complacency more than it attacks open hatred.

words.meaning: The idea that staying quiet about injustice makes a person part of it.
words.example: The slogan silence is violence asks bystanders to choose a side.

words.meaning: A long speech by one speaker, often expressing strong personal feeling.
words.example: Write your piece as a monologue delivered to an empty room.

units.name: Creating texts: Protest · Mentor text — the 1978 Sydney Mardi Gras riots

words.meaning: The basic rights of freedom and equality every citizen is entitled to.
words.example: The 1978 marchers argued that civil rights had to include everyone.

words.meaning: Widespread public disturbance caused by anger at conditions.
words.example: Arrests turned one night of protest into weeks of social unrest.

words.meaning: Unjustly harsh or restrictive; used to describe unfair social conditions.
words.example: Laws that punish who you are, not what you do, are oppressive.

words.meaning: Forced to leave home while staying in the same country, without safety or belonging.
words.example: People pushed out of their own suburb are internally displaced.

words.meaning: Safety or shelter from danger or persecution.
words.example: For many, the parade was the first place that felt like refuge.

words.meaning: An official statement of regret for past wrongdoing, made years or decades later.
words.example: The historic apology came thirty years after the arrests.

units.name: Creating texts: Protest · Reflective commentary

words.meaning: The piece of writing that explains and justifies the choices made in your own crafted text.
words.example: Your reflective commentary should name the mentor text you borrowed from.

translations.ur: غور و فکر پر مبنی تبصرہ

words.meaning: The process of writing, reviewing and rewriting a piece of work.
words.example: Keep every version, because drafting is evidence that the work is yours.

words.meaning: The level of formality and tone chosen for a piece of writing.
words.example: A protest placard and a letter to a senator need very different registers.

translations.vi: mức trang trọng của lời nói

words.meaning: A character or identity an author takes on for a piece, different from their own.
words.example: Writing in the persona of a 1978 marcher changes every word choice.

words.meaning: A deliberate choice made for a reason, rather than something that happened by accident.
words.example: Every intentional decision in your text needs a reason in your commentary.

units.name: High Ground · Characters and totems

words.meaning: The film's young Yolŋu hero, who survives a massacre and grows up between two worlds.
words.example: Gutjuk must choose between the mission station and his uncle's clan.

words.meaning: An animal or natural thing that stands for a person's spirit and their place in the clan.
words.example: A character's totem tells the audience which Country and clan they belong to.

words.meaning: A battle inside one character between two sets of values pulling opposite ways.
words.example: Gutjuk's psychomachia is the fight between revenge and reconciliation.

words.meaning: Making up for a past wrong and earning back your good name.
words.example: Travis hopes that protecting the boy will buy him some redemption.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Torn between two feelings or loyalties that pull against each other.
words.example: The tracker is conflicted: he serves the police and grieves for his own people.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Hurt in the body, or carrying a hurt in the mind that has not healed.
words.example: Every survivor in the film is wounded in some way.

words.meaning: Acting on a careful long-term plan instead of reacting in the moment.
words.example: His silence is strategic: he says nothing until he knows who is listening.

words.meaning: Paying close, careful attention to everything happening around you.
words.example: A watchful character notices the danger long before the patrol does.

units.name: High Ground · Truth and silence

words.meaning: Telling the truth without hiding parts of it or twisting them.
words.example: The film asks whether the nation has the honesty to name what happened.

words.meaning: Twisting the truth so that it gives a false picture.
words.example: The official report is a distortion of what the soldiers actually did.

words.meaning: Sharing in a wrong by helping it or by staying silent about it.
words.example: Saying nothing about the killings is its own kind of complicity.

words.meaning: Wiping something out of the record so later people never learn it happened.
words.example: Leaving the massacre out of the history books is an act of erasure.

parts.meaning: state or result of (makes a noun)

translations.es: estado o resultado de (forma un sustantivo)
translations.vi: trạng thái hoặc kết quả (tạo danh từ)

words.meaning: A first-hand account of what someone saw, given as evidence.
words.example: The survivor's testimony contradicts every official version of that day.

words.meaning: Making something confusing on purpose so that the truth stays hidden.
words.example: The officer's careful wording is obfuscation, not an explanation.

words.meaning: A made-up account of events, invented to replace the truth.
words.example: The report is a fabrication written to protect the men who fired.

words.meaning: Rewriting history to suit one side rather than to follow the evidence.
words.example: Calling an invasion a peaceful settlement is revisionism.

words.meaning: Refusing to accept that something true, and usually painful, really happened.
words.example: Denial kept the massacre out of the official record for a century.

words.meaning: A story told to challenge the official version of what happened.
words.example: The film offers a counter-narrative to the settlers' account of the frontier.

words.meaning: Being lawful, or being widely accepted as having the right to rule.
words.example: The patrol claims legitimacy, but its authority rests on the rifle.

units.name: High Ground · Justice and revenge

words.meaning: Punishment handed back to someone for the harm they did.
words.example: Western law calls it retribution; the clan calls it something else.

words.meaning: Harm done to someone in return for harm they caused, driven by anger.
words.example: The raids are vengeance for the killing of a whole family.

words.meaning: Proof that you were right all along, clearing you of blame.
words.example: The survivor's account is a vindication of everything he had claimed.

words.meaning: Putting right the harm done, often by giving back what was taken.
words.example: No amount of restitution can return the people who were killed.

words.meaning: An attack made to pay back an earlier attack.
words.example: Each reprisal makes the next one certain.

words.meaning: A Yolŋu process for settling a wrong and restoring peace between groups.
words.example: Makarrata offers an ending that punishment alone cannot.

words.meaning: Violence that keeps coming back, each act causing the next one.
words.example: The film traces cyclical violence across two generations.

words.meaning: Rebuilding a good relationship between groups after serious conflict.
words.example: Reconciliation asks more of both sides than an apology does.

units.name: High Ground · Colonisation and power

words.meaning: Taking and holding land or a country, usually by force.
words.example: For the clan, the mission station is part of an occupation.

words.meaning: A place newcomers build and live in on land that already had owners.
words.example: What the old maps call settlement, the film shows as invasion.

words.meaning: Someone who moves onto land already lived in by others and makes a home there.
words.example: The settler families see cattle country; the clan sees Country.

words.meaning: Entering a territory by force and taking control of it.
words.example: The film asks the audience to call it invasion, not settlement.

words.meaning: Being forced off your own land and away from home.
words.example: Displacement leaves the survivors living on someone else's terms.

words.meaning: Forcing a people under your control and keeping them there.
words.example: The patrol's real purpose is subjugation, not order.

words.meaning: Cruel or unfair use of power to keep a group of people down.
words.example: Mission rules are a quieter form of oppression than the rifle.

words.meaning: Complete control held by one group over another.
words.example: Domination is written into who is allowed to carry a weapon.

words.meaning: Wiping out a group's language, ceremonies and ways of living on purpose.
words.example: Banning a language inside the mission is culture erasure.

words.meaning: Using someone unfairly to get work, land or profit from them.
words.example: The station's unpaid labour is exploitation dressed up as care.

words.meaning: Having your land, property or rights taken away from you.
words.example: Dispossession is the wound the whole film grows from.

translations.fa: کسی که قدرت را در دست دارد

words.meaning: The official right to give orders and expect them to be obeyed.
words.example: Travis has authority on paper and almost none on Country.

words.meaning: A belief or system that treats one group as above all the others.
words.example: Racial supremacy is the assumption behind every order the officer gives.

units.name: High Ground · Culture and identity

words.meaning: The traditions, stories and culture handed down to you from earlier generations.
words.example: Gutjuk's heritage survives in the songs his uncle still sings.

words.meaning: The line of family and people you come from, going back through the generations.
words.example: His ancestry ties him to Country in a way the mission cannot undo.

words.meaning: Being cut off from your home, your culture or the people you belong to.
words.example: Mission life leaves the children in permanent dislocation.

words.meaning: Being pulled up by the roots from the culture and place you grew in.
words.example: Deracination is what the mission does to a boy raised on Country.

translations.ja: 根こそぎにされること

words.meaning: Being pushed to take on the dominant culture and give up your own.
words.example: Assimilation was official policy, not an accident.

words.meaning: The feeling of being fully accepted as part of a place or a people.
words.example: Belonging is exactly what the film's hero cannot find in either world.

words.meaning: Being stuck in between, not fully part of either of two worlds.
words.example: Gutjuk lives in liminality, at home in neither the mission nor the clan.

words.meaning: The Aboriginal peoples and languages of north-east Arnhem Land, where the film is set.
words.example: The Yolŋu characters speak their own language on screen.

units.name: High Ground · Loyalty and betrayal

words.meaning: Loyal support that you owe to a person, a group or a cause.
words.example: The tracker's allegiance is claimed by both sides at once.

words.meaning: Deep, lasting loyalty to a person or a belief.
words.example: The missionary's devotion does not stop her from doing harm.

words.meaning: Staying true to a person, a promise or a cause over time.
words.example: Faithfulness to family is what finally pulls the boy home.

words.meaning: Something you must do because of your job, the law or your conscience.
words.example: Travis hides behind duty when he is asked why he obeyed.

words.meaning: A serious betrayal of someone who trusted you.
words.example: Leading the patrol to the camp is treachery, whatever the orders said.

words.meaning: Failing to support someone you owed loyalty to.
words.example: Both sides accuse him of disloyalty; neither offers him a real choice.

words.meaning: Betraying your own country or ruler, especially by helping their enemies.
words.example: To the officer it is treason; to the clan it is coming home.

units.name: High Ground · Film techniques and metalanguage

words.meaning: A shot framed tightly on a face or object so we see small detail and feeling.
words.example: A close-up on the boy's eyes tells us more than any line of dialogue.

words.meaning: A shot taken from far away, so people look small against the landscape.
words.example: The long shot makes the patrol tiny against the ranges.

words.meaning: A shot filmed from straight above — in modern films usually flown by a drone.
words.example: A bird's-eye shot opens the film and shows how vast the Country is.

words.meaning: A shot that shows exactly what one character can see.
words.example: The point-of-view shot down the rifle sight puts us behind the trigger.

translations.vi: cảnh quay góc nhìn nhân vật
translations.ur: کردار کے نقطۂ نظر کا شاٹ

words.meaning: A camera looking down on someone, which usually makes them look small or weak.
words.example: A high camera angle turns the prisoner into someone helpless.

words.meaning: A camera looking up at someone, which usually makes them look powerful.
words.example: The low camera angle gives the officer a size he has not earned.

words.meaning: Everything placed inside the frame — setting, props, costume — and how it is arranged.
words.example: The mise-en-scène of the mission puts a fence between every two people.

words.meaning: Sound that belongs to the world of the story, so the characters hear it too.
words.example: Birdcall and gunfire are diegetic sound; the score is not.

translations.ja: ダイジェティックサウンド

words.meaning: Sound added for the audience only, which the characters cannot hear.
words.example: The music under the massacre is non-diegetic sound.

translations.ja: ノンダイジェティックサウンド
translations.tl: tunog mula sa labas ng eksena

words.meaning: A voice heard over a scene, speaking to us rather than to other characters.
words.example: A voiceover lets a character tell us what the images leave out.

words.meaning: A scene that jumps back to something that happened earlier in the story.
words.example: The flashback to 1919 explains everything the adults will not say.

words.meaning: How the separate shots are cut and ordered to build meaning and pace.
words.example: Fast editing turns the shootout into confusion the audience shares.

words.meaning: What characters wear, chosen to show their culture, their rank or a change in them.
words.example: His costume moves from mission shirt to clan paint and back again.

words.meaning: Using an object or an image to stand for a bigger idea.
words.example: The film uses the river as symbolism for the border between two worlds.

words.meaning: The effect a director is deliberately aiming for through the choices they make.
words.example: Ask what the directorial intent is behind holding that shot so long.

units.name: High Ground · Essay writing: contentions, ideas and values

words.meaning: The single argument your whole essay sets out to prove, in answer to the prompt.
words.example: Your contention should answer the prompt in one clear sentence.

words.meaning: A big concept a text keeps returning to, such as justice, guilt or identity.
words.example: Name the idea first, then show how the film explores it.

words.meaning: A belief about what is right that a text supports, questions or attacks.
words.example: The film endorses the value of truth-telling over comfortable silence.

words.meaning: A short phrase that names a complex idea more precisely than one word can.
words.example: 'Inherited guilt' is a sharper idea phrase than simply 'guilt'.

words.meaning: A difficulty inside an idea that stops a text from giving one simple answer.
words.example: The complication is that the man who saves the boy also destroyed his family.

words.meaning: A pull between two ideas or values that a text refuses to settle.
words.example: There is a tension between justice and revenge in almost every scene.

words.meaning: A verb naming what a director does with an idea, such as critiques or endorses.
words.example: Use a directorial intent verb: the director condemns the cover-up, he does not simply show it.

translations.ja: 監督の意図を表す動詞
translations.vi: động từ chỉ ý đồ đạo diễn
translations.ur: ہدایت کار کے مقصد کا فعل

units.name: Exploring Argument · Contention, tone and connotation

words.meaning: The attitude a writer or speaker shows through their words — angry, pleading, calm.
words.example: The tone shifts from reasonable to scornful in the final paragraph.

words.meaning: The feeling or idea a word carries beyond its plain dictionary meaning.
words.example: 'Crowd' and 'mob' name the same people, but 'mob' has a frightening connotation.

words.meaning: A softer word used in place of a blunt or unpleasant one.
words.example: 'Letting staff go' is a euphemism for sacking them.

words.meaning: The plain dictionary meaning of a word, before any feelings attach to it.
words.example: The denotation of 'home' is a place you live; the warmth is connotation.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Words chosen for the strong feelings they carry rather than for accuracy.
words.example: Calling the plan a betrayal is loaded language, not description.

words.meaning: Mocking; showing that you think something deserves to be laughed at.
words.example: A derisive tone invites readers to look down on the other side.

words.meaning: Meant to calm anger and bring the two sides of an argument together.
words.example: The writer ends on a conciliatory note, offering to meet halfway.

words.meaning: Bitterly sarcastic; harsh enough to sting the person it is aimed at.
words.example: A caustic tone can win agreement or lose the reader completely.

words.meaning: Expecting things to turn out badly.
words.example: A pessimistic tone warns the audience that nothing is going to improve.

words.meaning: Expecting things to turn out well.
words.example: The optimistic close leaves readers feeling the problem can be solved.

units.name: Exploring Argument · Persuasive techniques and rhetorical devices

words.meaning: A question asked for effect, when the answer is already obvious.
words.example: 'How much longer must families wait?' is a rhetorical question.

words.meaning: Persuading by making the audience feel something — fear, pity or pride.
words.example: The photograph of the flooded classroom is an appeal to emotion.

words.meaning: Persuading with logic and evidence rather than with feeling.
words.example: Three clear figures make an appeal to reason the council cannot ignore.

translations.fa: کسی که قدرت را در دست دارد

words.meaning: Persuading by quoting an expert or a trusted organisation.
words.example: Quoting the chief health officer is an appeal to authority.

words.meaning: A short personal story used to make an argument feel real.

words.meaning: A number offered as evidence that a claim is true.

words.meaning: Words like we and our that pull the audience onto the writer's side.

words.meaning: A spoken piece in which you argue your own position on a current issue.

words.meaning: Listening closely and showing it, ready to answer what was actually said.

words.meaning: How fast or slow you speak — one of the tools of persuasive delivery.

words.meaning: Stopping briefly so that an idea has room to land.

words.meaning: Extra force put on one word so that it stands out when you speak.

words.meaning: A shared talk in which people examine an issue together.

words.meaning: A spoken exchange between two people or two sides.

words.meaning: A formal argument in which two sides speak for opposing positions.

subjects.subtitle: Physics · motion, graphs & trigonometry — build each word!

units.name: Lesson 1 · Motion & its language

words.meaning: How fast something moves AND the direction it moves in.
words.example: The car's velocity was 20 m/s heading north.

words.meaning: How fast something moves, without saying the direction.
words.example: Her running speed was 5 metres per second.

words.meaning: The total length of the path something travels.
words.example: The distance around the oval is 400 metres.

words.meaning: The straight-line distance and direction from the start point to the end point.
words.example: My displacement from the door is 2 metres.

words.meaning: How long something takes, measured in seconds, minutes or hours.
words.example: The trip took a time of 3 hours.

words.meaning: How quickly velocity increases (speeding up).
words.example: The rocket's acceleration pushed us back into our seats.

words.meaning: How quickly velocity decreases (slowing down).
words.example: Braking caused a sharp deceleration.

words.meaning: Where something is located compared to a fixed point.
words.example: Her position is 5 metres from the wall.

words.meaning: The line or course along which something moves (e.g. north, left).
words.example: The wind changed direction suddenly.

words.meaning: The state of moving; a change of position over time.
words.example: The ball was in constant motion.

units.name: Lesson 2 · Graphs & lines

words.meaning: How steep a line is; the slope of a graph.
words.example: A steep gradient means the object is speeding up quickly.

words.meaning: The point where a line crosses an axis of a graph.
words.example: The y-intercept shows the starting position.

words.meaning: Making or relating to a straight line.
words.example: The graph was linear, so the speed stayed constant.

words.meaning: The steepness of a line; another word for gradient.
words.example: The slope of the line tells you the velocity.

words.meaning: Staying the same; not changing.
words.example: Uniform motion means the speed never changes.

words.meaning: Not moving; being still.
words.example: The ball was at rest before I kicked it.

words.meaning: A push or a pull that can change how something moves.
words.example: A force was needed to stop the trolley.

words.meaning: All the input values (x-values) a function can take.
words.example: The domain of the graph is time from 0 to 10 seconds.

words.meaning: A rule that links each input to exactly one output.
words.example: Distance is a function of time.

words.meaning: A function built from different pieces over different intervals.
words.example: The piecewise graph was flat, then sloped upward.

units.name: Lesson 3 · Data, trends & correlation

words.meaning: A quantity that can change or take different values.
words.example: Time is the variable on the horizontal axis.

words.meaning: How strongly two variables are related.
words.example: There is a positive correlation between time and distance.

words.meaning: Greater than zero; going up or to the right.
words.example: A positive gradient means the object moves forward.

words.meaning: Less than zero; going down or to the left.
words.example: A negative velocity means moving backward.

words.meaning: Facts and numbers collected for study.
words.example: We plotted the data on a graph.

words.meaning: To mark points on a graph.
words.example: Plot each point where time meets distance.

words.meaning: A maths statement that two things are equal, using an = sign.
words.example: The equation v = d/t links velocity, distance and time.

words.meaning: To say what will happen before it does, using evidence.
words.example: We can predict the position using the equation.

words.meaning: The general direction that data is heading.
words.example: The upward trend shows the object is speeding up.

units.name: Lesson 4 · Triangles & trigonometry

words.meaning: The amount of turn between two lines, measured in degrees.
words.example: The ramp meets the ground at a 30° angle.

words.meaning: The Greek letter θ, often used to name an unknown angle.
words.example: Find the value of theta in the triangle.

words.meaning: Next to; the side lying beside the angle you are using.
words.example: The adjacent side is next to the angle theta.

words.meaning: Across from; the side facing the angle you are using.
words.example: The opposite side is across from angle theta.

words.meaning: A comparison of two amounts, like 3 to 1.
words.example: Sine is the ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse.

words.meaning: In a right triangle, opposite side divided by hypotenuse.
words.example: Use sine to find the height of the ramp.

words.meaning: In a right triangle, adjacent side divided by hypotenuse.
words.example: Cosine links the adjacent side and the hypotenuse.

words.meaning: In a right triangle, opposite side divided by adjacent side.
words.example: Tangent connects the two shorter sides of the triangle.

words.meaning: At a right angle (90°) to something.
words.example: The wall is perpendicular to the floor.

words.meaning: The longest side of a right triangle, opposite the right angle.
words.example: The hypotenuse is always across from the 90° angle.

units.name: Extra vocab · Acceleration, Energy & Transfer

words.meaning: How quickly the speed or direction of an object changes.
words.example: The car's acceleration was 2 m/s² as it left the traffic lights.

words.meaning: Staying the same all the time; not changing.
words.example: The trolley moved at a constant speed along the flat track.

words.meaning: Describing a relationship where one quantity depends on another quantity multiplied by itself; its graph is a curve.
words.example: Distance against time is a quadratic curve when the acceleration is constant.

words.meaning: Changing by the same amount each step, so the graph is straight.
words.example: The graph of distance against time is linear when the speed is constant.

words.meaning: A line drawn through graph points to show their general pattern.
words.example: Draw a trendline through the points before you find the gradient.

words.meaning: A quantity that has both a size and a direction.
words.example: Velocity is a vector because it tells you the direction as well as the speed.

words.meaning: Greater than zero; in motion, in the direction chosen as forward.
words.example: A positive velocity means the object is moving to the right.

words.meaning: Less than zero; in motion, in the opposite direction to the one chosen as forward.
words.example: A negative acceleration means the object is slowing down while moving forward.

words.meaning: How steep a graph is; the rise divided by the run.
words.example: The slope of a distance-time graph shows the speed.

words.meaning: When two moving objects hit each other.
words.example: The two trolleys stuck together after the collision.

words.meaning: The ability to make things move or change; it is measured in joules.
words.example: The ball's energy changes from stored energy to moving energy as it falls.

words.meaning: The kind of energy an object has because it is moving.
words.example: A faster car has more kinetic energy than a slower car of the same mass.

words.meaning: Caused by the pull of a planet or other large object on things near it.
words.example: A book on a high shelf has gravitational potential energy.

words.meaning: Stored and ready to be used later.
words.example: A stretched spring has potential energy.

words.meaning: The rule that the total amount of energy stays the same; it is never made or destroyed.
words.example: Conservation of energy means the total energy before the collision equals the total after.

words.meaning: To move from one object or place to another.
words.example: Energy is transferred from the hot cup to the cold air.

words.meaning: A group of objects that we choose to study together.
words.example: In this system, the ball and the Earth exchange energy as the ball falls.

words.meaning: About heat.
words.example: Thermal energy moves from the hot tea into the cup.

words.meaning: Able to stretch or squash and then go back to its first shape.
words.example: A rubber band stores elastic potential energy when you stretch it.

words.meaning: Using measured numbers, not descriptions.
words.example: A quantitative result is 4.2 m/s, not 'quite fast'.

units.name: Extra vocab · Kinematics & Motion

words.meaning: Moving, or a change of position over time.
words.example: The motion of the trolley was recorded with a timer.

words.meaning: Where something is, measured from a starting point.
words.example: The position of the runner after 2 s was 10 m from the start.

words.meaning: The total length of the path something travels.
words.example: The runner's distance was 400 m, once around the track.

words.meaning: How far, and in which direction, an object is from where it started.
words.example: After walking 5 m east and then 5 m west, the student's displacement is zero.

words.meaning: How fast something moves, with no direction.
words.example: The speed of the cyclist was 6 m/s.

words.meaning: How fast something moves and in which direction.
words.example: A velocity of 5 m/s north is different from a velocity of 5 m/s south.

words.meaning: Happening at one exact moment.
words.example: The speedometer shows the instantaneous speed of the car.

words.meaning: A middle value found by sharing a total evenly; here, total distance divided by total time.
words.example: The average speed for the whole trip was 20 m/s.

words.meaning: Staying the same all the time; not changing.
words.example: The trolley moved at a constant speed along the flat track.

words.meaning: How steep a line is; the rise divided by the run.
words.example: The gradient of a distance-time graph is the speed.

words.meaning: A diagram that shows how two quantities are related, using points or a line.
words.example: We plotted a graph of distance against time.

words.meaning: The point where a line crosses an axis of a graph.
words.example: The intercept on the y-axis shows the starting position.

words.meaning: A number found by using an instrument, such as a ruler or a timer, with its unit.
words.example: Take three measurements of the time and find the average.

words.meaning: A careful experiment or search to find out how something works.
words.example: In our investigation we tested how the height of the ramp changed the speed.

words.meaning: A factor in an experiment that can change.
words.example: The variable we changed was the mass of the trolley.

words.meaning: In an experiment, the factor that you change on purpose.
words.example: The independent variable was the height of the ramp.

words.meaning: In an experiment, the factor that you measure to see if it changes.
words.example: The dependent variable was the time the trolley took to reach the bottom.

words.meaning: Kept the same on purpose so that the test is fair.
words.example: A controlled variable, such as the length of the track, stays the same.

words.meaning: A simple version, drawing or equation that shows how something works.
words.example: We used a model with constant speed to predict the finish time.

words.meaning: A rule written with letters and symbols, joined by an = sign.
words.example: Use the equation speed = distance ÷ time.

units.name: Cells & Organelles

words.meaning: the smallest living unit that all living things are made of.
words.example: A plant cell has a strong cell wall around it.

words.meaning: relating to cells, or made up of cells.
words.example: Cellular respiration releases energy inside the cell.

words.meaning: the jelly-like fluid inside a cell where the organelles sit and reactions happen.
words.example: The organelles float in the cytoplasm.

words.meaning: the last step of cell division, when the cytoplasm splits to make two separate cells.
words.example: After the nucleus divides, cytokinesis makes two new cells.

words.meaning: in biology: the control centre of a cell, which holds its DNA.
words.example: The nucleus contains the chromosomes.

words.meaning: relating to nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA, which carry genetic information.
words.example: DNA is a nucleic acid.

words.meaning: a long thread of DNA in the nucleus that carries many genes.
words.example: Humans have 46 chromosomes in most cells.

words.meaning: the loose mixture of DNA and protein in the nucleus before it coils into chromosomes.
words.example: Chromatin condenses into chromosomes before mitosis.

words.meaning: the molecule that carries the coded instructions for building and running a living thing.
words.example: DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder.

words.meaning: a section of DNA that carries the instructions for one trait or protein.
words.example: A gene controls whether the pea plant is tall or short.

words.meaning: a large molecule built from amino acids that does most of the work in a cell.
words.example: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions.

words.meaning: the cell structure that reads the genetic message and joins amino acids into a protein.
words.example: Ribosomes build proteins for the cell.

words.meaning: the organelles that release energy from food so the cell can use it.
words.example: Muscle cells contain many mitochondria.

words.meaning: cell division that makes two new cells with exactly the same chromosomes as the parent cell.
words.example: Your skin repairs itself by mitosis.

words.meaning: cell division that halves the chromosome number to make sex cells such as eggs and sperm.
words.example: Meiosis produces four cells with half the chromosomes.

words.meaning: a simple, usually single-celled organism whose DNA is not held inside a nucleus.
words.example: Bacteria are prokaryotes.

words.meaning: an organism whose cells keep their DNA inside a nucleus.
words.example: Plants, animals and fungi are all eukaryotes.

words.meaning: a picture of all of an organism's chromosomes, used to check for problems.
words.example: The karyotype showed an extra chromosome 21.

units.name: Genetics

words.meaning: a feature of a living thing, such as eye colour, that can be passed on to offspring.
words.example: Tongue rolling is a trait controlled by one gene.

words.meaning: to receive a trait from your parents through genes; heredity is this passing on of traits.
words.example: You inherit one allele for each gene from each parent.

words.meaning: passed from parents to their children through genes.
words.example: Haemophilia is a hereditary condition.

words.meaning: a change in the DNA that can make a new version of a gene.
words.example: A mutation created a new eye colour in the flies.

words.meaning: one of the different versions of the same gene.
words.example: The plant carries one tall allele and one short allele.

words.meaning: the set of alleles an organism carries for a trait.
words.example: The genotype Bb gives brown eyes.

words.meaning: the features you can actually see in an organism, produced by its genes and its environment.
words.example: Both BB and Bb give the same phenotype: brown eyes.

words.meaning: having two identical alleles for a gene, such as BB or bb.
words.example: A homozygous recessive plant is short.

words.meaning: having two different alleles for a gene, such as Bb.
words.example: Heterozygous plants are tall but carry the short allele.

parts.meaning: mixed offspring of two different types

words.meaning: the offspring of two parents that carry different alleles or come from different varieties.
words.example: Mendel crossed tall and short peas to make hybrids.

translations.ja: 育てられた/生み出された

words.meaning: having two identical alleles for a trait, so the same allele is always passed on.
words.example: The purebred white flowers always produced white offspring.

words.meaning: the allele that shows in the organism even when only one copy is present.
words.example: Brown eyes are dominant over blue.

words.meaning: an allele that only shows when the organism has two copies of it.
words.example: Blue eyes are recessive, so you need two blue alleles.

words.meaning: a person who carries a recessive allele for a condition but does not show it.
words.example: Both parents were carriers of cystic fibrosis.

words.meaning: how likely an outcome is, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain).
words.example: The probability of a girl is one half.

words.meaning: how possible it is that something will happen; the everyday word for probability.
words.example: There is a 25 percent chance the child has blue eyes.

words.meaning: a comparison of two amounts, like 3 to 1.
words.example: The cross gave a 3 : 1 ratio of tall to short plants.

words.meaning: a number out of 100, written with the % sign.
words.example: 50 percent of the offspring were carriers.

words.meaning: a grid used to work out the possible allele combinations in the offspring of a cross.
words.example: Draw a Punnett square to predict the offspring.

words.meaning: the young produced by a parent or a pair of parents.
words.example: The two tall plants had one short offspring.

words.meaning: all the members of a family line born at the same step, such as the parents or their children.
words.example: The F1 generation were all tall.

words.meaning: having a single set of chromosomes, as an egg or sperm cell does.
words.example: Human gametes are haploid, with 23 chromosomes.

parts.meaning: having a certain number of chromosome sets

words.meaning: having two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent.
words.example: Body cells are diploid.

parts.meaning: mixed offspring of two different types

words.meaning: a genetic cross that follows just one gene, or one pair of contrasting traits.
words.example: A monohybrid cross gives a 3 : 1 ratio.

parts.meaning: mixed offspring of two different types

words.meaning: a genetic cross that follows two different genes at the same time.
words.example: The dihybrid cross tracked seed colour and seed shape.

words.meaning: controlled by many genes working together.
words.example: Human height is polygenic.

words.meaning: An organism that produces offspring. In a Punnett square the parents' alleles are written outside the grid, one parent along the top and one down the side.
words.example: Both parents were carriers, so one in four of their offspring had the recessive trait.

units.name: Ecology & Zoo

words.meaning: the study of how living things interact with each other and with their environment.
words.example: We studied pond ecology on the excursion.

words.meaning: all the living things in an area together with their non-living surroundings, working as one unit.
words.example: A coral reef is a rich ecosystem.

words.meaning: living, or coming from living things.
words.example: Plants and animals are biotic factors.

words.meaning: non-living; abiotic factors include water, light, temperature and soil.
words.example: Temperature is an abiotic factor in the pond.

words.meaning: the natural home of a plant or animal, where it finds food, shelter and space.
words.example: The koala's habitat is eucalypt forest.

words.meaning: everything living and non-living that surrounds an organism.
words.example: Pollution changed the environment of the river.

words.meaning: all the members of one species living in the same place at the same time.
words.example: The kangaroo population fell after the drought.

words.meaning: in ecology: all the different populations living together in one place.
words.example: The forest community includes trees, birds and insects.

words.meaning: a group of similar living things that can breed together and produce fertile young.
words.example: Lions and tigers are different species.

words.meaning: a feature that helps a living thing survive in its environment.
words.example: Thick fur is an adaptation to the cold.

words.meaning: an animal that hunts and eats other animals.
words.example: The owl is a predator of mice.

words.meaning: an animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal.
words.example: Rabbits are the prey of foxes.

words.meaning: an animal that eats only meat.
words.example: A lion is a carnivore.

words.meaning: an animal that eats only plants.
words.example: Cows are herbivores.

words.meaning: an animal that eats both plants and meat.
words.example: Humans and bears are omnivores.

words.meaning: a living thing that makes its own food, such as a plant using sunlight.
words.example: Plants are autotrophs at the start of the food chain.

words.meaning: a living thing that must eat other organisms to get its food.
words.example: All animals are heterotrophs.

words.meaning: a close living relationship between two different species.
words.example: Coral and algae live in symbiosis.

words.meaning: a relationship between two species where both of them benefit.
words.example: Bees and flowers are an example of mutualism.

words.meaning: a relationship where one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.
words.example: Barnacles on a whale show commensalism.

words.meaning: a relationship where one species benefits by harming the other.
words.example: Fleas on a dog are an example of parasitism.

words.meaning: a living thing that lives on or in another organism and harms it while taking its food.
words.example: A tapeworm is a parasite.

words.meaning: the organism that a parasite lives on or in.
words.example: The dog is the host for the tick.

words.meaning: a step in a food chain, showing how far energy has passed from the producers.
words.example: Plants are the first trophic level.

words.meaning: a diagram showing how energy passes from one living thing to the next as food.
words.example: Grass, rabbit and fox make a simple food chain.

words.meaning: a network of connected food chains showing all the feeding links in an ecosystem.
words.example: Draw a food web for the wetland.

words.meaning: the variety of different living species found in an area.
words.example: Clearing the forest reduced its biodiversity.

words.meaning: the scientific study of animals.
words.example: She studied zoology at university.

units.name: Epidemiology / Pandemic Links

words.meaning: an outbreak of a disease that spreads across many countries at the same time.
words.example: COVID-19 became a pandemic in 2020.

words.meaning: a sudden rise in the number of cases of a disease in one area or country.
words.example: There was a measles epidemic in the city.

words.meaning: always present in a particular place or population at a steady level.
words.example: Malaria is endemic in some tropical countries.

words.meaning: any organism or particle that causes disease, such as a virus or bacterium.
words.example: Washing your hands removes pathogens.

words.meaning: a condition that stops the body working normally and makes a person unwell.
words.example: Vaccines protect us from many diseases.

words.meaning: when a pathogen enters the body and multiplies, causing illness.
words.example: The cut became red because of an infection.

words.meaning: caused by a pathogen and able to be passed on to other people.
words.example: Influenza is an infectious disease.

words.meaning: able to spread from person to person, often by close contact.
words.example: Chickenpox is very contagious.

words.meaning: the body's ability to resist a particular infection or disease.
words.example: You gain immunity after a vaccination.

words.meaning: a medicine that trains the immune system to fight a disease before you catch it.
words.example: The flu vaccine is given every year.

words.meaning: the study of populations and how their size and make-up change.
words.example: Demography helps us predict future health needs.

words.meaning: the number of people living in each unit of area, such as people per square kilometre.
words.example: Disease spreads faster where population density is high.

words.meaning: numbers collected from data, and the study of how to collect and understand them.
words.example: The statistics showed cases rising each week.

words.meaning: How fast something changes. A rate is an amount for each unit of time, such as 60 new cases per day.
words.example: The rate of new infections fell from 60 per day to 20 per day.
words.origin: From Latin rata (reckoned, calculated), in the phrase pro rata parte — “according to the calculated part”.

words.meaning: Describing something that makes you believe a wrong thing, even when it does not exactly tell a lie.
words.example: The graph was misleading because the y-axis started at 90, not at 0.

units.name: Biology vocabulary — build the words

words.meaning: the smallest living unit that all living things are made of.
words.example: A plant cell has a strong cell wall around it.

words.meaning: a long thread of DNA in the nucleus that carries many genes.
words.example: Humans have 46 chromosomes in most cells.

words.meaning: the jelly-like fluid inside a cell where the organelles sit and reactions happen.
words.example: The organelles float in the cytoplasm.

words.meaning: the molecule that carries the coded instructions for building and running a living thing.
words.example: DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder.

words.meaning: a section of DNA that carries the instructions for one trait or protein.
words.example: A gene controls whether the pea plant is tall or short.

words.meaning: the set of alleles an organism carries for a trait.

words.meaning: the features you can actually see in an organism, produced by its genes and its environment.

words.meaning: a large molecule built from amino acids that does most of the work in a cell.
words.example: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions.

words.meaning: a feature of a living thing, such as eye colour, that can be passed on to offspring.
words.example: Tongue rolling is a trait controlled by one gene.

words.meaning: a spiral shape, like the twisted ladder shape of DNA.

words.meaning: the passing of traits from parents to their offspring through genes.
words.example: Heredity explains why you look like your parents.

words.meaning: a change in the DNA that can make a new version of a gene.

words.meaning: a small structure inside a cell that does a particular job.

words.meaning: the copying of DNA so that each new cell gets a full set.

words.meaning: the differences between individuals of the same species.

words.meaning: one of the different versions of the same gene.

words.meaning: a person who carries a recessive allele for a condition but does not show it.

words.meaning: having two different alleles for a gene, such as Bb.

words.meaning: having two identical alleles for a gene, such as BB or bb.

words.meaning: the passing of genes, and the traits they control, from parents to offspring.
words.example: We drew a diagram to show the inheritance of eye colour.

words.meaning: the young produced by a parent or a pair of parents.

words.meaning: an allele that only shows when the organism has two copies of it.
