translations.zh-Hans: 用于生产更多财富的资本
translations.zh-Hant: 用於生產更多財富的資本

words.meaning: An economic system based on private ownership and the pursuit of profit.
words.example: Under capitalism the mill owner kept the profits and paid the wages.

words.meaning: A history idea: comparing what stayed the same with what became different over a period.
words.example: Use continuity and change to compare village life in 1750 and in 1850.

translations.vi: tính liên tục và sự thay đổi

words.meaning: The lasting effects an event or period leaves behind for later times.
words.example: One legacy of the Industrial Revolution is the modern city.

translations.vi: di sản của một thời kỳ

units.name: Making a Nation · Set 1: Colonisation and colonial society

words.meaning: One country settling in another territory and taking control of it and its people.
words.example: Colonisation of the continent began at Sydney Cove in 1788.

translations.ja: 植民地化 (しょくみんちか)

words.meaning: All the lands, including the Australian colonies, once ruled or controlled by Britain.
words.example: At its height the British Empire covered a quarter of the world.

words.meaning: A territory that is governed by another country.
words.example: Victoria became a separate colony in 1851.

words.meaning: A colony set up to hold convicts sent from another country.
words.example: New South Wales began as a penal colony.

words.meaning: Taking land and resources away from the people they belong to.
words.example: Dispossession of First Nations land followed each new frontier.

words.meaning: Violent clashes between colonists and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples over land.
words.example: Frontier conflict spread inland as settlers took up grazing runs.

words.meaning: A sudden movement of many people to an area after gold is found there.
words.example: The gold rush tripled Victoria's population in ten years.

translations.ro: a se ghemui/a apăsa în jos

words.meaning: A settler who occupied and used large areas of land, often without legal title.
words.example: A squatter could hold more land than a whole village of farmers.

units.name: Making a Nation · Set 2: Federation and nation-building

words.meaning: The joining of Australia's six separate colonies into one nation in 1901.
words.example: Federation created a national parliament for the first time.

words.meaning: The set of rules and principles that says how a country is governed.
words.example: The Constitution divides power between the states and the Commonwealth.

words.meaning: The official name of the Australian nation created at Federation.
words.example: The Commonwealth of Australia came into being on 1 January 1901.

translations.ps: هغه شی چې باید ترسره شي

words.meaning: A vote in which all the voters decide a single question.
words.example: Changing the Constitution needs a referendum, not just a new law.

words.meaning: Laws brought in soon after Federation that restricted non-European immigration.
words.example: The White Australia Policy shaped who could settle here for seventy years.

words.meaning: Strong pride in and loyalty to your own nation.
words.example: Nationalism grew in the colonies in the years before Federation.

words.meaning: A colony or territory running its own affairs instead of being run from outside.
words.example: The eastern colonies won self-government in the 1850s.

units.name: Making a Nation · Set 3: Immigration and national identity

words.meaning: The movement of people into a country to live there permanently or long-term.
words.example: Post-war immigration brought people to Australia from across Europe.

words.meaning: A past policy that pressured minority and Indigenous groups to drop their own culture.
words.example: Assimilation policies punished children for speaking their own language.

words.meaning: A policy or society that values many different cultures living together.
words.example: Multiculturalism replaced assimilation as government policy in the 1970s.

words.meaning: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children taken from their families under past policies.
words.example: The Stolen Generations were the subject of the 2008 National Apology.

words.meaning: The false legal idea that Australia belonged to nobody before Europeans arrived.
words.example: The Mabo decision overturned terra nullius in 1992.

translations.ur: ٹیرا نولیئس (بے مالک زمین کا نظریہ)

words.meaning: Building a respectful relationship between First Nations and other Australians.
words.example: Reconciliation asks for truth-telling as well as good intentions.

units.name: World War I · Set 1: Causes, outbreak and Australia's involvement

words.meaning: The web of agreements that bound the European powers to defend each other in war.
words.example: The alliance system turned one murder into a continent-wide war.

words.meaning: The belief that a country should build strong armed forces and be ready to use them.
words.example: Militarism drove the great powers into an arms race before 1914.

words.meaning: Extending a country's power by taking colonies or controlling other territories.
words.example: Imperialism put the great powers in competition for the same territories.

words.meaning: The murder of an important public or political figure.
words.example: The assassination in Sarajevo set off the crisis of July 1914.

words.meaning: Getting armed forces ready and moving them into position for war.
words.example: Once mobilisation began, the railway timetables were hard to stop.

translations.zh-Hans: 列表 / 列表 / 列表 lit6 biu2
translations.zh-Hant: 列表 / 列表 / 列表 lit6 biu2

words.meaning: Formally joining the armed forces.
words.example: Enlistment was high in 1914 and fell away after Gallipoli.

words.meaning: The volunteer army Australia raised to fight overseas in World War I.
words.example: Every soldier in the Australian Imperial Force (AIF) was a volunteer.

translations.ja: オーストラリア帝国軍

words.meaning: The 1915 campaign on a Turkish peninsula where Australian and New Zealand troops suffered heavy losses.
words.example: The landing at Gallipoli is remembered every 25 April.

words.meaning: The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, and the soldiers who served in it.
words.example: ANZAC stands for Australian and New Zealand Army Corps.

words.meaning: The main line of fighting between Allied and German forces in France and Belgium.
words.example: Most Australian casualties came on the Western Front, not at Gallipoli.

units.name: World War I · Set 2: Australia's home front

words.meaning: The civilian side of a country during a war, away from the fighting.
words.example: On the home front, women took over jobs the soldiers had left.

words.meaning: Forcing people by law to serve in the armed forces.
words.example: Conscription applied at home, but never to overseas service in this war.

words.meaning: The bitter argument and two failed votes, in 1916 and 1917, on compulsory overseas service.
words.example: Both times the conscription referendum went to the voters, it was defeated.

translations.ja: 徴兵制をめぐる国民投票
translations.vi: cuộc trưng cầu dân ý về quân dịch

words.meaning: Official limits on how much of a scarce good each person may buy.
words.example: Rationing kept sugar and meat on the shelves for everyone.

translations.vi: chế độ phân phối định lượng

words.meaning: Persuading and signing up people to join the armed forces.
words.example: Recruitment marches went from town to town looking for volunteers.

words.meaning: Biased or misleading information spread to promote a cause, especially in wartime.
words.example: Wartime propaganda made the enemy look monstrous and the cause look simple.

words.meaning: A person who chooses to serve without being forced to.
words.example: Every Australian who served overseas in this war was a volunteer.

words.meaning: A person killed, wounded, captured or missing as a result of war.
words.example: One battalion reported three hundred casualties in a single morning.

words.meaning: A soldier who has come home from active service.
words.example: Every returned serviceman was promised help finding work.

units.name: World War I · Set 3: Women on the WWI home front

words.meaning: The paid and unpaid jobs women took on at home to support the war effort.
words.example: Home-front roles ranged from filling shells to knitting socks.

words.meaning: Weapons and military supplies, especially ammunition.
words.example: Factories switched from making kettles to making munitions.

words.meaning: A person employed making weapons and ammunition, often a woman during this war.
words.example: A munitions worker filled shells with explosive for twelve hours a day.

translations.vi: công nhân nhà máy đạn dược

words.meaning: A nickname for British women munitions workers whose skin turned yellow from TNT.
words.example: The newspapers called them canary girls because of the stain on their hands.

words.meaning: A humanitarian organisation that gave medical and practical help to soldiers and families.
words.example: The Red Cross packed parcels for prisoners of war.

words.meaning: Knitted and packed items such as socks, food and clothing sent out to soldiers.
words.example: Country branches sewed and packed comforts every week.

words.meaning: Organising activities to collect money for a cause.
words.example: Fundraising fetes paid for ambulances and hospital beds.

words.meaning: A feather handed to a man to accuse him of cowardice for not enlisting.
words.example: Some women handed a white feather to any young man not in uniform.

words.meaning: Being given the right to vote.
words.example: War work strengthened the argument for the enfranchisement of women in Britain.

translations.vi: việc được trao quyền bầu cử

words.meaning: A moment historians judge to have changed the direction of events.
words.example: Was the war a turning point for women's work, or only a pause?

words.meaning: A history idea: working out what altered and what stayed the same across a period.
words.example: Judge change and continuity by comparing women's jobs in 1913 and in 1920.

translations.vi: sự thay đổi và tính liên tục

units.name: World War I · Set 4: Repatriation and Australia after the war

words.meaning: The agreement to stop fighting, signed on 11 November 1918, that ended the war.
words.example: News of the Armistice brought crowds into the streets.

words.meaning: Bringing soldiers or other people home to their own country after a war.
words.example: Repatriation of the whole force took more than a year.

words.meaning: Releasing soldiers from military service and returning them to civilian life.
words.example: Demobilisation put thousands of men into a job market with no jobs.

words.meaning: Keeping people or goods apart from others to stop a disease spreading.
words.example: Returning troopships were held in quarantine outside the harbour.

words.meaning: An outbreak of disease that spreads across many countries or the whole world.
words.example: The influenza pandemic of 1919 killed more Australians than Gallipoli.

words.meaning: A treatment such as a vaccination, given to protect a person against a disease.
words.example: Inoculation was offered to soldiers before they boarded the ship home.

words.meaning: A government program after the war that gave returned soldiers land to farm.
words.example: Many blocks in the Soldier Settlement Scheme were too small to live on.

translations.vi: Chương trình định cư cho binh sĩ
translations.tl: Programa sa Paninirahan ng mga Sundalo

words.meaning: Something built to honour and remember those who served or died in a war.
words.example: Almost every country town in Victoria has its own war memorial.

words.meaning: A burial ground for soldiers killed in a conflict, often near where they fought.
words.example: The war cemetery holds headstones in long, even rows.

units.name: World War I · CAT 3: Significance and historical argument

words.meaning: A judgement of how important an event was, based on its impact and how long it lasted.
words.example: Argue the historical significance of Gallipoli; do not just retell the landing.

words.meaning: The overall argument or position a piece of writing sets out to prove.
words.example: State your contention in the first paragraph, then defend it.

words.meaning: Evidence created at the time of an event by someone who was there.
words.example: A soldier's diary is a primary source; a textbook chapter is not.

words.meaning: A later account or analysis of an event, built from other evidence.
words.example: Use a secondary source to check what your primary source leaves out.

words.meaning: The particular interpretation a historian brings to their account of the past.
words.example: Two accounts of the same battle can differ because of the historian's viewpoint.

translations.vi: quan điểm của nhà sử học

words.meaning: An effect felt soon after an event.
words.example: One short-term impact of enlistment was a shortage of farm workers.

words.meaning: An effect that is still felt long after an event.
words.example: The long-term impact of the war can be read in every town's memorial.

words.meaning: Facts, data or source material used to support an argument.
words.example: Every point in a paragraph needs evidence, not just an opinion.

words.meaning: Explaining what evidence means and why it matters, rather than just describing it.
words.example: Add analysis after the evidence: say what it proves about your contention.

units.name: The Holocaust · Set 1: Nazi ideology and rise to power

words.meaning: The ideology of the National Socialist party in Germany, built on extreme nationalism and racism.
words.example: Nazism promised order and blamed minorities for Germany's problems.

words.meaning: The leader of Nazi Germany from 1933 to 1945.
words.example: Adolf Hitler was appointed Chancellor in January 1933.

words.meaning: A system of government in which the state controls both public and private life.
words.example: Under totalitarianism there is no legal opposition and no free press.

words.meaning: An authoritarian, extremely nationalist political system that crushes opposition.
words.example: Fascism took power in Italy before it took power in Germany.

words.meaning: Hostility towards or prejudice against Jewish people.
words.example: Nazi antisemitism moved from insults to laws to violence.

words.meaning: Nazi films, posters and radio used to spread hateful ideas and build support for the regime.
words.example: Nazi propaganda repeated the same few images until they felt like facts.

translations.ja: ナチスのプロパガンダ
translations.vi: tuyên truyền của Đức Quốc xã

words.meaning: Laws of 1935 that took German citizenship and rights away from Jewish people.
words.example: The Nuremberg Laws made discrimination part of the legal system.

units.name: The Holocaust · Set 2: Persecution, ghettos and the path to genocide

words.meaning: Hostile and unfair treatment of a person or group, usually because of who they are.
words.example: Persecution began with boycotts and ended in the camps.

words.meaning: A walled-off part of a city where Jewish people were forced to live under Nazi rule.
words.example: Families were moved into the ghetto and the gates were closed behind them.

words.meaning: Treating a person or group unfairly because of who they are.
words.example: Discrimination was written into German law after 1935.

words.meaning: The November 1938 night of organised Nazi violence against Jewish people and their property.
words.example: After Kristallnacht, thousands of Jewish men were arrested.

words.meaning: The deliberate, planned destruction of a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
words.example: Genocide is a crime under international law.

words.meaning: A camp where the Nazis imprisoned people, usually under brutal conditions.
words.example: Political opponents were sent to a concentration camp before the war began.

words.meaning: A camp built by the Nazis for the single purpose of mass killing.
words.example: An extermination camp was built for killing, not for holding prisoners.

units.name: The Holocaust · Set 3: The Holocaust, resistance and memory

words.meaning: The Nazi murder of about six million Jewish people and millions of others during WWII.
words.example: The Holocaust is studied so that its warning signs are recognised.

words.meaning: The forced removal of people from a country or area, often to the camps.
words.example: Deportation trains left the ghetto week after week.

words.meaning: Acts, large or small, by which people opposed or defied Nazi persecution.
words.example: Hiding a neighbour was resistance, and it carried a death sentence.

parts.meaning: state or result of (makes a noun)

translations.es: estado o resultado de (forma un sustantivo)
translations.vi: trạng thái hoặc kết quả (tạo danh từ)

words.meaning: A first-hand account given by someone who lived through the Holocaust.
words.example: Survivor testimony is a primary source that historians treat with great care.

translations.vi: lời kể của người sống sót
translations.ur: زندہ بچ جانے والے کی گواہی

words.meaning: The freeing of people held captive, such as camp prisoners at the end of the war.
words.example: Soldiers who filmed the liberation wanted the world to have proof.

words.meaning: A ceremony or act that remembers and honours victims or events.
words.example: Commemoration keeps the names, not just the numbers.

words.meaning: A phrase expressing the promise that genocide must never be allowed to happen again.
words.example: Never Again is a promise that each generation has to keep.

units.name: Humanities Skills · Essay writing structure

words.meaning: The main claim or position an essay sets out to prove.
words.example: Your contention should answer the question in one clear sentence.

words.meaning: A three-step plan for an introduction: background, argument, then main points.
words.example: Use BAM so your introduction says what the whole essay will argue.

translations.vi: BAM (bối cảnh, luận điểm, ý chính)
translations.ur: بی اے ایم (پس منظر، دلیل، اہم نکات)

words.meaning: A four-step plan for a body paragraph: topic sentence, evidence, analysis, link.
words.example: Check every paragraph against TEAL before you hand the essay in.

translations.ja: TEAL（主題文・根拠・分析・連結）
translations.vi: TEAL (câu chủ đề, bằng chứng, phân tích, liên kết)
translations.ur: ٹی ای اے ایل (موضوعی جملہ، شواہد، تجزیہ، ربط)
translations.am: ቲኤኤል (ርዕሰ ዓረፍተ ነገር፣ ማስረጃ፣ ትንተና፣ ማገናኛ)

words.meaning: The opening sentence of a paragraph, which states its main idea.
words.example: A topic sentence should name the idea, not the source.

translations.ja: トピックセンテンス（主題文）

words.meaning: A set phrase used to begin a sentence, for example to introduce evidence.
words.example: Keep a list of sentence starters for introducing evidence and for linking back.

words.meaning: Explaining history by linking what happened to what made it happen.
words.example: Show cause and effect: militarism built the armies that made war possible.

words.meaning: A linking word such as however or therefore that shows how two ideas relate.
words.example: A transition word tells the reader whether you are adding or disagreeing.

words.meaning: How smoothly and logically the ideas in a piece of writing hold together.
words.example: Cohesion comes from linking words and from repeating your key terms.

units.name: Humanities Skills · Historical inquiry and source analysis

words.meaning: Any material, such as a document, image or object, used as evidence about the past.
words.example: Name the source before you say what it shows.

words.meaning: Evidence created at the time of an event by someone who was present.
words.example: A recruitment poster from 1915 is a primary source.

words.meaning: An account of an event written later, using other evidence.
words.example: Your textbook is a secondary source about the war.

words.meaning: A one-sided view that favours one side of an issue.
words.example: Bias does not make a source useless; it makes it useful in a different way.

words.meaning: The viewpoint of one particular person or group.
words.example: A soldier's letter and a general's report give two perspectives on one day.

words.meaning: How far a source can be trusted, judging by who created it and why.
words.example: Test reliability by asking who made the source and who it was made for.

words.meaning: To support a claim by checking it against another, independent source.
words.example: Corroborate the diary with a newspaper report from the same week.

words.meaning: The guiding question that directs a piece of historical research.
words.example: A good inquiry question can be answered with evidence, not with an opinion.

words.meaning: Comparing what stayed the same with what became different across a period of time.
words.example: Continuity and change works best when you compare two fixed dates.

translations.vi: tính liên tục và sự thay đổi

words.meaning: Working out what led to an event and what followed from it.
words.example: Separate cause and consequence: one comes before the event, one after.

units.name: Humanities Skills · Geographic, civic and economic concepts

words.meaning: Using resources so that today's needs are met without harming future generations.
words.example: Sustainability asks what a decision costs the people who come after us.

words.meaning: The way people, places and environments are linked and affect one another.
words.example: Interconnection explains how a drought in one place raises food prices in another.

words.meaning: The natural surroundings in which people, plants and animals live.
words.example: Every land-use decision changes the environment somehow.

words.meaning: A particular part of the Earth's surface, known by its natural and human features.
words.example: Describe the place using both its landforms and its people.

words.meaning: The level at which a geographic issue is examined, from local to global.
words.example: Change the scale and the same problem can look solved or hopeless.

translations.vi: thành viên của một quốc gia

words.meaning: Taking part responsibly in community life and in democratic processes.
words.example: Active citizenship is more than voting once every three years.

words.meaning: Taking part in activities that support public life, such as voting or volunteering.
words.example: Civic participation can start with a petition to the local council.

translations.vi: sự tham gia của công dân

words.meaning: How comfortable, healthy and well-off people are, judged by income and quality of life.
words.example: A rising standard of living is not the same thing as a fairer society.

words.meaning: Giving up one thing in order to gain another, especially in an economic choice.
words.example: Every budget is a trade-off between spending now and saving for later.

units.name: Analysing a text

words.meaning: The main character of a story, whose choices drive what happens.
words.example: The protagonist of the novel is a fifteen-year-old girl who refuses to give up.

words.meaning: The character or force that works against the protagonist.
words.example: The antagonist is not evil — he simply wants the same thing as the hero.

words.meaning: The way a writer builds a character, through actions, speech, thoughts and description.
words.example: Notice how the characterisation of the father changes after chapter six.

words.meaning: The voice that tells the story to the reader.
words.example: The narrator is a child, so we only see what a child would notice.

words.meaning: All-knowing — an omniscient narrator knows every character's thoughts.
words.example: An omniscient narrator tells us what both brothers are thinking.

words.meaning: Clues placed early in a text that hint at what will happen later.
words.example: The broken clock on the first page is foreshadowing the accident.

words.meaning: A scene that jumps back to something that happened before the main story.
words.example: The flashback explains why the family left their village.

words.meaning: Using an object or image to stand for a bigger idea.
words.example: The symbolism of the caged bird suggests she is not free.

words.meaning: An image, idea or word that keeps coming back through a whole text.
words.example: Water is a motif in this novel: it appears in almost every chapter.

words.meaning: Placing two very different things side by side so the difference stands out.
words.example: The juxtaposition of the party and the funeral makes both scenes stronger.

words.meaning: The feelings and ideas a word suggests, beyond its dictionary meaning.
words.example: 'Cheap' and 'affordable' cost the same, but 'cheap' has a negative connotation.

words.meaning: The plain dictionary meaning of a word, with no extra feeling attached.
words.example: The denotation of 'home' is simply a place where someone lives.

words.meaning: The feeling that a place or scene creates for the reader.
words.example: The rain and the empty streets build a lonely atmosphere.

words.meaning: The big idea about life that a text explores.
words.example: One theme of the novel is that belonging can be chosen, not inherited.

words.meaning: The most tense moment of a story, where the main problem comes to a head.
words.example: The climax comes when she finally opens the letter.

words.meaning: A conclusion you work out from clues, because the text does not say it directly.
words.example: We make the inference that he is frightened, because his hands are shaking.

units.name: Persuasion and argument

words.meaning: The art of using language to persuade an audience.
words.example: The speech is full of rhetoric designed to make the crowd angry.

words.meaning: A question asked for effect, where no answer is expected.
words.example: 'Do we really want dirty beaches?' is a rhetorical question.

words.meaning: The main point of view a writer or speaker is arguing for.
words.example: Her contention is that the school day should start later.

words.meaning: A short personal story used to make a point feel real.
words.example: He opens with an anecdote about his own first day in Australia.

words.meaning: How believable and trustworthy a writer or speaker seems.
words.example: Quoting a doctor gives the article more credibility.

words.meaning: Deliberate exaggeration for effect, not meant to be taken literally.
words.example: 'This will destroy our city forever' is hyperbole.

words.meaning: Chosen to stir strong feelings in the reader.
words.example: Emotive language like 'innocent children' makes us feel protective.

words.meaning: Making the reader feel part of the same group as the writer.
words.example: Inclusive words like 'we' and 'our community' pull the reader in.

words.meaning: A reply that argues against the other side's point.
words.example: Her rebuttal shows why the cost argument does not hold up.

words.meaning: Unfairly favouring one side instead of treating both fairly.
words.example: The article shows bias, because it only quotes people who agree.

words.meaning: A broad claim about a whole group, made from very little evidence.
words.example: 'Teenagers never listen' is a generalisation.

words.meaning: Saying the same word or phrase again so that it sticks in the mind.
words.example: The repetition of 'not fair' hammers the point home.

words.meaning: An argument put forward against your own position.
words.example: A strong essay answers the counterargument instead of ignoring it.

words.meaning: A move in an argument that targets the reader's feelings or values.
words.example: The photograph of the puppy is an appeal to our sympathy.

words.meaning: The act of getting someone to agree with you or to do something.
words.example: Advertising is persuasion with pictures as well as words.

words.meaning: The attitude a writer's voice shows — angry, calm, joking or serious.
words.example: The tone becomes sarcastic in the third paragraph.

units.name: Poetry

words.meaning: A group of lines in a poem, set apart by a space — like a paragraph.
words.example: The mood of the poem changes in the final stanza.

words.meaning: Language that builds pictures, sounds or smells in the reader's mind.
words.example: The imagery of dust and cracked earth makes you feel the drought.

words.meaning: Saying that one thing IS another, to show something about it.
words.example: 'Her voice was thunder' is a metaphor.

words.meaning: A comparison of two things using 'like' or 'as'.
words.example: 'Quiet as a closed door' is a simile.

words.meaning: Giving human qualities to something that is not human.
words.example: 'The wind argued with the trees' is personification.

words.meaning: Repeating the same beginning sound in words that are close together.
words.example: 'Silver stars slipped' uses alliteration.

words.meaning: Repeating the same vowel sound inside nearby words.
words.example: 'Deep green sea' uses assonance.

words.meaning: A word that sounds like the noise it names.
words.example: 'Buzz', 'crash' and 'hiss' are onomatopoeia.

words.meaning: When a sentence steps over the end of one line and continues on the next.
words.example: The enjambment makes you read on quickly, without stopping.

words.meaning: A poem of fourteen lines with a set rhyme pattern.
words.example: Shakespeare's sonnet ends with two rhyming lines.

words.meaning: The beat you can hear in a line of poetry when you read it aloud.
words.example: The rhythm speeds up in the last two lines.

words.meaning: Matching sounds at the ends of words, often at the ends of lines.
words.example: The rhyme at the end of every second line ties the poem together.

words.meaning: Poetry written with no fixed rhyme pattern and no regular beat.
words.example: The poem is free verse, so the lines can be any length.

words.meaning: A line or group of lines repeated through a poem or song.
words.example: The refrain comes back after every stanza.

words.meaning: The feeling a poem creates in the reader.
words.example: Short lines and dark words create a tense mood.

units.name: Film and media

words.meaning: The art of filming: what the camera does with movement, light and framing.
words.example: The cinematography keeps the character small inside a huge landscape.

words.meaning: A series of short shots edited together to show time passing or one idea.
words.example: A training montage shows months of work in thirty seconds.

words.meaning: A shot taken very near the subject, usually a person's face.
words.example: The close-up on her eyes shows fear without any dialogue.

words.meaning: The position the camera films from, which changes how we see a character.
words.example: A low camera angle makes the villain look powerful.

words.meaning: How a shot is arranged: what is included, what is left out, and where.
words.example: The framing puts the fence right between the two friends.

words.meaning: How light and shadow are used in a shot to create a feeling.
words.example: Harsh lighting makes the hospital scene feel cold.

words.meaning: All the music and sound that goes with the images in a film.
words.example: The soundtrack goes silent just before the crash.

words.meaning: A voice we hear over the images, spoken by someone we cannot see.
words.example: The voiceover tells us what the character is really thinking.

words.meaning: The way a text shows a group, a place or an idea to its audience.
words.example: The film's representation of teenagers is not very fair.

words.meaning: A fixed, over-simple idea about what everyone in a group is like.
words.example: The clever scientist with thick glasses is a tired stereotype.

words.meaning: A film that sets out to show real people and real events.
words.example: The documentary follows one family for a whole year.

words.meaning: The people a text is made for.
words.example: This advertisement's audience is clearly teenage boys.

words.meaning: A type of text with its own familiar features — horror, comedy, romance.
words.example: You can name the genre from the first scene: it is a thriller.

words.meaning: A text made to sell something or to change what people do.
words.example: We analysed an advertisement for a mobile phone.

words.meaning: The channels that carry information to large numbers of people.
words.example: The media reported the same story in very different ways.

units.name: Creative writing

words.meaning: The opening of a story, where the reader meets the characters, place and time.
words.example: Keep the orientation short: two sentences can set the whole scene.

words.meaning: The problem that upsets things and gets the story moving.
words.example: The complication starts when the bus never arrives.

words.meaning: The ending, where the problem is sorted out in some way.
words.example: Your resolution does not have to be happy, but it must feel earned.

words.meaning: The order of events in a story, and how each one leads to the next.
words.example: Plan your plot before you write the first draft.

words.meaning: The words that characters speak to each other.
words.example: Good dialogue shows us who a character is without explaining.

words.meaning: A long speech by one character, alone or to other people.
words.example: She wrote a monologue in the voice of the younger sister.

words.meaning: Language used for the picture it makes, not its literal meaning.
words.example: 'Drowning in homework' is figurative, not literal.

words.meaning: Full of detail, so the reader can see, hear or feel the scene.
words.example: Add descriptive detail about the smell of the kitchen.

words.meaning: Writing an early version that you expect to change later.
words.example: Spend one lesson drafting and the next lesson improving it.

words.meaning: Going back over your writing to improve the ideas, order and wording.
words.example: In revision she cut the whole first paragraph.

words.meaning: The last check of a piece of writing for spelling and punctuation mistakes.
words.example: Leave five minutes for proofreading before you hand it in.

words.meaning: An ending that stops at a tense moment, so the reader must keep going.
words.example: End the chapter on a cliffhanger.

words.meaning: The nervous feeling of not knowing what will happen next.
words.example: Short sentences build suspense.

words.meaning: How well the parts of a piece of writing hold together.
words.example: Linking words give a paragraph coherence.

words.meaning: So clear and strong that it feels alive to the reader.
words.example: One vivid detail is worth three ordinary ones.

units.name: The Curious Incident · speaking words

words.meaning: What a text makes you think or feel, and why.
words.example: My personal response is that it's sad, because …

words.meaning: Give a reason that shows your view is fair.
words.example: Justify that. Where does the book say so?

words.meaning: The words or facts you point to when you back up what you say.
words.example: What would count as evidence for that?

words.meaning: Say someone's idea again in your own words.
words.example: So you think he'd rather be accurate than kind.

translations.vi: diễn giải lại bằng lời riêng

words.meaning: Work out what someone means from the clues, without being told.
words.example: I infer from that that you think he's lying.

words.meaning: Suggest something without saying it directly.
words.example: You're implying she had no choice.

words.meaning: Put an idea in a different way so it can be seen differently.
words.example: Do you mean a good father overall, or good at the daily stuff?

words.meaning: Admit that part of the other side's point is true.
words.example: Fair, he does look after him. I still say the lie is too big.

words.meaning: Add detail or an example to an idea.
words.example: Can you elaborate? What makes it calm?

words.meaning: Speaking one at a time and handing the talk on.
words.example: Your turn, Mia. What did you think?

words.meaning: How formal or casual your speaking is, matched to who is listening.
words.example: Same idea, but in the register you'd use to the class.

translations.vi: mức trang trọng của lời nói

units.name: The Curious Incident · Chapters 2 to 37

words.meaning: Saying one thing is another thing to show what it is like.
words.example: This means that the word metaphor is a metaphor.

words.meaning: Close to, but not exactly.
words.example: Mr Jeavons wears brown shoes that have approximately 60 tiny circular holes in each of them.

words.meaning: Loyal; staying true to someone.
words.example: Also, dogs are faithful and they do not tell lies because they cannot talk.

words.meaning: A senior police officer; someone whose job is to look closely at things.
words.example: He was an inspector. I could tell because he wasn't wearing a uniform.

words.meaning: Exactly.
words.example: And what, precisely, were you doing in the garden?

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Completely tired; used up.
words.example: Drawn has three meanings: drawn with a pencil, exhausted, and pulled across.

words.meaning: A person who kills someone on purpose.
words.example: In a murder mystery novel someone has to work out who the murderer is and then catch them.

words.meaning: Everything that exists: all of space and everything in it.
words.example: Prime numbers are like life. They are very logical but you could never work out the rules, even if you spent all your time thinking about them.

units.name: The Curious Incident · Chapters 41 to 73

words.meaning: A person you do not know.
words.example: I don't like talking to strangers. This is not because of Stranger Danger.

words.meaning: A person who finds out who did something by looking for clues.
words.example: Then I decided to do some detective work.

words.meaning: Making you think something is wrong; not to be trusted.
words.example: I asked if she had seen anything suspicious on Thursday evening which might be a clue.

words.meaning: A careful search to find out the truth.
words.example: Thank you for helping me with my investigation.

words.meaning: Very bad; shocking.
words.example: I heard about it yesterday. Dreadful. Dreadful.

words.meaning: Friendly talk that is not questions and answers.
words.example: Mrs Alexander was doing what is called chatting, where people say things to each other which aren't questions and answers and aren't connected.

words.meaning: A disagreement, or a reason given for a view.
words.example: Especially if those things were numbers or an argument.

words.meaning: To do with the way a person acts.
words.example: This was because of the stress of looking after someone who has Behavioural Problems like I have.

units.name: The Curious Incident · Chapters 79 to 109

translations.fa: نگاه کردن یا در نظر گرفتن
translations.ps: کتل یا په پام کې نیول

words.meaning: Knowing something by feeling, without working it out.
words.example: But if you use your intuition you think that chance is 50-50.

words.meaning: Silly enough to laugh at.
words.example: You are to stop this ridiculous bloody detective game right now.

words.meaning: Clever; quick to understand.
words.example: To be a good astronaut you have to be intelligent and I'm intelligent.

words.meaning: Simple; easy to follow.
words.example: These problems were difficult and interesting but there was always a straightforward answer at the end.

words.meaning: Going onto someone's land without permission.
words.example: You are not to go trespassing in other people's gardens.

words.meaning: Beyond what nature can explain; ghostly.
words.example: This means that the Hound of the Baskervilles is not a supernatural being but a real dog.

words.meaning: Talk between two or more people.
words.example: I find it hard to have a conversation with people I don't know.

words.meaning: Sad because you are away from home.
words.example: You have to be someone who would like being on their own in a tiny spacecraft thousands of miles away, and not get homesick.

units.name: The Curious Incident · Chapters 113 to 151

words.meaning: A question asked for effect, not for an answer.
words.example: How stupid are you? This is what Siobhan says is called a rhetorical question.

words.meaning: Imagined as a possibility, not real.
words.example: This graph is hypothetical. It doesn't show real frogs.

words.meaning: Being shown or uncovered; in a camera, letting light in.
words.example: Harold Snelling, who was an expert in fake photography, said the figures showed movement during the exposure.

words.meaning: Stopped someone in the middle of speaking.
words.example: But Father interrupted me and said, 'Don't give me that.'

words.meaning: Afraid.
words.example: And Siobhan asked if I was frightened about going home, and I said I wasn't.

words.meaning: Found out something that was hidden.
words.example: My book was where I had kept all the clues that I had discovered.

words.meaning: All the animals or people living in a place.
words.example: Here is a formula for a population of animals.

words.meaning: Things that cannot be explained yet.
words.example: Lots of things are mysteries. But that doesn't mean there isn't an answer to them.

units.name: The Curious Incident · Chapters 157 to 179

words.meaning: A little person; the imagined 'self' inside the head.
words.example: They think that this person is their special human mind, which is called a homunculus, which means a little man.

translations.ja: ホムンクルス（頭の中の小人）
translations.vi: người tí hon (cái 'tôi' tưởng tượng trong đầu)
translations.ur: ننھا انسان (ذہن میں تصور کیا گیا 'میں')
translations.ps: وړوکی سړی (په سر کې انګېرل شوی 'ځان')
translations.fr: petit homme (le « moi » imaginé dans la tête)
translations.es: hombrecillo (el 'yo' imaginado dentro de la cabeza)

words.meaning: A choice made after thinking.
words.example: I did this by thinking of all the things I could do and deciding whether they were the right decision or not.

words.meaning: A test done to find something out.
words.example: You can tell this because of an experiment which I saw on TV in a series called How the Mind Works.

words.meaning: Made of many parts; hard to understand.
words.example: But the mind is just a complicated machine.

words.meaning: A sudden danger that needs action now.
words.example: Father got a phone call from a lady whose cellar had flooded and he had to go out and fix it because it was an emergency.

words.meaning: In the end, after a long time.
words.example: Eventually he got really cross and he told me I was being stupid.

words.meaning: Write your answer as a formula or expression using the letters you are given.
words.example: Express the perimeter in terms of x.

words.meaning: Change something into the form the question asks for. 'Write as' means the same.
words.example: Express 0.35 as a percentage.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Command and instruction words (2)

words.meaning: Work out or find an answer, usually by a method you have to show.
words.example: Determine the size of the missing angle.

translations.zh-Hans: 解决 / 解決 / 解決 gaai2 kyut3
translations.zh-Hant: 解決 / 解決 / 解決 gaai2 kyut3

words.meaning: Find the value or values that make an equation or inequality true.
words.example: Solve 2x − 7 = 11.

words.meaning: Obtain a rule or formula by reasoning through the steps.
words.example: Derive a formula for the number of matchsticks in pattern n.

words.meaning: Change the way a formula is written, usually so a different letter is on its own.
words.example: Rearrange A = lw to make w the subject.

words.meaning: Write the answer down directly; you do not need to show working.
words.example: State the coordinates of the origin.

words.meaning: Give an answer straight away, without full working.
words.example: Write down the highest common factor of 12 and 18.

words.meaning: Prove that a given statement is true by working through the steps.
words.example: Show that the three angles of this triangle add to 180°.

words.meaning: Use logical steps to show that something is always true, not just true once.
words.example: Prove that the sum of two even numbers is always even.

words.meaning: Explain in words what you notice, or what a shape, graph or pattern looks like.
words.example: Describe the pattern in the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15.

words.meaning: Explain what a graph, table or set of data actually means.
words.example: Interpret what the steep part of the travel graph tells you.

words.meaning: Sort things into groups according to their properties.
words.example: Classify each triangle as scalene, isosceles or equilateral.

words.meaning: Fill in the missing parts of a table, a sentence or a diagram.
words.example: Complete the table of values for y = 2x + 1.

words.meaning: Change a quantity from one unit or form into another.
words.example: Convert 250 cm into metres.

words.meaning: Pick out and name the correct part, feature or answer.
words.example: Identify the coefficient in the term 7x.

words.meaning: Say how two or more things are the same and how they differ, often using numbers.
words.example: Compare the mean and the median of the two data sets.

words.meaning: Represent a real situation using maths — a diagram, an equation or a graph.
words.example: Model the phone plan with the equation C = 20 + 0.5n.

words.meaning: Explore a maths problem by trying examples and looking for a pattern.
words.example: Investigate what happens to the area when you double the side length.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Everyday words with a different maths meaning (1)

words.meaning: In maths, an organised grid of rows and columns showing data or values — not furniture.
words.example: Complete the table of values before you plot the points.

words.meaning: In maths, how many times a number is multiplied by itself — not strength or electricity.
words.example: In 5³ the power is 3, so 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.

words.meaning: In maths, a number that multiplied by itself a set number of times gives another number — not part of a plant.
words.example: The square root of 49 is 7.

words.meaning: In maths, the answer when you multiply numbers together — not a thing made to be sold.
words.example: The product of 6 and 7 is 42.

words.meaning: In maths, the answer when one number is subtracted from another — not just how two things are unalike.
words.example: The difference between −3 and 5 is 8.

words.meaning: In maths, the answer when numbers are added together — not an amount of money.
words.example: The sum of 12, 8 and 5 is 25.

words.meaning: In maths, the average: add all the values and divide by how many there are — not 'unkind'.
words.example: Find the mean of 4, 6, 8 and 10.

words.meaning: In maths, a whole number that cannot be divided evenly by 2 — not 'strange'.
words.example: 7, 9 and 11 are odd numbers.

words.meaning: In maths, a whole number that can be divided evenly by 2 — not 'level' or 'fair'.
words.example: Every even number ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

words.meaning: In maths, the number raised to a power, or the bottom side of a shape — not just the bottom of something.
words.example: In 5³ the base is 5 and the index is 3.

words.meaning: In maths, a flat surface on a 3D shape — not the front of your head.
words.example: A cube has six square faces.

words.meaning: In maths, the amount of space a 3D shape takes up, measured in cubic units — not loudness.
words.example: Find the volume of a box 3 cm by 4 cm by 5 cm.

words.meaning: In maths, a unit for measuring the size of an angle — not a university qualification.
words.example: A right angle measures 90 degrees.

words.meaning: In maths, one part of an expression, separated by a plus or minus sign — not part of the school year.
words.example: How many terms are in 3x + 2y − 5?

words.meaning: In maths, a group of numbers, letters and signs with no equals sign — not a look on a face.
words.example: Simplify the expression 4x + 2x.

words.meaning: In maths, exactly the same shape but a different size, with matching angles — not just 'alike'.
words.example: The two triangles are similar, so their sides are in the same ratio.

words.meaning: In maths, a whole number greater than 1 with exactly two factors, itself and 1 — not 'excellent'.
words.example: 13 is prime because only 1 and 13 divide into it.

words.meaning: In maths, a whole number that divides evenly into another number — not just something that affects a result.
words.example: The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.

words.meaning: In maths, the small raised number showing how many times the base is multiplied by itself — not a list in a book.
words.example: In 2⁵ the index is 5, and the plural of index is indices.

words.meaning: In maths, the point (0, 0) where the x-axis and the y-axis cross — not where something came from.
words.example: The line y = 4x passes through the origin.

words.meaning: In maths, a flat surface that keeps going in every direction — not an aeroplane.
words.example: Plot the point (−2, 3) on the number plane.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Everyday words with a different maths meaning (2)

words.meaning: In maths, a transformation that flips a shape over a line, like a mirror image — not a thought.
words.example: Draw the reflection of the triangle in the y-axis.

words.meaning: In maths, a transformation that turns a shape around a fixed point by a given angle — not just spinning.
words.example: Describe the rotation that maps shape A onto shape B.

words.meaning: In maths, a transformation that slides a shape without turning or flipping it — not changing language.
words.example: The translation moves every point 3 units right and 2 units down.

words.meaning: In maths, the difference between the highest and lowest values in a data set — not a variety.
words.example: The range of 4, 9, 11 and 20 is 16.

words.meaning: In maths, the value that appears most often in a data set — not a style or a setting.
words.example: The mode of 2, 3, 3, 3 and 7 is 3.

words.meaning: In maths, the ratio between a distance on a map or model and the real distance — not weighing equipment.
words.example: A scale of 1 : 100 means 1 cm on the map is 100 cm in real life.

words.meaning: In maths, a number less than zero — not 'bad' or 'pessimistic'.
words.example: Adding a negative number gives the same answer as subtracting.

words.meaning: In maths, a number greater than zero — not 'good' or 'optimistic'.
words.example: The answer is positive because two negatives multiply to give a positive.

words.meaning: In maths, a number that can be written as a fraction of two whole numbers — not 'sensible'.
words.example: 0.75 is rational because it is the same as 3/4.

words.meaning: In maths, a number that cannot be written as an exact fraction — not 'making no sense'.
words.example: π and √2 are irrational numbers.

words.meaning: In maths, everything in the sample space that is not the event you want — not praise, which is 'compliment'.
words.example: If P(A) = 0.3, the complement of A has a probability of 0.7.

words.meaning: In maths, one possible result of a probability experiment — not the result of any situation.
words.example: Tossing a coin has two outcomes: heads or tails.

words.meaning: In maths, one repeat of a probability experiment — not a court case or a test run.
words.example: Each spin of the spinner counts as one trial.

words.meaning: In maths, a set of one or more outcomes in a probability experiment — not a party.
words.example: The event 'rolling an even number' has three outcomes.

words.meaning: In maths, the whole group being studied in a survey — not only the people living in a place.
words.example: The population is every Year 8 student; the sample is 30 of them.

words.meaning: In maths, a smaller group chosen from the population to represent it — not a small taste.
words.example: Choose a random sample of 20 students from the year level.

words.meaning: In maths, a comparison of two quantities measured in different units — not just speed or a fee.
words.example: A rate of 60 km/h means 60 kilometres travelled in each hour.

words.meaning: In maths, money paid for borrowing money, or earned for saving it — not curiosity.
words.example: Work out the interest earned on $500 at 4% per year.

words.meaning: In maths, the exact amount or percentage taken off the marked price — not any reduction.
words.example: A 20% discount on $80 saves you $16.

words.meaning: In maths, the amount of money left in an account — not staying steady or being fair.
words.example: After the withdrawal, the balance was $340.

words.meaning: In maths, the new shape produced after a transformation — not just any picture.
words.example: Label the image A′B′C′ after the reflection.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Chapters 5A–5I: Algebraic language, fractions and factorising

words.meaning: A letter used in place of a number in algebra.
words.example: In 3x, the pronumeral is x.

words.meaning: A letter that stands for a number that can change.
words.example: The variable in this equation is x.

words.meaning: A group of numbers, letters and signs with no equals sign.
words.example: Simplify the expression 4x + 2x.

words.meaning: One part of an expression, separated by a plus or minus sign.
words.example: How many terms are in 3x + 2y - 5?

words.meaning: The number in front of a letter that multiplies it.
words.example: In 7x, the coefficient is 7.

words.meaning: A number in an expression that never changes.
words.example: In 4x + 9, the constant is 9.

words.meaning: Putting a number in place of a letter to work out the value.
words.example: Use substitution to find the answer when x = 5.

words.meaning: Having the same value, even though it looks different.
words.example: 2x + 4 and 2(x + 2) are equivalent.

words.meaning: The operation of putting numbers or terms together to find a total.
words.example: Use addition to collect the like terms.

words.meaning: The operation of taking one number or term away from another.
words.example: Use subtraction to simplify 8x - 3x.

words.meaning: The operation of multiplying numbers or terms together.
words.example: Use multiplication to expand the brackets.

words.meaning: The operation of splitting a number into equal parts.
words.example: Simplify the fraction using division.

words.meaning: A number written as one number over another, like 3 over 4.
words.example: Add these two fractions together.

words.meaning: The bottom number of a fraction.
words.example: The denominator of 3 over 5 is 5.

words.meaning: The top number of a fraction.
words.example: The numerator of 3 over 5 is 3.

words.meaning: A group of numbers, pronumerals and operation signs with no equals sign.
words.example: Write an algebraic expression for five more than x.

words.meaning: Terms with exactly the same pronumeral to the same power, so they can be added together.
words.example: Collect the like terms in 6x + 2y + 3x.

words.meaning: Terms whose pronumerals or powers are different, so they cannot be added together.
words.example: 5x and 5y are unlike terms, so leave them apart.

words.meaning: Two expressions that look different but always give the same value.
words.example: Show that 3(x + 2) and 3x + 6 are equivalent expressions.

words.meaning: A fraction with a pronumeral on the top, on the bottom, or on both.
words.example: Simplify the algebraic fraction 6x over 3.

words.meaning: Multiplying every term inside the brackets by the term outside, until no brackets are left.
words.example: Start by expanding brackets: 4(x + 5) becomes 4x + 20.

words.meaning: Writing an expression as a product of its factors — the opposite of expanding.
words.example: Factorising 6x + 9 gives 3(2x + 3).

words.meaning: A factor that every term in an expression shares.
words.example: Take out the common factor 5 from 5x + 10.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Chapters 7A–7E, 7I–7J: Solving equations and inequalities

words.meaning: A maths sentence with an equals sign that you can solve.
words.example: Solve the equation 2x + 1 = 9.

words.meaning: Having the same value, even though it looks different.
words.example: 2x + 4 and 2(x + 2) are equivalent.

words.meaning: A number written as one number over another, like 3 over 4.
words.example: Add these two fractions together.

words.meaning: The top number of a fraction.
words.example: The numerator of 3 over 5 is 3.

words.meaning: The bottom number of a fraction.
words.example: The denominator of 3 over 5 is 5.

words.meaning: A letter that stands for a number that can change.
words.example: The variable in this equation is x.

words.meaning: A maths sentence that uses signs like < or > instead of equals.
words.example: Solve the inequality 3x > 12.

words.meaning: The value of the letter that makes the equation true.
words.example: Check that x = 4 is the solution.

words.meaning: A group of numbers, letters and signs with no equals sign.
words.example: Simplify the expression 4x + 2x.

words.meaning: Something you do to numbers, like adding or multiplying.
words.example: Do the same operation on both sides.

words.meaning: To keep both sides of an equation equal.
words.example: Keep the equation in balance by doing the same to both sides.

words.meaning: The small raised number that shows how many times to multiply.
words.example: In 2 to the power of 5, the index is 5.

words.meaning: The result of multiplying a number by itself several times.
words.example: Write 3 to the power of 4.

words.meaning: The number that is multiplied by itself in a power.
words.example: In 2 to the power of 3, the base is 2.

words.meaning: The raised number in a power, which is another word for index.
words.example: Add the exponents when you multiply two powers.

words.meaning: To find the product of two numbers or terms.
words.example: Multiply both sides by 3.

words.meaning: To split a number into equal parts.
words.example: Divide both sides by 4.

words.meaning: A number that divides exactly into another number.
words.example: 3 and 4 are factors of 12.

words.meaning: A number in an expression that never changes.
words.example: In 4x + 9, the constant is 9.

words.meaning: The number in front of a letter that multiplies it.
words.example: In 7x, the coefficient is 7.

words.meaning: An operation that undoes another one, the way subtraction undoes addition.
words.example: Use the inverse operation and subtract 4 from both sides.

words.meaning: Solving an equation by working backwards through the operations, undoing each one.
words.example: Solve 3x + 2 = 14 by backtracking.

translations.hi: पीछे से हल करने की विधि

words.meaning: Different equations that have exactly the same solution.
words.example: 2x = 8 and x = 4 are equivalent equations.

words.meaning: All the values that make an inequality true.
words.example: The solution set for x > 3 is every number bigger than 3.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Chapter 1A–1D: Whole numbers, operations and factors

words.meaning: A number with no fraction or decimal part, such as 0, 1, 2 or 3.
words.example: Write down the whole numbers between 4.2 and 8.9.

words.meaning: A whole number that can be positive, negative or zero, with no fractions or decimals.
words.example: Is −6 an integer? Yes, because it has no decimal part.

words.meaning: The value a digit has because of its position in a number.
words.example: In 3407 the place value of the 4 is 400.

words.meaning: The rule that you can add or multiply numbers in either order and get the same answer.
words.example: The commutative law tells you that 7 × 4 = 4 × 7.

words.meaning: The rule that you can group added or multiplied numbers any way you like and still get the same answer.
words.example: By the associative law, (2 + 5) + 8 = 2 + (5 + 8).

words.meaning: The rule for multiplying a number by a bracket: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
words.example: Use the distributive law to work out 6 × 23 as 6 × 20 + 6 × 3.

words.meaning: A set method with clear steps for solving one type of problem.
words.example: Use the written algorithm to multiply 46 by 27.

words.meaning: Breaking a number into parts, such as tens and units, to make a calculation easier.
words.example: By partitioning, 47 + 36 becomes 40 + 30 and then 7 + 6.

words.meaning: Adjusting one number up and the other down to make a calculation easier, then correcting it.
words.example: By compensating, work out 68 + 39 as 68 + 40 − 1.

words.meaning: A quick approximate calculation, usually done by rounding the numbers first.
words.example: Use estimation to check that 412 × 19 is about 8000.

words.meaning: Whether one number can be divided by another with nothing left over.
words.example: The divisibility test for 3 is that the digits add to a multiple of 3.

words.meaning: A whole number greater than 1 with only two factors: 1 and itself.
words.example: Is 51 a prime number? No, because 3 × 17 = 51.

words.meaning: A whole number greater than 1 that has more than two factors.
words.example: 12 is a composite number because 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 all divide into it.

words.meaning: Writing a number as a product of prime numbers only.
words.example: The prime factorisation of 60 is 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.

translations.vi: phân tích thừa số nguyên tố

words.meaning: A diagram that breaks a number down step by step into its prime factors.
words.example: Draw a factor tree for 72.

words.meaning: The largest number that divides evenly into two or more numbers, written HCF.
words.example: The highest common factor of 12 and 18 is 6.

words.meaning: The smallest number that two or more numbers all divide evenly into, written LCM.
words.example: The lowest common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12.

words.meaning: The result of multiplying a number by a whole number.
words.example: 15 is a multiple of 5 because 5 × 3 = 15.

words.meaning: In a division, the number that is being divided.
words.example: In 56 ÷ 7, the dividend is 56.

words.meaning: In a division, the number you are dividing by.
words.example: In 56 ÷ 7, the divisor is 7.

words.meaning: The answer you get when one number is divided by another.
words.example: In 56 ÷ 7, the quotient is 8.

words.meaning: The amount left over when one number does not divide evenly into another.
words.example: 57 ÷ 7 gives 8 with a remainder of 1.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Chapter 1E–1H: Negative integers and order of operations

words.meaning: A whole number that is less than zero, such as −3.
words.example: Put the negative integers −5, −2 and −8 in order from smallest.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: Another name for a positive or negative number: it shows size and direction.
words.example: The directed number −4 means 4 units to the left of zero.

words.meaning: A line with the numbers marked in order, used to compare, add and subtract integers.
words.example: Use a number line to work out −3 + 5.

words.meaning: Two numbers the same distance from zero but on different sides of it.
words.example: 5 and −5 are opposite numbers, so they add to zero.

words.meaning: The size of a number when you ignore its sign.
words.example: The absolute value of −7 is 7.

words.meaning: The agreed order for a calculation: brackets, indices, then × and ÷, then + and − (BODMAS).
words.example: Follow the order of operations to work out 4 + 3 × 2.

translations.vi: thứ tự thực hiện phép tính

words.meaning: Putting a number in place of a letter to work out the value.
words.example: Use substitution to find 2a − b when a = 5 and b = −3.

words.meaning: A pair of numbers, (x, y), that gives the exact position of a point on the number plane.
words.example: Plot the coordinate (−2, 3).

words.meaning: The horizontal number line on the Cartesian plane.
words.example: Every point on the x-axis has a y-value of 0.

words.meaning: The vertical number line on the Cartesian plane.
words.example: The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 4).

words.meaning: One of the four regions that the x-axis and y-axis divide the number plane into.
words.example: The point (−2, 3) lies in the second quadrant.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Chapter 2A–2D: Angles, lines, triangles and quadrilaterals

words.meaning: The amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point, measured in degrees.
words.example: Measure this angle with a protractor and write the answer in degrees.

words.meaning: An angle smaller than 90°, so it looks sharp and narrow.
words.example: The 35° corner of this triangle is an acute angle.

words.meaning: An angle of exactly 90°, like the corner of a page.
words.example: Mark the right angle with a small square, not with an arc.

words.meaning: An angle between 90° and 180°.
words.example: Is 145° an acute angle or an obtuse angle?

words.meaning: An angle of exactly 180°, which makes a straight line.
words.example: Angles on a straight line add to a straight angle, 180°.

words.meaning: An angle between 180° and 360°.
words.example: To find the reflex angle, subtract the smaller angle from 360°.

translations.ro: a se rostogoli / a se întoarce

words.meaning: A full turn all the way around, equal to 360°.
words.example: Angles at a point add to one revolution, so they total 360°.

translations.vi: cuộc cách mạng; vòng quay trọn vẹn

words.meaning: Two angles that add up to 90°.
words.example: If one of two complementary angles is 35°, the other is 55°.

words.meaning: Two angles that add up to 180°.
words.example: The supplementary angles 110° and 70° together make a straight line.

words.meaning: The equal angles that sit across from each other where two straight lines cross.
words.example: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so x = 62°.

words.meaning: A line that cuts across two or more other lines.
words.example: Label the transversal before you name the pairs of angles.

words.meaning: Lines that always stay the same distance apart and never meet.
words.example: The arrows on the diagram show that these are parallel lines.

words.meaning: Lines that cross each other at a right angle of 90°.
words.example: Perpendicular lines meet at 90°, so mark the corner with a square.

words.meaning: Equal angles on opposite sides of a transversal between parallel lines, in a Z shape.
words.example: Alternate angles in a Z shape are equal, so y = 74°.

words.meaning: Angles on the same side of a transversal between parallel lines; they add to 180°.
words.example: Co-interior angles add to 180°, so subtract 115° from 180°.

words.meaning: Equal angles in matching positions where a transversal crosses parallel lines, in an F shape.
words.example: Corresponding angles are equal, so the missing angle is also 48°.

words.meaning: A flat shape with three straight sides and three angles.
words.example: Find the third angle of the triangle by subtracting the other two from 180°.

words.meaning: A triangle with all three sides equal and all three angles 60°.
words.example: Every angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°.

words.meaning: A triangle with exactly two equal sides and two equal angles.
words.example: The two base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.

words.meaning: A triangle with no equal sides and no equal angles.
words.example: A scalene triangle has three different side lengths.

words.meaning: The total of all the inside angles of a shape: 180° in a triangle, 360° in a quadrilateral.
words.example: Use the angle sum of a triangle to find the missing value.

words.meaning: The angle outside a shape between one side and the extension of the next side.
words.example: The exterior angle equals the two opposite inside angles added together.

words.meaning: A flat shape with four straight sides.
words.example: The angle sum of any quadrilateral is 360°.

words.meaning: A quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides.
words.example: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal in length.

words.meaning: A parallelogram with all four sides the same length.
words.example: A square is a rhombus whose angles are all right angles.

words.meaning: A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides.
words.example: Find the area of the trapezium from its two parallel sides and its height.

words.meaning: A quadrilateral with two pairs of equal sides next to each other.
words.example: The diagonals of a kite cross at right angles.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Chapter 2E–2G: Polygons, solids and 3D coordinates

words.meaning: A flat shape with three or more straight sides.
words.example: A polygon with eight sides is called an octagon.

words.meaning: A polygon with all sides equal and all angles equal.
words.example: Each angle of a regular polygon with six sides is 120°.

words.meaning: A shape in which every inside angle is less than 180°, so no corner caves in.
words.example: A convex shape has no corner pointing inwards.

words.meaning: A shape with at least one inside angle bigger than 180°, so one corner caves in.
words.example: This concave shape has one angle of 220°.

words.meaning: A corner point where two or more edges meet; more than one are called vertices.
words.example: Count the vertices of the cube before you use Euler's formula.

words.meaning: The straight line where two faces of a 3D shape meet.
words.example: A cube has twelve edges, all the same length.

words.meaning: A flat surface of a 3D shape.
words.example: Each face of a cube is a square.

words.meaning: A 3D shape whose faces are all flat polygons; more than one are called polyhedra.
words.example: Is a cylinder a polyhedron? No, because its side is curved.

words.meaning: The rule for any polyhedron: faces plus vertices minus edges equals 2.
words.example: Check your counting with Euler's formula, F + V − E = 2.

translations.ja: オイラーの多面体定理

words.meaning: Three numbers (x, y, z) that fix the position of a point in space.
words.example: Plot the three-dimensional coordinates (2, 3, 5) on the axes.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · 3D Space: nets, views and drawing solids

words.meaning: A flat pattern that folds up to make a 3D shape.
words.example: Draw the net of a cube using six equal squares.

words.meaning: A drawing on a grid of triangles or dots that makes a solid look 3D on flat paper.
words.example: Use dot paper for the isometric drawing of the prism.

words.meaning: What a 3D object looks like from straight above.
words.example: Draw the plan view of the tower as you would see it from above.

words.meaning: The view of a 3D object seen from straight in front or from the side.
words.example: Sketch the front elevation and the side elevation of this solid.

words.meaning: The flat shape you see when you slice straight through a solid.
words.example: The cross-section of this prism is a triangle.

words.meaning: A set of flat views — plan, front and side — that show a 3D object accurately.
words.example: An orthographic drawing shows the three views side by side.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Chapter 3A–3C: Fractions

words.meaning: A number that shows part of a whole, written as one number over another.
words.example: Write three parts out of eight as the fraction 3/8.

words.meaning: The top number of a fraction, which counts how many parts you have.
words.example: In 5/8 the numerator is 5.

words.meaning: The bottom number of a fraction, which names how many equal parts the whole is cut into.
words.example: In 5/8 the denominator is 8.

words.meaning: Fractions that look different but have exactly the same value.
words.example: Show that 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent fractions.

words.meaning: A fraction written so the top and bottom share no common factor except 1.
words.example: Write 12/18 in its simplest form.

words.meaning: A fraction whose top number is bigger than its bottom number.
words.example: Change the improper fraction 7/4 into a mixed number.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: A whole number written together with a fraction.
words.example: Write 7/4 as the mixed number 1 3/4.

words.meaning: A fraction turned upside down; a number times its reciprocal equals 1.
words.example: To divide by 2/3, multiply by its reciprocal, 3/2.

words.meaning: The smallest number that every denominator in the question divides into; short form LCD.
words.example: The lowest common denominator of 1/4 and 1/6 is 12.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Chapter 3D–3F: Decimals

words.meaning: A number that uses a decimal point to show parts smaller than one.
words.example: Write 3/4 as the decimal 0.75.

words.meaning: The position of a digit after the decimal point.
words.example: Round 4.567 to two decimal places.

words.meaning: A decimal that stops after a certain number of digits.
words.example: Explain why 0.25 is a terminating decimal but 0.333... is not.

words.meaning: A decimal in which a digit or a group of digits repeats forever.
words.example: Write 1/3 as the recurring decimal 0.333...

translations.zh-Hans: 四舍五入 / 四捨五入 / 四捨五入 sei3 se2 ng5 jap6
translations.zh-Hant: 四捨五入 / 四捨五入 / 四捨五入 sei3 se2 ng5 jap6

words.meaning: Writing a number to a given number of decimal places or significant figures.
words.example: Rounding 8.472 to one decimal place gives 8.5.

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Chapter 3G–3K: Percentages

words.meaning: A number out of 100, written with the % sign.
words.example: Write 0.35 as a percentage.

words.meaning: How much a quantity has grown, given as a percentage of the starting amount.
words.example: A rise from 40 to 50 is a percentage increase of 25%.

words.meaning: How much a quantity has shrunk, given as a percentage of the starting amount.
words.example: A fall from 50 to 40 is a percentage decrease of 20%.

words.meaning: The rise or fall in a quantity, written as a percentage of the starting value.
words.example: Divide the change by the original amount to find the percentage change.

translations.fr: une façon de faire quelque chose
translations.hi: किसी काम को करने का तरीका

words.meaning: A way of solving a problem by finding the value of one unit first, then scaling up.
words.example: Use the unitary method: find the cost of one pen, then of twelve.

translations.vi: phương pháp quy về đơn vị
translations.es: método de reducción a la unidad

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Chapter review: profit, loss and exact decimals

words.meaning: The price a business pays to buy or make an item, before selling it; short form CP.
words.example: Subtract the cost price from the selling price to find the profit.

words.meaning: The price an item is actually sold for; short form SP.
words.example: If the mark-up is 40%, what is the selling price?

words.meaning: The amount added to the cost price to set the selling price.
words.example: A $20 mark-up on a $50 jacket gives a selling price of $70.

words.meaning: An amount taken off the marked price, given as money or as a percentage.
words.example: Find the sale price of a $60 shirt after a 15% discount.

words.meaning: The money gained when the selling price is higher than the cost price.
words.example: Selling for $70 what cost $50 gives a profit of $20.

words.meaning: The money lost when the selling price is lower than the cost price.
words.example: Selling for $40 what cost $50 gives a loss of $10.

words.meaning: Out of every hundred; a fraction whose denominator is 100.
words.example: Twenty per cent means 20 out of every 100.

words.meaning: A decimal written with no rounding at all, such as 0.5.
words.example: Give the answer in exact decimal form, not rounded to two places.

words.meaning: A decimal that carries on forever without ending.
words.example: Dividing 1 by 7 gives a non-terminating decimal.

words.meaning: A never-ending decimal in which a digit or group of digits repeats.
words.example: Two thirds is the recurring decimal 0.666...

words.meaning: A decimal with a fixed, limited number of digits after the point.
words.example: One eighth gives the terminating decimal 0.125.

words.meaning: A number that cannot be written exactly as a fraction.
words.example: Both π and √2 are irrational numbers.

words.meaning: An irrational number left in root form, such as √3.
words.example: Leave the answer as the surd √5 instead of rounding it.

words.meaning: A 10% Australian government tax added to the price of most goods and services; short form GST.
words.example: Add 10% Goods and Services Tax to find the price a customer pays.

translations.vi: thuế hàng hóa và dịch vụ
translations.fr: taxe sur les biens et services

units.name: Year 8 Maths · Real-world finance: banking, interest and pay

words.meaning: Money paid upfront on a purchase, or money put into a bank account.
words.example: A $200 deposit on a $1000 bike leaves $800 still to pay.

words.meaning: Money taken out of a bank account.
words.example: After a $50 withdrawal the balance is $450.

words.meaning: Money earned on savings, or charged on a loan, usually written as a percentage rate.
words.example: How much interest does $2000 earn at 4% per annum?

words.meaning: Interest worked out only on the original amount, at the same rate each period.
words.example: Simple interest on $500 at 6% for three years is $90.

words.meaning: For each year; used for a yearly rate such as 5% p.a.
words.example: The savings account pays 3% per annum.

words.meaning: Pay given to a salesperson as a percentage of the value of what they sell.
words.example: A 4% commission on $12 000 of sales is $480.

words.meaning: Regular pay for work, usually worked out for each hour.
words.example: At a wage of $25 an hour, what does a six-hour shift pay?

words.meaning: A fixed amount of pay for a whole year, split into equal regular payments.
words.example: A salary of $78 000 is paid in twelve equal monthly amounts.

translations.am: ለወደፊት ገቢና ወጪ የተዘጋጀ የገንዘብ እቅድ
translations.es: plan financiero para ingresos y gastos futuros
