units.name: Civics

words.meaning: A system where the people choose their leaders by voting.
words.example: Australia is a democracy because citizens vote in elections.

words.meaning: The elected group that makes the laws for a country or state.
words.example: The Australian Parliament meets in Canberra.

words.meaning: The monarch's representative in an Australian state, who signs new laws.
words.example: The governor signs a bill so that it becomes law.

words.meaning: A member of the government in charge of one area, such as health or education.
words.example: The education minister visited our school.

words.meaning: The party or parties in Parliament that are not in government.
words.example: The opposition asks the government questions in Parliament.

words.meaning: The set of basic rules for how a country is run.
words.example: The Australian Constitution sets out the powers of the federal Parliament.

words.meaning: A group of states that join together under one national government but keep some powers.
words.example: Australia became a federation in 1901.

words.meaning: The group of senior ministers who make the government's main decisions.
words.example: The Prime Minister meets with cabinet every week.

words.meaning: A small group chosen to look closely at an issue and report on it.
words.example: A committee of the Senate studied the new law.

words.meaning: More than half of the votes or people.
words.example: The party won a majority of the seats.

words.meaning: The area a member of Parliament represents, and the voters who live there.
words.example: Each electorate has one member in the House of Representatives.

words.meaning: A person who lives in an area and is represented by its member of Parliament.
words.example: A constituent wrote to the member about the local park.

translations.ps: هغه شی چې باید ترسره شي

words.meaning: A national vote to change the Australian Constitution.
words.example: A referendum needs a majority of voters in a majority of states.

words.meaning: A written request signed by many people, asking leaders to take action.
words.example: Students signed a petition for a new crossing.

words.meaning: Trying to persuade politicians to support a cause.
words.example: Lobbying by farmers led to the new water rules.

words.meaning: Keeping things apart, such as keeping the powers of government in different groups.
words.example: The separation of powers stops one group having too much control.

words.meaning: The ability or right to control or influence others.
words.example: Parliament has the power to make laws.

words.meaning: A vote where people choose their leaders.
words.example: Australians vote in a federal election about every three years.

words.meaning: To do with government and how a country is run.
words.example: A political party shares ideas about how to run the country.

words.meaning: Not belonging to a party; free from control by others.
words.example: An independent member does not belong to a party.

words.meaning: The part of government that puts laws into action, led by the Prime Minister and ministers.
words.example: The executive carries out the laws made by Parliament.

words.meaning: The part of government that makes the laws, which is Parliament.
words.example: The legislative branch debates and passes bills.

words.meaning: The part of government that decides court cases, using the courts and judges.
words.example: The judicial branch includes the High Court.

words.meaning: A plan of action that a government or group agrees to follow.
words.example: The party announced a new health policy.

words.meaning: The right to act, speak and choose without being controlled.
words.example: Freedom of speech is important in a democracy.

words.meaning: From or to do with another country.
words.example: Foreign aid helps countries after a disaster.

words.meaning: Help, such as money or food, given to people in need.
words.example: Australia sent aid after the flood.

words.meaning: A legal member of a country, with rights and duties.
words.example: A citizen over 18 must vote in Australia.

words.meaning: The group of people who run a country or state and make decisions for it.
words.example: The state government looks after public schools and hospitals.

words.meaning: A person chosen to speak and act for a group of people.
words.example: Each representative speaks for the people of their area.

words.meaning: To do with a whole country.
words.example: The national government is in Canberra.

words.meaning: The natural world around us: land, water, air, plants and animals.
words.example: The council made a plan to protect the local environment.

words.meaning: Being a legal member of a country, with rights and duties.
words.example: Voting is part of good citizenship.

words.meaning: A country with its own independent government.

units.name: Shogunate Japan · Set 3: Historical significance and glossary

words.meaning: the military government of Japan, led by the shogun
words.example: The Tokugawa shogunate ruled Japan for over 250 years.

parts.meaning: an estate held under a lord

words.meaning: a system where people are given land and protection in return for loyalty and service
words.example: Under feudalism, samurai served their lord in exchange for land.

words.meaning: controlled from one place by one leader or government
words.example: The shogun built a centralised government at Edo.

words.meaning: the group of people with the power to rule a country and make its laws
words.example: The shogun's government controlled the daimyo closely.

words.meaning: a system that ranks people in order from most powerful to least
words.example: In the Japanese hierarchy, merchants were ranked below farmers.

words.meaning: when some groups have far more money, rights or power than others
words.example: There was great inequality between samurai and peasants.

words.meaning: farming: growing crops and raising animals
words.example: Rice agriculture supported most of Japan's people.

words.meaning: all the people living in a place
words.example: The population of Edo grew to over one million.

words.meaning: one way of explaining what evidence from the past means
words.example: Historians offer more than one interpretation of the shogun's rule.

words.meaning: to do with the past and the study of it
words.example: We used historical sources to learn about samurai life.

words.meaning: the cutting down of large areas of forest
words.example: Building cities and castles caused deforestation in Japan.

words.meaning: a policy of keeping a country closed off from other countries
words.example: Japan's isolationism kept out most foreign traders for 200 years.

words.meaning: Another name for the shogun's military government; it literally means 'tent government'.
words.example: Officials of the bakufu carried the shogun's orders out to every domain.

words.meaning: A territory ruled by a daimyo; the Japanese word for it is han.
words.example: Each domain collected its own rice tax and kept its own soldiers.

words.meaning: Japan's traditional royal ruler, who kept ceremonial and religious authority while the shogun held military power.
words.example: The emperor remained in Kyoto while the shogun governed from Edo.

words.meaning: A warrior or official who served a lord and stayed loyal to him.
words.example: A daimyo rewarded his most trusted retainer with land of his own.

words.meaning: A set of ideas from China that taught order, duty, rank and education.
words.example: Neo-Confucianism gave the four-tier class system its moral argument.

words.meaning: The accepted ranking of social groups within a society.
words.example: The status order placed samurai at the top and merchants at the bottom.

words.meaning: How important a person or event was, judged by how much changed, how many people, and for how long.
words.example: To judge historical significance, ask what would be different if Ieyasu had lost.

words.meaning: The lasting effects or influence that remain after a person or event.
words.example: The legacy of the shogunate can still be seen in the street plan of Tokyo.

words.meaning: A limit or exception added to a claim so that it is more accurate.
words.example: Add a qualification: the peace helped most people, though merchants stayed low in status.

words.meaning: One test of significance: whether it changed who held power or how people lived then.
words.example: Judge importance at the time by what people alive in 1600 actually noticed.

words.meaning: One test of significance: how long the effects of an event or person lasted.
words.example: The duration of the Tokugawa peace, over 250 years, makes it highly significant.

units.name: Business & Economics

words.meaning: anywhere buyers and sellers meet to trade goods and services
words.example: Prices are set by buyers and sellers in the market.

words.meaning: something used to make goods and services, such as land, workers or money
words.example: Water is an important natural resource.

words.meaning: deciding how resources are shared out and what they are used for
words.example: The allocation of resources decides what gets produced.

words.meaning: when there are not enough resources to satisfy everyone's wants
words.example: Scarcity means we must choose what to buy.

words.meaning: when businesses try to win the same customers
words.example: Competition between shops keeps prices lower.

words.meaning: a person who buys and uses goods and services
words.example: A consumer has the right to a refund for a faulty product.

words.meaning: a person or business that makes goods or provides services
words.example: The producer sells the bread to local shops.

words.meaning: how much of a good consumers want to buy at a given price
words.example: Demand for ice cream rises in summer.

words.meaning: how much of a good producers are willing to sell at a given price
words.example: Bad weather reduced the supply of wheat.

words.meaning: the money a person earns from work or other sources
words.example: She saves part of her income each week.

words.meaning: money the government collects from people and businesses to pay for services
words.example: Taxation pays for hospitals, roads and schools.

words.meaning: a plan for how much money you will earn and how much you will spend
words.example: Make a budget so you do not spend more than you earn.

words.meaning: putting money into something now in order to earn more money later
words.example: The company made an investment in new machines.

words.meaning: a chance to do something; the choice you give up is the opportunity cost
words.example: Working on Saturday was a good opportunity to earn money.

words.meaning: something that puts a person or business in a better position than others
words.example: Being close to the station is an advantage for the shop.

units.name: Shogunate Japan · Set 1: Tokugawa Ieyasu's rise to power

words.meaning: The top military ruler of Japan, who held the real power with the emperor's blessing.
words.example: The shogun governed from Edo while the emperor stayed in Kyoto.

words.meaning: The government run by a shogun and his officials.
words.example: The Tokugawa shogunate held power for more than 250 years.

words.meaning: A powerful regional lord who ruled his own land and commanded samurai.
words.example: Every daimyo had to leave his family in Edo as a guarantee of loyalty.

words.meaning: A trained warrior in old Japan who served a lord.
words.example: A samurai was expected to put loyalty to his lord above his own life.

words.meaning: Japan's 'Warring States' age, when rival lords fought because no one held central power.
words.example: The Sengoku Jidai ended once one family finally controlled the whole country.

words.meaning: A person held by another lord as a guarantee that their family will stay loyal; also called a ward.
words.example: Ieyasu spent much of his childhood as a hostage in a rival lord's household.

words.meaning: An agreement between two leaders or groups to support each other.
words.example: The alliance lasted only as long as both lords needed it.

words.meaning: A partnership between regional lords for military or political benefit.
words.example: One daimyo alliance could put thousands of samurai into a single army.

words.meaning: Bringing separate, rival territories together under one ruler.
words.example: Unification took three leaders and more than fifty years of fighting.

words.meaning: Being seen as having the proper, accepted right to hold power.
words.example: The emperor's title gave the shogun legitimacy in the eyes of the daimyo.

words.meaning: The passing of a role or title on to the next person, often within a family.
words.example: Ieyasu planned the succession early so that his son would keep control.

units.name: Shogunate Japan · Set 2: Achievements of the Tokugawa shogunate

words.meaning: The city Ieyasu made his headquarters; it was later renamed Tokyo.
words.example: Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world.

words.meaning: The Tokugawa way of governing: central rule by the shogun plus locally run daimyo domains.
words.example: Under the Bakuhan system a lord ran his own land but obeyed the shogun.

words.meaning: Passed down within one family, from parent to child.
words.example: The title of shogun became hereditary in the Tokugawa family.

words.meaning: The 'Laws for the Military Houses': rules the shogunate used to control daimyo and samurai.
words.example: The Buke shohatto even set out when a lord could repair his castle.

translations.tl: batas para sa mga angkang militar

words.meaning: The ranked order of Tokugawa society: samurai, then farmers, then artisans, then merchants.
words.example: In the four-tier class system the richest merchants still ranked lowest.

translations.tl: apat na antas na sistemang panlipunan

words.meaning: A policy of limiting contact and trade with other countries.
words.example: Japan's isolationism closed almost every port to foreign ships.

words.meaning: The long period of internal peace in Japan under the Tokugawa shoguns.
words.example: Historians call those two centuries without civil war the Pax Tokugawa.

words.meaning: Managing relationships and agreements between different countries or powers.
words.example: Careful diplomacy kept one Dutch trading post open through the closed years.

words.meaning: The 1868 change that ended the shogunate and returned formal power to the emperor.
words.example: The Meiji Restoration opened Japan to rapid industrial change.

words.meaning: A town that grew around a lord's castle as its centre of trade and government.
words.example: Merchants and artisans crowded into the castle town below the walls.

units.name: Medieval Europe · Topic 1: The Dark Ages

words.meaning: An older name for the early medieval period, once wrongly thought to have no progress.
words.example: Historians avoid the name Dark Ages because monasteries kept learning alive.

words.meaning: Relating to the Middle Ages, the period in Europe from about 500 to 1500 CE.
words.example: A medieval village was built around the lord's manor and the church.

words.meaning: Something that stays the same across a period of time.
words.example: Farming shows continuity: the tools barely changed for centuries.

words.meaning: The order in which events happened, from earliest to latest.
words.example: Put the events in chronological order to build a clear chronology.

words.meaning: A gradual loss of power, wealth or importance.
words.example: The decline of Rome left Europe without one central government.

words.meaning: When an armed force enters another territory to seize control of it.
words.example: The Viking invasion changed who ruled much of northern England.

units.name: Medieval Europe · Topic 2: Social structure (the feudal system)

parts.meaning: an estate held under a lord

words.meaning: The medieval system where land was given in exchange for loyalty and military service.
words.example: The feudal system tied every person to someone above them and below them.

words.meaning: A king or queen who rules a country.
words.example: The monarch granted land to nobles who promised him soldiers.

words.meaning: A person of high birth or rank, usually owning large amounts of land.
words.example: A noble owed the king armed knights in return for his estates.

words.meaning: A person granted land and protection by a lord in return for loyalty and service.
words.example: The vassal knelt and promised service to his lord.

words.meaning: A warrior granted land in return for military service to a lord.
words.example: A knight trained for years before he could fight on horseback.

words.meaning: A poor medieval farm worker; a serf was a peasant bound to land he did not own.
words.example: The peasant handed over part of every harvest to the manor.

words.meaning: Officials of the Church, such as priests, bishops and monks.
words.example: Only the clergy could read Latin, so they wrote most of the records.

words.meaning: A document of 1215 that limited the English king's power and set out basic legal rights.
words.example: Magna Carta forced the king to accept that he too was under the law.

words.meaning: The estate of land controlled by a lord and worked by peasants.
words.example: The whole village belonged to the manor and to its lord.

words.meaning: A system that ranks people or groups from highest to lowest status.
words.example: In the medieval hierarchy the king sat at the top and peasants at the base.

units.name: Medieval Europe · Topic 3: Daily life

words.meaning: Practices that keep a person or a place clean and healthy.
words.example: Poor hygiene in crowded towns helped disease spread quickly.

words.meaning: Activities such as feasts, music, jousting and fairs, done for enjoyment.
words.example: Medieval entertainment needed no money, only a market square.

words.meaning: An organisation of skilled workers in one trade who set shared rules and standards.
words.example: The bakers' guild decided who was allowed to sell bread in the town.

words.meaning: A simple piece of medieval clothing worn over the body.
words.example: A peasant wore a woollen tunic tied at the waist with a cord.

words.meaning: A long shirt made of chain mail, worn for protection in battle.
words.example: The hauberk reached the knees and weighed more than ten kilograms.

words.meaning: A padded jacket worn under armour for extra protection.
words.example: Without a gambeson, chain mail would bruise the wearer badly.

words.meaning: Armour made of small metal rings joined together.
words.example: Chain mail turned a sword's edge but not the force of the blow.

words.meaning: Armour made of solid metal plates, used later in the medieval period.
words.example: Plate armour was shaped so that blows would slide off it.

words.meaning: A lighter style of helmet used in the late medieval period.
words.example: The barbute left the face open so the wearer could see and breathe.

words.meaning: The general quality of a person's housing, food and comfort.
words.example: Living conditions in a lord's castle were nothing like those in a peasant's hut.

units.name: Medieval Europe · Topic 4: Crime and punishment

words.meaning: A medieval way of deciding guilt by a dangerous physical test, believed to show God's judgement.
words.example: In trial by ordeal, a burn that healed cleanly was taken as proof of innocence.

words.meaning: A medieval way of settling a dispute or accusation through a fight.
words.example: A noble could demand trial by combat instead of facing the court.

translations.vi: phân xử bằng đấu tay đôi

words.meaning: The courts, punishments and customs used to deal with crime in the Middle Ages.
words.example: The medieval justice system relied on the village itself to catch offenders.

translations.vi: hệ thống tư pháp trung cổ
translations.ps: د منځنیو پیړیو د عدالت نظام

words.meaning: To use extra evidence to support or confirm a claim.
words.example: A second chronicle corroborates the account of the battle.

words.meaning: Evidence created at the time of an event by someone who was there.
words.example: A letter written during the battle is a primary source.

words.meaning: A later account or interpretation of an event, based on other evidence.
words.example: The textbook chapter on Hastings is a secondary source.

words.meaning: A one-sided view that favours a particular side or opinion.
words.example: A monk writing for the new king is likely to show bias.

words.meaning: The point of view of a particular person or group in the past.
words.example: The Norman perspective on Hastings is very different from the Saxon one.

units.name: Medieval Europe · Topic 5: The Black Death

words.meaning: A deadly disease that spread rapidly across medieval Europe.
words.example: The bubonic plague killed perhaps a third of the people in Europe.

words.meaning: A disease outbreak that spreads across a very wide area, often across many countries.
words.example: The Black Death was a pandemic, not just a local outbreak.

words.meaning: A sign in the body that shows a person is unwell.
words.example: The first symptom was a painful swelling under the arm.

words.meaning: The place or source where an outbreak first began.
words.example: Most historians place the origin of the plague in Central Asia.

words.meaning: Actions taken to stop something harmful, such as a disease, from spreading.
words.example: Medieval prevention included burning herbs, which did nothing at all.

words.meaning: A large drop in the number of people living in an area.
words.example: Depopulation left whole villages empty after the plague passed.

words.meaning: A rise in the pay workers receive, often because workers are in short supply.
words.example: Wage inflation followed the plague because so few labourers were left.

words.meaning: When there are not enough workers to do the jobs that need doing.
words.example: The labour shortage let peasants demand better pay for the first time.

words.meaning: The ranked structure of groups within a society, from highest to lowest.
words.example: The Black Death shook the social hierarchy that feudalism depended on.

words.meaning: A result or effect that follows from an event or an action.
words.example: One consequence of the plague was higher wages for those who survived.

parts.meaning: an estate held under a lord

words.meaning: The system of land for loyalty and service, which weakened after the Black Death.
words.example: Feudalism lost its grip once peasants could bargain over their wages.

units.name: Medieval Europe · Source analysis skills: Hastings and the Black Death

words.meaning: The study of how history is written and interpreted.
words.example: Historiography asks why two writers tell the same battle so differently.

words.meaning: Facts, sources or details used to support a conclusion.
words.example: Quote evidence from the source before you explain what it shows.

words.meaning: One person's explanation of what a source or an event means.
words.example: Two historians can read the same chronicle and reach a different interpretation.

words.meaning: How trustworthy or accurate a source is.
words.example: Question the reliability of a chronicle written for the winning side.

words.meaning: How much a source helps you answer the particular question you are asking.
words.example: A biased source still has usefulness: it shows what people believed.

words.meaning: A description of an event given by someone who saw it happen.
words.example: An eyewitness account is close to the event but may still be one-sided.

words.meaning: The link between why something happened and what happened as a result.
words.example: Map cause and effect before you plan your essay paragraphs.

words.meaning: A sudden, disorganised retreat by a defeated army.
words.example: The chronicle describes a rout, with soldiers throwing down their shields.

words.meaning: The level of confidence and spirit within a group, especially an army.
words.example: Losing their leader destroyed the army's morale.

words.meaning: The taking of control of a country or territory by force.
words.example: The Norman conquest changed England's language and who owned its land.

units.name: Renaissance Italy · Topics 1–2: Origins and daily life

words.meaning: The 'rebirth' of art, learning and culture in Europe, beginning in Italy from the 1300s.
words.example: The Renaissance began in wealthy Italian cities, not in royal courts.

words.meaning: An independent city that governs itself and the area around it.
words.example: Florence was a city-state with its own laws, coins and army.

words.meaning: A wealthy person who pays to support an artist or a thinker.
words.example: Without a patron, a painter could not afford paint or assistants.

words.meaning: City government run through the trade guilds rather than by a single ruler.
words.example: Under guild government, wool merchants helped choose the city's officials.

words.meaning: Ancient Greek and Roman culture and ideas, which Renaissance thinkers studied and admired.
words.example: Artists copied statues from the classical world to learn the human body.

words.meaning: In Renaissance Italy, the household that shaped a person's status and marriage.
words.example: A young woman's family, not the woman herself, chose her husband.

words.meaning: A group treated as separate from the main society, often with fewer rights.
words.example: Jewish residents were a social minority, restricted to one part of the city.

words.meaning: A young person learning a trade or craft under a skilled master.
words.example: An apprentice ground colours for years before touching a canvas.

words.meaning: Money or property given by a bride's family to the groom's family at marriage.
words.example: A large dowry could buy a daughter a match with a richer family.

units.name: Renaissance Italy · Topics 3–4: Achievements, spread and legacy

words.meaning: A Renaissance way of thinking that focused on human ability, achievement and classical learning.
words.example: Humanism put people, not only saints, at the centre of art.

words.meaning: In art, a technique that makes a flat picture look three-dimensional — not a point of view.
words.example: Lines drawn towards a single point give the painting its perspective.

words.meaning: The money and support a patron gives to artists or scholars.
words.example: Medici patronage paid for many of Florence's best-known works.

words.meaning: A new idea, method or invention.
words.example: Oil paint was an innovation that let artists blend colours slowly.

parts.meaning: a mark pressed onto a surface

words.meaning: A machine, developed by Gutenberg, that produced books quickly and cheaply.
words.example: The printing press spread new ideas faster than any preacher could.

words.meaning: A widespread shift in ideas, art or beliefs across a society.
words.example: The Renaissance was a cultural movement, not a single event.

words.meaning: The way beliefs, styles or knowledge travel from one place or group to another.
words.example: The spread of Renaissance ideas followed traders and printed books north.

words.meaning: The later arrival of Renaissance ideas and art from Italy into England.
words.example: The English Renaissance gave us the theatres Shakespeare wrote for.

translations.ja: イギリス・ルネサンス

units.name: Law and Justice · Topic 1: Why we need laws and how they are made

words.meaning: An official rule that everyone in a society must follow, enforced by the government.
words.example: Breaking a law can lead to a charge in court, not just a detention.

words.meaning: An instruction about how to behave that is not always backed by government enforcement.
words.example: A rule about wearing a hat at lunch is made by the school, not by parliament.

words.meaning: Law made by a parliament and written down as an Act.
words.example: Statutory law can change quickly, because parliament can pass a new Act.

words.meaning: Law made by judges through their decisions in court cases.
words.example: Common law grows case by case, as judges decide new problems.

words.meaning: The group of elected representatives who make the laws for a country or state.
words.example: Parliament debated the bill for three days before voting.

words.meaning: A proposed law that parliament is still considering — not a bill you pay in a shop.
words.example: A bill becomes an Act only once both houses pass it.

words.meaning: A past court decision that later, similar cases are expected to follow.
words.example: The judge followed a precedent set by a higher court.

words.meaning: The ranked structure of courts, from lower courts up to the Supreme Court.
words.example: The court hierarchy decides which court hears a serious case.

translations.vi: hệ thống thứ bậc tòa án

translations.ps: هغه شی چې باید ترسره شي

words.meaning: A public vote on one question, such as a change to the constitution.
words.example: Changing the Constitution needs a referendum, not just a vote in parliament.

units.name: Law and Justice · Topic 2: Criminal and civil law

words.meaning: The law dealing with offences against the whole community, brought to court by the state.
words.example: Criminal law covers theft, assault and dangerous driving.

words.meaning: The law that settles disputes between individuals or organisations.
words.example: A neighbour who sues over a broken fence is using civil law.

words.meaning: A serious crime, tried by a judge and jury in a higher court.
words.example: Armed robbery is an indictable offence, heard in the County Court.

words.meaning: A minor crime, dealt with quickly by a magistrate in a lower court.
words.example: Speeding is a summary offence, so no jury is needed.

words.meaning: To bring a legal case against a person accused of breaking the law.
words.example: The state decided to prosecute the driver for dangerous driving.

words.meaning: The person or organisation being accused or sued in a court case.
words.example: The defendant sat with her lawyer while the charges were read.

words.meaning: The person who brings a civil case against someone else in court.
words.example: The plaintiff claimed the builder had never finished the job.

translations.fr: transformé en / ayant la forme de
translations.ur: میں تبدیل شدہ / شکل رکھنے والا

words.meaning: A person charged with a crime, who must be proven guilty.
words.example: The accused is treated as innocent until the jury decides.

words.meaning: A court system in which two opposing sides each argue their case before an independent judge or jury.
words.example: In the adversary system the judge listens, rather than investigating.

units.name: Law and Justice · Topic 3: Principles of justice

words.meaning: The principle that the law applies equally to everyone, including the government.
words.example: The rule of law means a prime minister can be taken to court too.

words.meaning: A court hearing without bias, where both sides get a proper chance to be heard.
words.example: A fair trial needs an impartial jury and time to prepare a defence.

words.meaning: Having a lawyer put your case for you in court.
words.example: Without legal representation, an accused person has to argue alone.

words.meaning: Free or low-cost legal help from the government for people who cannot afford a lawyer.
words.example: Legal aid makes the right to a lawyer real, not just an idea.

words.meaning: The principle that a person is treated as innocent until they are proven guilty.
words.example: The presumption of innocence puts the work of proving guilt on the prosecution.

words.meaning: The responsibility to prove a claim, which in a criminal case rests on the prosecution.
words.example: The burden of proof never moves across to the accused.

words.meaning: The official decision reached in a trial, such as guilty or not guilty.
words.example: The jury took two days to reach a verdict.

words.meaning: The offence of driving so carelessly or dangerously that it causes another person's death.
words.example: Culpable driving carries a far heavier sentence than speeding.

words.meaning: Illegally supplying, moving or selling banned drugs.
words.example: Trafficking is treated much more seriously than possessing a small amount.

words.meaning: Entering a building without permission, meaning to steal or commit another offence inside.
words.example: Burglary can be charged even if nothing is actually taken.

units.name: Law and Justice · Topic 4: Imposing a sentence

words.meaning: In law, the punishment a court decides for a person found guilty — not a group of words.
words.example: The judge handed down a sentence of two years in prison.

words.meaning: Being sent to prison as a punishment.
words.example: Imprisonment is usually kept for the most serious offences.

words.meaning: A court order to do supervised work or treatment in the community instead of going to prison.
words.example: A community correction order can include unpaid work and counselling.

translations.vi: lệnh cải tạo tại cộng đồng

words.meaning: Helping an offender change their behaviour so that they do not offend again.
words.example: Rehabilitation is one reason a judge may order treatment rather than prison.

words.meaning: Genuine regret and sorrow for having done something wrong.
words.example: The offender showed real remorse, and the judge shortened the sentence.

words.meaning: A circumstance that makes an offence look less serious and can lower the sentence.
words.example: Pleading guilty early is a mitigating factor at sentencing.

words.meaning: A circumstance that makes an offence look more serious and can raise the sentence.
words.example: Using a weapon is an aggravating factor at sentencing.

words.meaning: A statement describing how a crime affected a victim, which the court considers when sentencing.
words.example: The victim impact statement was read aloud before the sentence was set.

translations.vi: bản khai tác động đối với nạn nhân
translations.es: declaración de impacto de la víctima

words.meaning: Early release from prison under strict conditions, before the full sentence is served.
words.example: He was released on parole after serving half his sentence.

words.meaning: The harshest punishment the law allows for a particular offence.
words.example: The maximum penalty is rarely given for a first offence.

words.meaning: An earlier finding of guilt already recorded against a person.
words.example: A prior conviction can push the court towards a longer sentence.

units.name: Place and Liveability · Lessons 1.1–2.1: factors of liveability

words.meaning: How suitable and pleasant a place is to live in.
words.example: We ranked five cities for liveability using climate, safety and services.

words.meaning: The usual, long-term weather pattern of a place.
words.example: Melbourne's climate is mild, with cool winters and warm summers.

words.meaning: The day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere, such as today's rain or wind.
words.example: Weather changes hourly; climate is measured over thirty years.

words.meaning: A graph showing a place's average monthly temperature and rainfall together.
words.example: Read the bars on the climograph for rainfall and the line for temperature.

words.meaning: How clean and healthy the natural surroundings of a place are.
words.example: Smog and polluted rivers lower a city's environmental quality.

words.meaning: The basic physical systems a place needs, such as roads, water and electricity.
words.example: Without reliable infrastructure, a growing city cannot supply clean water.

words.meaning: Harmful substances released into the air, water or land.
words.example: Air pollution from traffic is worst near the city centre.

words.meaning: The number of people living in each square kilometre of an area.
words.example: Population density is high in the inner city and low out on the farms.

units.name: Place and Liveability · Lessons 2.2–3.3: safety, healthcare and education

words.meaning: How secure a place is from crime, conflict and political unrest.
words.example: Safety and stability matter as much as income when we rank a city.

words.meaning: The services and systems that look after people's physical and mental health.
words.example: Free healthcare raises life expectancy across a whole population.

words.meaning: A measure of a country's development that combines life expectancy, education and income.
words.example: Norway sits near the top of the Human Development Index.

translations.vi: Chỉ số Phát triển Con người

words.meaning: The average number of years a person born in a place is expected to live.
words.example: Life expectancy rises when clean water and healthcare improve.

words.meaning: The percentage of people in a place who can read and write.
words.example: A high literacy rate usually goes with strong schooling.

words.meaning: The total value of the goods and services a country produces in a year.
words.example: Gross domestic product shows the size of an economy, not how fairly it is shared.

words.meaning: A bad condition that pushes people to leave a place.
words.example: War and drought are push factors for migration.

words.meaning: A good condition that attracts people to move to a place.
words.example: Jobs and safe schools act as pull factors for a growing city.

units.name: Place and Liveability · Case study: a least-liveable city (Harare)

words.meaning: A level of poverty where food, clean water and shelter cannot reliably be met.
words.example: Families in extreme poverty spend almost all their income on food.

words.meaning: Systems for dealing with waste and sewage so that people stay healthy.
words.example: Poor sanitation spreads disease quickly through crowded suburbs.

words.meaning: A crowded urban area with poor housing and very few services.
words.example: Whole families share a single room in the slum.

words.meaning: Public disorder or protest inside a country, sometimes turning violent.
words.example: Civil unrest closed the city's markets for a week.

words.meaning: A comparison of cities using measures such as safety, healthcare and environment.
words.example: The liveability ranking placed the city near the bottom of the list.

translations.ja: 住みやすさランキング
translations.vi: bảng xếp hạng mức độ đáng sống
translations.ps: د اوسېدو د وړتیا درجه بندي

units.name: Changing Nations · Lessons 1.1–1.4: urban and rural living and the megacity

words.meaning: The growing share of a country's people who live in cities rather than the countryside.
words.example: Urbanisation in Asia has been faster than anywhere else on earth.

words.meaning: To do with cities and towns.
words.example: An urban area has shops, transport and dense housing.

words.meaning: To do with the countryside, away from the cities and towns.
words.example: Rural towns often lose their young people to the cities.

words.meaning: A city with more than ten million people.
words.example: Tokyo was the world's first megacity.

words.meaning: The way a country's towns and cities are spread out and linked together.
words.example: Australia's urban settlement pattern hugs the coast.

translations.vi: mô hình phân bố đô thị

words.meaning: The spreading of a city outwards into the farmland around it.
words.example: Urban sprawl adds an hour to the drive into work.

words.meaning: The outer edge of a city, where urban and rural land meet.
words.example: New housing estates are built on the urban fringe.

units.name: Changing Nations · Lessons 2.1–2.3: migration and the Jakarta case study

words.meaning: The movement of people from one place to live in another.
words.example: Migration reshaped the city's suburbs within a single generation.

words.meaning: The movement of people from one place to another inside the same country.
words.example: Internal migration from farms to cities drives urbanisation.

words.meaning: The movement of people from one country to another.
words.example: International migration needs a visa; internal migration does not.

words.meaning: A person forced to leave their country because of war, persecution or disaster.
words.example: A refugee cannot safely return home.

words.meaning: The movement of people into a country in order to live there.
words.example: Immigration has supplied most of Australia's population growth.

words.meaning: The movement of people out of a country to live somewhere else.
words.example: Emigration from the village left only the oldest residents behind.

words.meaning: A fast rise in the share of people living in cities, often faster than services can grow.
words.example: Rapid urbanisation leaves new arrivals without water or sewerage.

words.meaning: Housing built without official planning approval, often on the edge of a city.
words.example: An informal settlement can appear on unused land within weeks.

words.meaning: Too many people living or working in too small a space.
words.example: Overcrowding spreads illness and makes study at home almost impossible.

words.meaning: The clustering of a country's people into one or a few very large cities.
words.example: Urban concentration means a single city can hold a tenth of the nation.

units.name: Economics and Business · Week 5: business success and social enterprise

words.meaning: A person who starts and runs a new business and carries the financial risk.
words.example: The entrepreneur pitched her idea to a panel of investors.

words.meaning: The activity of setting up and running new businesses.
words.example: Entrepreneurship needs an idea, some capital and a tolerance for risk.

words.meaning: The special strength that lets a business do better than its rivals.
words.example: Free delivery gave the shop a competitive advantage over the chain stores.

parts.meaning: wealth used to produce more wealth

translations.es: riqueza usada para producir más riqueza
translations.fa: ثروتی که برای تولید ثروت بیشتر به‌کار می‌رود
translations.fr: richesse utilisée pour produire plus de richesse
translations.hi: अधिक धन बनाने हेतु प्रयुक्त धन
translations.ps: شتمني چې د نورې شتمنۍ د تولید لپاره کارول کیږي
translations.ro: avere folosită pentru a produce mai multă avere
translations.ru: богатство, используемое для производства ещё большего богатства
translations.tl: yaman na ginagamit para lumikha ng higit pang yaman
translations.ur: دولت جو مزید دولت پیدا کرنے کے لیے استعمال ہو
translations.vi: của cải dùng để tạo ra thêm của cải
translations.zh-Hans: 用于生产更多财富的资本
translations.zh-Hant: 用於生產更多財富的資本

words.meaning: An investor who puts money into a new business in return for a share of it.
words.example: The venture capitalist offered money for twenty per cent of the company.

translations.ja: ベンチャーキャピタリスト

words.meaning: Money put into a business or project in the hope of a gain later.
words.example: The investment paid for new ovens and a delivery van.

words.meaning: A business that trades to make money mainly in order to support a social or environmental cause.
words.example: The cafe is a social enterprise: every dollar of profit trains a new apprentice.

words.meaning: An organisation that raises money mainly through donations, not trade, to support a cause.
words.example: A charity relies on donations; a social enterprise sells something.

translations.vi: tổ chức từ thiện phi lợi nhuận

words.meaning: The money a business has left once its costs are taken out of its income.
words.example: Income of $900 minus costs of $650 leaves a profit of $250.

units.name: Economics and Business · Week 6: mission, demographics and competition

words.meaning: A short statement of what a company does now and why it exists.
words.example: Their mission statement is one sentence about feeding students well.

translations.ja: ミッション・ステートメント

words.meaning: A short statement of what a company hopes to become in the future.
words.example: A vision statement looks years ahead; a mission statement describes today.

translations.ja: ビジョン・ステートメント

words.meaning: The measurable facts about a population, such as age, gender and income.
words.example: The demographics of the suburb show many families with young children.

words.meaning: The particular group of customers a business aims to sell to.
words.example: Their target market is teenagers who skate.

words.meaning: A smaller group inside a market that shares similar needs.
words.example: Gluten-free buyers are one market segment for a bakery.

translations.ro: a căuta / a se îndrepta spre

words.meaning: Businesses selling very similar products to the same customers.
words.example: Two burger shops on one street are in direct competition.

translations.ro: a căuta / a se îndrepta spre

words.meaning: Businesses selling different products that meet the same customer need.
words.example: A cinema and a bowling alley are indirect competition for a Friday night.

translations.ro: a căuta / a se îndrepta spre

words.meaning: Rivalry between businesses trying to win the same customers — not a contest with a prize.
words.example: Competition between the two shops pushed prices down.

units.name: Economics and Business · Week 7: cost-benefit, promotion and branding

words.meaning: Weighing the costs of each option against its benefits to decide which is best.
words.example: A cost-benefit analysis showed that a second baker would pay for herself.

translations.vi: phân tích chi phí - lợi ích

words.meaning: One of the different options being compared when making a decision.
words.example: List every alternative before you weigh the costs and the benefits.

words.meaning: A chance to meet a need that no business is meeting yet.
words.example: No late-night pharmacy nearby was the business opportunity they spotted.

words.meaning: Using social media platforms to promote a brand or a product.
words.example: Their social media marketing reached more teenagers than a newspaper ad would.

translations.ja: ソーシャルメディア・マーケティング
translations.vi: tiếp thị qua mạng xã hội

words.meaning: An organised set of actions aimed at one marketing goal.
words.example: The winter campaign ran for six weeks across three platforms.

words.meaning: The name, symbol and identity that make a company's products recognisable.
words.example: A strong brand lets customers pick the product out of a crowded shelf.

parts.meaning: a sign that shows or identifies something

words.meaning: Legal protection for a brand name, logo or symbol.
words.example: Once the trademark is registered, no rival may copy the logo.

words.meaning: A symbol or design that stands for a company or brand.
words.example: The logo still works in one colour, so it prints on a paper cup.

words.meaning: The overall image and personality a company presents to its customers.
words.example: Their brand identity is friendly, cheap and local.

translations.ja: ブランドアイデンティティ

units.name: Economics and Business · Week 8: managing a business

words.meaning: The abilities needed to run and organise a business effectively.
words.example: Planning the roster is a management skill, not a baking skill.

words.meaning: Giving tasks to other people who have the skills to do them.
words.example: Good delegation frees the owner to plan instead of stacking shelves.

translations.hi: अभ्यास के माध्यम से तैयार करना
translations.ja: 練習によって準備する
translations.ps: د تمرین له لارې چمتو کول
translations.vi: chuẩn bị thông qua luyện tập

words.meaning: Teaching employees the skills they need to do their jobs well.
words.example: Two hours of staff training halved the mistakes at the till.

words.meaning: The ability to guide, motivate and direct a group of people.
words.example: Her leadership showed when she stayed calm through the busiest hour.

words.meaning: The ability to communicate and work well with other people.
words.example: Interpersonal skills matter most in a job that faces customers.

translations.vi: kỹ năng giao tiếp cá nhân
translations.ps: د خلکو سره د اړیکو مهارتونه

units.name: Economics and Business · Revision: resources, scarcity, tax and consumer law

words.meaning: Anything used to produce goods or services.
words.example: Land, workers and machines are all resources.

words.meaning: A resource that comes from the earth, such as water, oil or timber.
words.example: Iron ore is the natural resource behind most of Australia's exports.

words.meaning: The human effort, physical or mental, used to produce goods and services.
words.example: A cafe's biggest labour resource is the staff who cook and serve.

words.meaning: The tools, machines and equipment used to help produce goods and services.
words.example: The new oven is a capital resource, not a natural one.

words.meaning: The problem that resources are limited while people's wants are not.
words.example: Scarcity forces every economy to choose what to produce.

words.meaning: Giving up one thing in order to get another.
words.example: Choosing the cheaper supplier is a trade-off against quality.

words.meaning: The amount of a good or service that producers are willing to sell.
words.example: A frost cut the supply of strawberries and prices rose.

words.meaning: How much of a good or service buyers want to buy.
words.example: Demand for umbrellas jumps the moment it rains.

words.meaning: A tax charged on the money a person earns.
words.example: Income tax is taken out of your pay before you ever see it.

words.meaning: A tax system in which people who earn more pay a higher rate of tax.
words.example: Under a progressive tax, the first slice of your income is taxed least.

words.meaning: The government body that enforces fair trading and protects consumers in Australia.
words.example: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission can fine a business for false advertising.

translations.zh-Hans: 澳大利亚竞争与消费者委员会
translations.zh-Hant: 澳洲競爭及消費者委員會
translations.ja: オーストラリア競争・消費者委員会
translations.vi: Ủy ban Cạnh tranh và Người tiêu dùng Úc
translations.tl: Komisyon sa Kompetisyon at Konsyumer ng Australia
translations.ps: د آسټراليا د سيالۍ او پېرودونکو کمیسیون
translations.ro: Comisia Australiană pentru Concurență și Consumatori
translations.ru: Австралийская комиссия по конкуренции и защите прав потребителей
translations.fr: Commission australienne de la concurrence et de la consommation
translations.es: Comisión Australiana de Competencia y Consumo

words.meaning: An automatic legal right that protects you when you buy goods or services.
words.example: A consumer guarantee applies even when the shop offers no warranty of its own.

words.meaning: A promise from the maker to repair or replace a faulty product for a set time.
words.example: The manufacturer's warranty covers the phone for two years.

translations.vi: bảo hành của nhà sản xuất

words.meaning: A dishonest scheme designed to trick people out of money or personal information.
words.example: If an offer seems too good to be true, treat it as a scam.

words.meaning: A scam that tricks people into giving away personal or bank details, usually through fake messages.
words.example: The phishing email copied the bank's logo exactly.

words.meaning: Using someone else's personal details without permission, usually to get money.
words.example: Identity theft can start with a single stolen password.

words.meaning: A scam that tricks people into putting money into a fake or worthless opportunity.
words.example: An investment scam always promises huge returns with no risk.

units.name: Humanities Skills · Source analysis and historical inquiry

words.meaning: Any material — a document, image or object — used as evidence about the past.
words.example: Name the source before you quote anything from it.

words.meaning: Evidence created at the time of an event by someone who was there.
words.example: A soldier's own diary is a primary source.

words.meaning: An account or analysis of an event written later, using other evidence.
words.example: Your textbook is a secondary source about the Renaissance.

words.meaning: A one-sided view that favours a particular side or opinion.
words.example: A poster made by one side in a war shows obvious bias.

words.meaning: The viewpoint of one person or group, shaped by their situation.
words.example: A peasant's perspective on the shogun differs from a samurai's.

words.meaning: The guiding question that a piece of research sets out to answer.
words.example: Write your inquiry question before you collect any sources.

words.meaning: To support a claim by checking it against another, independent source.
words.example: Two letters from different towns corroborate the account.

words.meaning: How far a source can be trusted to give accurate information.
words.example: Question the reliability of a report written thirty years after the event.

words.meaning: A judgement of how important an event, person or development was.
words.example: Explain the significance of the printing press for ordinary readers.

units.name: Humanities Skills · Democracy, sustainability and citizenship concepts

words.meaning: A system of government in which power comes from the people, usually through voting.
words.example: In a democracy, a government that loses an election must hand over power.

translations.vi: thành viên của một quốc gia

words.meaning: A legally recognised member of a country, with rights and responsibilities.
words.example: Every Australian citizen over eighteen must vote.

words.meaning: The set of rules that establishes how a country is governed.
words.example: The Constitution can only be changed by a referendum.

words.meaning: Using resources so that today's needs are met without harming future generations.
words.example: Sustainability asks what the forest will look like in fifty years.

words.meaning: The way people, places and environments are linked and affect one another.
words.example: Interconnection explains how a drought overseas raises prices here.

translations.vi: thành viên của một quốc gia

words.meaning: Taking part responsibly in your community and in democratic processes.
words.example: Active citizenship can be as simple as joining a local clean-up.

units.name: Particles

words.meaning: A very small piece of matter.
words.example: A particle of water is too small to see.

words.meaning: Anything that takes up space and has mass.
words.example: Solids, liquids and gases are all kinds of matter.

words.meaning: Matter that keeps its shape and does not flow.
words.example: In a solid, the particles are packed close together and only shake in place.

words.meaning: Matter that flows and takes the shape of its container.
words.example: Water is a liquid at room temperature.

words.meaning: Matter that spreads out to fill any container.
words.example: The particles in a gas are far apart.

words.meaning: The form that matter takes: solid, liquid or gas.
words.example: Water changes state when it freezes.

words.meaning: A feature that describes a material, such as its colour or hardness.
words.example: Hardness is a property of many metals.

words.meaning: Changing from one place to another.
words.example: Particles in a gas have fast, random movement.

words.meaning: The ability to make things move or change; it is measured in joules.
words.example: The ball's energy changes from stored energy to moving energy as it falls.

words.meaning: The way things are placed in a pattern or order.
words.example: In a solid the arrangement of particles is regular.

words.meaning: The gaps left between things.
words.example: The spacing between particles is large in a gas.

words.meaning: A quick shaking back and forth in the same place.
words.example: The particles in a solid have vibration but do not change place.

words.meaning: Making something hotter by adding energy.
words.example: Heating makes the particles move faster.

words.meaning: Making something colder by taking energy away.
words.example: Cooling a gas can turn it into a liquid.

words.meaning: How much mass is packed into a certain volume.
words.example: A solid usually has a higher density than a gas because its particles are closer.

words.meaning: Getting bigger in size or volume.
words.example: Expansion of the liquid makes the thermometer reading rise.

words.meaning: Getting smaller in size or volume.
words.example: Contraction happens when a metal rod cools.

words.meaning: To become different.
words.example: A change of state happens when ice melts.
